Return with daylight and use Bob's Cove or another formed stop for the final walk. Let the lake road remain the experience instead of squeezing it between Queenstown bookings.

sections.heading: The Glenorchy road is the attraction
body: The 45 kilometres from Queenstown along the lake is one of the great drives in the country, with a series of signed viewpoints that are all worth stopping at. Bennett's Bluff in particular deserves more than a slow drive past.

It is also narrow with tight corners and considerable cyclist and tourist traffic. Allow well over an hour each way with stops, and take particular care in a large vehicle at the pull-offs, which are small.
tips: Allow over an hour each way
Bennett's Bluff is the stop to make
Pull-offs are small for campervans

sections.heading: Camping near Queenstown is constrained
body: Queenstown Lakes District enforces freedom camping restrictions strictly, with defined zones, certification requirements and early morning patrols. This is not a district where an unmarked lay-by is a reasonable gamble, and infringements here are common.
The DOC sites at Twelve Mile Delta and Moke Lake are the practical options close to town and fill early in summer. Both are worth arriving at in the early afternoon rather than at dusk.

sections.heading: Paradise and the Dart Valley
body: Beyond Glenorchy the road turns to gravel and continues towards Paradise and the Dart. It is passable in a normal vehicle in good conditions but includes fords that become impassable after rain, and many rental agreements prohibit it.
Check your agreement and the conditions before going, and turn around at any ford where you cannot see the bottom. The scenery is genuinely exceptional and it is not worth a recovery bill or worse.
tips: Gravel with fords beyond Glenorchy
Many rentals prohibit this road
Never cross a ford you cannot see into

sections.heading: Doing Queenstown without the adrenaline budget
body: The town is built around paid adventure activities and it is easy to spend several hundred dollars a day. It is equally possible to have an excellent few days on the Queenstown Hill and Ben Lomond walks, the lakefront, the Gardens and a swim, none of which cost anything.
If you want one paid activity, the Shotover jet and the gondola are the most reliably weather-independent. Skydiving and paragliding cancel frequently, so book them early in your stay.

sections.heading: Walks from Glenorchy
body: The Routeburn Track starts near Glenorchy and the first section to Routeburn Flats makes an excellent day walk without needing hut bookings. The full crossing is a Great Walk requiring booking well in advance and transport at both ends.

Lake Sylvan and the Rees-Dart valley tracks give quieter options with easier access, and the Glenorchy Walkway around the lagoon is flat, short and has the best views of the head of the lake for minimal effort.

The Routeburn road and the valley roads beyond Glenorchy are gravel and subject to closure and flooding. Check DOC alerts and your rental agreement, and be aware that the Routeburn car park fills early in summer.

sections.heading: Weather and the lake
body: Lake Wakatipu generates its own wind and the afternoon breeze up the lake is reliable enough to plan around. Mornings are usually calmer, which matters for kayaking, photography and anything on the water.
Winter brings the ski fields and a completely different town, with the Crown Range requiring chains and Glenorchy road conditions worth checking before setting out.
tips: Mornings are calmest on the lake
Crown Range needs chains in winter

wanaka-haast-pass-route.title: Wānaka to Haast Pass: Drive, Stops and Camping Guide
wanaka-haast-pass-route.description: Drive Wānaka to Haast over the Main Divide in three days: lakeshore stops, short forest walks, river viewpoints and where to camp along the pass.
wanaka-haast-pass-route.imageAlt: Haast Pass road through native forest
wanaka-haast-pass-route.intro: Wānaka to Haast is a half-day transfer only if nothing is closed and nothing invites a walk. Three days creates room for Makarora, the pass waterfalls and a patient arrival on the wet western side.

sections.heading: Wānaka to Makarora
body: Leave Wānaka with fuel and groceries, then follow Lake Hāwea and the head of Lake Wānaka without racing the curves. Use signed lookouts, because roadside shoulders disappear quickly.
Makarora offers the natural overnight break and access to short walks or longer backcountry trips. Check sandflies, river conditions and accommodation hours before settling in.

sections.heading: Across Haast Pass
body: The pass road can close for snow, slips, fallen trees or crashes. Review Waka Kotahi updates immediately before departure and keep enough supplies to wait or turn back.
Waterfall and Blue Pools tracks change with maintenance and flood damage. Follow the current DOC notice and barriers rather than assuming a famous stop is open because vehicles are parked nearby.

sections.heading: Haast coast
body: The western side is wetter, greener and more exposed to sandflies. A roofed stay or powered site can be worth the money when several days of rain have soaked the vehicle.
Choose the next move only after checking the coast road north. Haast is a place to reset fuel, food and expectations, not merely the end of the pass.

sections.heading: Haast Pass is the lowest of the alpine crossings
body: At 563 metres it is the lowest road pass over the Southern Alps, which makes it the most reliable of the three in winter. It is still subject to closure from slips and snow, and the western descent is steep with tight corners and frequent one-lane bridges.
Check the NZTA status before crossing, particularly after heavy rain. When it closes there is no short alternative; the detour is back through Wānaka and around, which is most of a day.
tips: Lowest alpine pass at 563 metres
Steep western descent with tight corners
No short detour when it closes

sections.heading: The roadside walks are the point
body: Blue Pools, Fantail Falls, Thunder Creek Falls and the Haast Pass lookout are all short walks close to the road, and together they turn a two-hour drive into a satisfying day. Blue Pools is the standout, with a swing bridge and genuinely startling water clarity.

The Blue Pools bridge and track have been closed for reconstruction at various points, so check the current DOC status. Do not jump from the bridge; it is prohibited and people have been seriously injured doing it.

sections.heading: Wānaka is the calmer alternative to Queenstown
body: An hour from Queenstown with a similar lake and mountains, Wānaka has a fraction of the intensity and noticeably better value. Roys Peak is the famous walk and is a hard six hours return with a queue at the viewpoint in summer.
Diamond Lake and the Isthmus Peak track give comparable views with far fewer people. The lone tree in the lake is five minutes from town and busiest at sunrise, which is also when it is worth seeing.
tips: Roys Peak is six hard hours
Isthmus Peak has the same views, fewer people
Wānaka is better value than Queenstown

sections.heading: Sandflies begin at the pass
body: The eastern side around Wānaka and Hāwea is largely sandfly-free, and the moment you descend the western side that changes completely. Haast and the coast beyond it are serious sandfly country and the transition is abrupt.
Have repellent accessible in the cab rather than packed in the back before you start the descent. Stopping at Thunder Creek Falls without it is a memorable mistake.

sections.heading: Lake Hāwea and the Neck
body: The road runs along Lake Hāwea then crosses the narrow isthmus known as the Neck between the two lakes before following Lake Wānaka north. The viewpoint at the Neck looks down both lakes at once and is one of the better roadside stops in the country.
Hāwea is quieter than Wānaka with a good lakefront campground and considerably fewer people. It works well as a base if Wānaka is full or expensive, and it is only fifteen minutes further on.

Makarora, at the northern end, is the last settlement before the pass and has fuel, a cafe and camping. It is also the departure point for flights and jet boat trips into the Siberia Valley if you want a day out of the vehicle.

sections.heading: Where to stop for the night
body: Camping options thin out considerably between Makarora and Haast, and the DOC sites along the pass are basic with no reception. Fill water and fuel at Makarora rather than assuming something appears.
Haast township itself has fuel, a shop and accommodation but very little else. Treat it as a service stop rather than a destination.
tips: Fill up at Makarora
Haast is a service stop, not a destination

southern-scenic-route-camping.title: Southern Scenic Route camping guide
southern-scenic-route-camping.description: Wild Catlins beaches, southern towns and Fiordland gateways between Dunedin and Queenstown.
southern-scenic-route-camping.imageAlt: Catlins coast on the Southern Scenic Route
southern-scenic-route-camping.intro: The Southern Scenic Route links more than 600 kilometres of coast, forest and lake country. Seven days gives the Catlins two nights, keeps Fiordland from becoming a detour and leaves room for southern weather.

sections.heading: Dunedin through the Catlins
body: Stock up in Dunedin, then use Balclutha or Owaka as the practical entry to the Catlins. Waterfalls and beaches sit on side roads that turn a short map distance into a full afternoon.
At Nugget Point, Curio Bay and wildlife beaches, follow seasonal access and keep well away from sea lions, penguins and nesting birds. Darkness and wildlife make late coastal driving a poor trade.

sections.heading: Invercargill and the south
body: Invercargill provides repairs, groceries and indoor options after wet days. Bluff adds a satisfying geographic marker, but it should not replace time for local museums, food or a vehicle reset.
If travelling to Rakiura, park or book the vehicle according to ferry arrangements and expect Foveaux Strait weather to change schedules. Keep a flexible mainland night.

sections.heading: Te Anau to Queenstown
body: Use Te Anau for Fiordland rather than driving Milford Sound as a day trip from Queenstown. Fuel, road conditions and avalanche controls need checking before the early start.
Finish via the lakes to Queenstown with enough margin for traffic and roadworks. A shorter last day preserves the concentration needed after a week of narrow roads.

sections.heading: The Catlins are the reason to take this route
body: Between Balclutha and Invercargill the coastline holds Nugget Point, Purakaunui Falls, Cathedral Caves and Curio Bay, and it sees a fraction of the traffic of the main highway. The road includes unsealed sections and everything takes longer than the map suggests.
Give the Catlins two days rather than one. Compressed into a single transit it becomes a series of car park visits, which is exactly what the route is not for.
tips: Two days for the Catlins
Some sections are unsealed
Far quieter than the main highway

sections.heading: Cathedral Caves and Curio Bay run on the tide
body: Cathedral Caves are only accessible around two hours either side of low tide, the access road is privately managed with an entry fee and seasonal opening, and it closes entirely outside the season. Turning up without checking is the standard disappointment here.

Curio Bay's petrified forest is also tide-dependent, and the yellow-eyed penguins come ashore in the evening. Keep well back and behind the roped areas, because disturbance keeps them at sea and away from their chicks.

sections.heading: Wildlife here needs distance
body: Nugget Point has fur seals and sea lions, Curio Bay has hoiho, and sea lions haul out on beaches throughout the region. New Zealand sea lions are large, fast over short distances and will charge if you get between them and the water.
Twenty metres is the minimum for seals and sea lions, and considerably more for penguins coming ashore. Never position yourself between an animal and the sea, and keep dogs away entirely.
tips: Twenty metres minimum from sea lions
Never block the route to the water
Penguins will not land if you are visible

sections.heading: Weather from the south
body: This coast faces the Southern Ocean and gets weather straight off it. It can be genuinely cold and wind-driven at any time of year, and a warm Invercargill afternoon means nothing about conditions at Slope Point an hour later.
Carry warm and windproof layers regardless of the season, and choose sheltered campsites. An exposed pitch on this coast in a southerly is not a good night.

sections.heading: The Otago Peninsula and Dunedin
body: The peninsula east of Dunedin has the world's only mainland royal albatross colony at Taiaroa Head, along with sea lions, fur seals and yellow-eyed penguins. The albatross centre is a paid tour and the birds are visible year-round, with the best flying in windy conditions.

The peninsula road is narrow, winding and slow, hugging the harbour edge with almost no shoulder. It is not a comfortable drive in a large campervan and the high road over the ridge is the easier alternative in either direction.

Dunedin itself has the Otago Museum, Speight's brewery and Baldwin Street, and it is the last full-service city before Invercargill. Restock properly here, because the Catlins have very limited shops.

sections.heading: Invercargill and Bluff
body: Invercargill is the last full-service city and the natural restock before Fiordland or the ferry to Rakiura. Bluff, half an hour south, is the signpost at the end of the country and the departure point for Stewart Island.
Bluff oysters are in season roughly March to August and are genuinely worth the detour when they are. Outside that, the town is quiet and the drive is mostly about having reached the end.
tips: Restock in Invercargill
Bluff oysters run March to August

fiordland-camping-road-trip.title: Fiordland camping road trip from Te Anau
fiordland-camping-road-trip.description: Deep lakes, rain-fed waterfalls and remote roads built around a stable Te Anau base.
fiordland-camping-road-trip.imageAlt: Fiordland mountains reflected in dark water
fiordland-camping-road-trip.intro: Fiordland is easier when the campsite stays put. Base around Te Anau for four nights, then let weather and road conditions decide the order of Milford Sound, Manapouri and the walking days.

sections.heading: Build the base
body: Choose a Te Anau holiday park for services or an approved DOC campsite that matches the vehicle and water needs. Book summer dates early and never use a trailhead as an improvised overnight site.
Buy food and fuel before each long day. There are no ordinary fuel stations on the Milford Road, and reception is unreliable through much of the national park.

sections.heading: Milford Road
body: Check road status, avalanche controls and weather before leaving. Drive early, use designated stops and remember that the same beautiful waterfalls can signal intense rain and rising water.
A cruise booking does not protect against a closed road. Keep the operator informed, allow generous travel time and accept that Fiordland sometimes replaces the plan with weather.

sections.heading: Walking and recovery
body: Use the Kepler Track edges, lakefront and shorter DOC walks for flexible days. Longer tramps require hut bookings, backcountry equipment and a forecast suited to the full route.
Dry boots, refill water and rest between major outings. Fiordland's scale is best absorbed with spare time, not from a vehicle that returns to Te Anau exhausted every night.

sections.heading: The Milford road is a serious drive
body: State Highway 94 from Te Anau to Milford is 119 kilometres, takes at least two hours each way without stops, has no fuel, no reception for most of its length, and is subject to avalanche closure in winter and spring. It is also one of the best drives anywhere.
Leave early, fill up in Te Anau, and allow a full day for the return trip with stops at Mirror Lakes, the Chasm and the Eglinton Valley. Do not attempt it as an afternoon addition to another day.
tips: No fuel and no reception on the road
Two hours each way minimum
Full day for the return trip

sections.heading: Winter avalanche control closes the road
body: Between roughly May and November the Milford road operates under an avalanche risk programme, with scheduled closures and mandatory chain carriage at times. Closures can be announced at short notice and the road can shut with vehicles at Milford, requiring an overnight stay.

Check the status on the morning you travel, carry chains if required, and never drive past a closure barrier. The avalanche paths above that road are large and the control programme exists because of a genuine history of them.

sections.heading: Rain makes Milford better
body: Milford Sound receives around seven metres of rain a year and the waterfalls that make it extraordinary only run properly when it is raining. A clear day gives you the peaks; a wet day gives you hundreds of temporary falls down the cliff faces.
Book a cruise regardless of the forecast, take a waterproof layer and go outside on the deck. Travellers who cancel because of rain are cancelling the better version of the experience.
tips: Waterfalls need rain to run
Book the cruise regardless of forecast
Go out on deck, take waterproofs

sections.heading: Camping and the sandflies
body: There are DOC campsites through the Eglinton Valley along the road, which are the practical option since accommodation at Milford itself is very limited. Freedom camping near the fiords is not permitted, and the restriction is enforced.
Fiordland sandflies are the worst in the country and Milford's are legendary. Repellent is not optional here, and setting up camp in the Eglinton at dusk without it is genuinely unpleasant.

sections.heading: Doubtful Sound and the alternative to Milford
body: Doubtful Sound is larger, quieter and reached by a boat across Lake Manapouri followed by a bus over Wilmot Pass, which makes it a full day and considerably more expensive than Milford. In exchange you see almost no other vessels.

For travellers who have the time and budget, the overnight cruises on either sound are the version most people remember. They book out well ahead in summer and are weather-dependent like everything else here.
Manapouri itself is a quieter base than Te Anau with a good campground and the Kepler Track trailhead nearby. If Te Anau is full, it is twenty minutes away and usually has space.

sections.heading: Te Anau as a base
body: Te Anau has the services, the DOC visitor centre for track and weather information, and the accommodation that Milford lacks. Almost everyone bases here and drives out, which is the sensible arrangement.
The Te Anau glow worm caves are a boat trip across the lake and work well as an evening activity, particularly on a day when the weather ruled out something else.
tips: Base in Te Anau, not Milford
DOC visitor centre for track info

nelson-abel-tasman-golden-bay.title: Abel Tasman Camping: Campsites, Bookings and Route
nelson-abel-tasman-golden-bay.description: Abel Tasman Coast Track campsites must be booked all year ($21 NZ, up to $31 international). Tide windows, Tōtaranui and a Nelson to Golden Bay route.
nelson-abel-tasman-golden-bay.imageAlt: Golden beach in Abel Tasman National Park
nelson-abel-tasman-golden-bay.intro: Six days gives Nelson one night, Abel Tasman two and Golden Bay enough time to justify crossing Tākaka Hill. The route works best when water transport replaces some road kilometres and the final coast remains flexible.

sections.heading: Nelson to Marahau
body: Use Nelson for supplies and a city night, then pause in Māpua or Motueka before Marahau. Summer traffic is slow and camps near the national park book early.
Reserve water taxis, campsites and huts through the correct operator or DOC system. Tides affect several coastal track crossings, so the day's schedule should begin with the tide table.

sections.heading: Over Tākaka Hill
body: Fuel in Motueka and cross the hill in daylight. The road is steep, winding and tiring for large vehicles, with winter ice or storm damage possible.
Tākaka makes the practical base for food and weather decisions. Te Waikoropupū Springs has strict contact restrictions that protect its water, and every barrier should be treated as non-negotiable.

sections.heading: Golden Bay north
body: Pūponga and Farewell Spit sit farther from services than they appear. Join an authorised tour where access is restricted and avoid driving onto tidal sand.
Keep the final night near Tākaka if a ferry or flight follows. Crossing the hill and reaching Nelson or Picton under time pressure removes the calm that makes Golden Bay worth visiting.

sections.heading: Abel Tasman is a booking exercise
body: The coast track's 4 huts and 18 campsites must be booked in advance all year round, and they sell out for the summer season well ahead. Great Walk campsites cost $21 per adult a night for New Zealanders and $21 to $31 for international visitors, depending on the season. Water taxis run from Marahau and Kaiteriteri and are the standard way to combine a walk with a return, which also has to be booked.

Decide the shape of your walk before you book anything: one-way with a taxi pickup, a day walk from Marahau, or a multi-day with hut or campsite nights. Each has different booking requirements and they interlock.
tips: Track sites and huts book out early
Water taxis need booking too
Decide the shape before booking

sections.heading: Tidal crossings are not optional timing
body: The track crosses tidal estuaries at Torrent Bay, Bark Bay and Awaroa. DOC gives Torrent Bay and Bark Bay a window of 2 hours either side of low tide, with all-tide tracks around both, but Awaroa Inlet has no way round: cross it in daylight, within 1 hour 30 minutes before and 2 hours after low tide. Missing the window means a long wait or a high-tide alternative track, and people are caught out on this regularly.
Get the tide table when you book and plan the day around it rather than around distance. The estuary crossings dictate your start time, not your preference.

sections.heading: Tākaka Hill and Golden Bay
body: The road over Tākaka Hill is steep, winding and slow, and it is the only route into Golden Bay. It takes longer than the distance suggests and is a real workout in a campervan, but the bay on the other side is worth the effort.

Te Waikoropupū Springs are among the clearest freshwater springs measured anywhere and are culturally significant to Ngāti Tama and Te Ātiawa. The water is not to be entered, and the boardwalk keeps you off it.
tips: Tākaka Hill is the only way in
No entry to the Pupu Springs water
Allow well over the estimated time

sections.heading: Farewell Spit and the far north of the island
body: The spit is a wetland of international importance and vehicle access beyond the first section is restricted to a licensed tour operator. Wharariki Beach, reached by a twenty minute walk across farmland, is the more accessible highlight and frequently the better one.
Check the tide for Wharariki, because the arches and the seal pups in the rock pools are only reachable at lower water. The walk crosses private farmland, so keep to the track and close the gates.

sections.heading: Nelson and the Great Taste Trail
body: Nelson is one of the sunniest places in the country, with a substantial arts and food scene, and the Great Taste Trail is a mostly flat cycle route linking wineries, breweries and cafes between the city, Māpua and Motueka. Bike hire and shuttle services make a one-way day easy.
The Saturday market in Nelson is one of the better ones in the country and worth planning around. Māpua wharf, on the trail, has a cluster of good food and a passenger ferry across the estuary.
Nelson also works as the restock point before Golden Bay, since the shops beyond Tākaka are limited and everything has to cross the hill. Do the big shop here rather than in Motueka.

sections.heading: When to go
body: Abel Tasman is at its best from December to March and is correspondingly full, with track sites booked months ahead. Shoulder season gives you the same coast with availability and cooler water.
Nelson regularly ranks among the sunniest places in New Zealand, so even outside summer the odds of good weather here are better than in most of the South Island.
tips: Book December to March far ahead
Shoulder season is much easier

arthurs-pass-camping-route.title: Arthur's Pass Camping Route: Christchurch to the West Coast
arthurs-pass-camping-route.description: Drive Christchurch to the West Coast over Arthur's Pass: braided rivers, alpine walks, where to camp on the way, and what the pass road demands.
arthurs-pass-camping-route.imageAlt: Arthur's Pass highway beneath alpine peaks
arthurs-pass-camping-route.intro: State Highway 73 is a crossing that deserves two or three days. Castle Hill, Arthur's Pass Village and the Otira descent each reward daylight, while snow, wind and kea require more attention than the distance alone suggests.

sections.heading: Canterbury approach
body: Leave Christchurch after checking the pass forecast and road status. Stop at Castle Hill only in the formed parking area and respect cultural and conservation guidance among the limestone formations.
Lake Pearson and other camps have exact rules for vehicles, fires and facilities. Confirm the selected site before arrival and carry water suitable for a basic alpine night.

sections.heading: Arthur's Pass Village
body: Use the village as the walking base and visit the DOC centre for current track advice. Alpine routes range from short valley walks to serious mountaineering terrain, and names alone do not show the difference.
Kea are intelligent and destructive around unattended gear. Never feed them, secure loose objects and protect rubber or exposed fittings without harming the birds.

sections.heading: Otira to the coast
body: Descend cautiously through the viaduct and steep grades, using lower gears instead of riding the brakes. Ice, wind and heavy vehicles can change the character of the road quickly.
Reach Hokitika or Greymouth before dark for a full reset. If the pass closes, wait or use a properly planned alternative rather than searching for an unsealed shortcut.

sections.heading: The highest of the three alpine crossings
body: At 920 metres, Arthur's Pass is the highest and most weather-affected of the main alpine road crossings. The Otira Gorge section on the western side is steep with a viaduct, and snow, ice and high wind close it regularly in winter.
Check the NZTA status before you leave, carry chains in winter, and treat a closure as a reason to reroute rather than wait. The Lewis Pass and Haast Pass alternatives are both long detours.
tips: Highest main alpine crossing at 920 m
Otira Gorge is steep with a viaduct
Carry chains in winter

sections.heading: Kea will damage your vehicle
body: The kea at Arthur's Pass and Otira are intelligent, curious and destructive, and they will strip rubber seals, windscreen wipers, roof racks and anything soft on a parked vehicle. This is not a small risk; it is the normal outcome of leaving a van unattended in the car parks.
Never feed them, because human food is what has drawn them to car parks and roads where they are killed. Pack away anything loose, and expect them to open a bag you thought was secure.

sections.heading: The walks are short and steep
body: Devils Punchbowl Falls is an hour return and mostly steps. Avalanche Peak is a serious alpine day with genuine exposure and no shelter, and it should not be attempted in poor weather or without proper gear despite being a signposted track from the village.

Castle Hill, on the eastern approach, is an easy walk through limestone formations and works well as a break on the drive. It is also a significant site for Ngāi Tahu, so keep to the tracks and treat it accordingly.
tips: Avalanche Peak is a real alpine route
Devils Punchbowl is an hour of steps
Castle Hill is an easy roadside stop

sections.heading: Village services are minimal
body: Arthur's Pass village has a small store, a cafe and limited fuel, and it is not a place to rely on for a full restock. Fill up in Springfield on the eastern side or Kumara on the western side, and carry food for the crossing.
The DOC campsites near the village are basic and can be very cold, sitting at altitude even in summer. Bring warmer bedding than the Canterbury Plains would suggest.

sections.heading: The TranzAlpine as an alternative
body: The TranzAlpine train follows roughly the same corridor between Christchurch and Greymouth and is widely rated one of the best rail journeys anywhere. It works as a return day trip from Christchurch without a vehicle, or as a way to see the pass in weather that makes driving unpleasant.

If you are driving, the viewpoints at the Otira Viaduct lookout and the Bealey Valley give you the scale of the pass without a long walk. Both have parking and both are places where kea will investigate your vehicle.

Coming from the east, Castle Hill and the Cave Stream Scenic Reserve break up the drive. Cave Stream is a genuine cave walk-through requiring a torch, warm clothing and care with water levels, and it should not be attempted after rain.

sections.heading: Where to break the crossing
body: Arthur's Pass village is the obvious stop but it is small, cold and often full. Springfield on the eastern side and Kumara or Hokitika on the western side both have more options and better services.
If the pass is closed or the forecast is poor, the Lewis Pass to the north is the alternative crossing and a good drive in its own right, with hot pools at Maruia along the way.
tips: Village is small and often full
Lewis Pass is the alternative crossing

banks-peninsula-camping-weekend.title: Banks Peninsula Camping Weekend From Christchurch
banks-peninsula-camping-weekend.description: A camping weekend on Banks Peninsula from Christchurch: volcanic harbours, steep bays, Akaroa, and the narrow roads to plan around.
banks-peninsula-camping-weekend.imageAlt: Akaroa Harbour and Banks Peninsula hills
banks-peninsula-camping-weekend.intro: Banks Peninsula is close enough for a weekend and slow enough to feel farther away. The best route chooses one harbour, one camp and one major walk instead of chasing every steep bay road.

sections.heading: Choose the harbour
body: Lyttelton and the inner harbour suit a gentle first day, while Akaroa makes the stronger base for the outer peninsula. Leave Christchurch before weekend traffic and expect cyclists on narrow roads.
Little River is the last easy pause before the summit road. Strong wind, fog and stock traffic can make a modest climb demanding in a high-sided campervan.

sections.heading: Akaroa base
body: Park the vehicle and explore Akaroa on foot or by harbour trip. Marine wildlife operators follow different schedules according to sea conditions, so retain a land-based walk as the backup.
Camp only at authorised sites around the harbour and bays. Council restrictions, private property and narrow access remove many places that look possible on a satellite image.

sections.heading: Outer bays
body: Okains Bay and other outer roads involve steep grades and limited turning room. Confirm vehicle suitability and campsite access before descending, because reversing a large rig uphill is not a backup plan.
Return before late Sunday traffic or add another night. A short geographic distance does not guarantee a quick journey across the peninsula.

sections.heading: The peninsula roads are steep and narrow
body: Banks Peninsula is an eroded volcano and the roads reflect that: steep gradients, tight hairpins and narrow shelf sections, particularly on the routes to Okains Bay, Le Bons Bay and over the Summit Road. They are sealed but demanding in a large vehicle.

The Summit Road is the scenic option and considerably slower than the direct route to Akaroa via Little River. Take the highway out and the Summit Road back if you want both without doubling the driving time.
tips: Steep hairpins and narrow shelf roads
Summit Road is slow but worth it
Highway out, Summit Road back

sections.heading: Akaroa and the Hector's dolphins
body: Akaroa Harbour is home to Hector's dolphins, the smallest and one of the rarest marine dolphins in the world, and the harbour cruises are among the more reliable wildlife encounters in the country. They are also weather-dependent and book out when cruise ships are in port.
Check whether a cruise ship is scheduled before planning your day. On those days the village is extremely busy and the harbour trips fill with ship passengers.

sections.heading: The bays are better than the town
body: Okains Bay, Le Bons Bay and Pigeon Bay are quieter than Akaroa, have basic campgrounds, and give you the peninsula the way it is worth experiencing. Okains Bay also has a well-regarded Māori and colonial museum that is worth the stop.
Facilities in the bays are limited and there is no supermarket outside Akaroa. Restock in Christchurch or Akaroa before heading over the hill to a bay for the night.
tips: Restock before heading to the bays
Okains Bay museum is worth a stop
Bays are quieter than Akaroa

sections.heading: An easy weekend from Christchurch
body: The whole peninsula is within ninety minutes of Christchurch, which makes it the standard local weekend and means the campgrounds fill on Friday evenings in summer and over long weekends. Booking ahead matters more than the short distance suggests.
It also works well as the first or last stop of a South Island trip, since it is close enough to the airport to fit either side of a flight without a long drive.

sections.heading: Lyttelton and the harbour side
body: Lyttelton, through the road tunnel from Christchurch, has recovered from the earthquakes into a good small port town with a Saturday market and a working harbour. The Bridle Path over the hill is a solid hour's walk with views over both the city and the harbour.

Governors Bay and Diamond Harbour on the southern side of Lyttelton Harbour are quieter than the Akaroa side and reachable by ferry from Lyttelton as a foot passenger, which avoids the winding road entirely.

The Port Hills between the city and the harbour have extensive walking and mountain biking, and the Summit Road along them gives the overview of the whole peninsula before you commit to driving down into it.

sections.heading: Getting there and the tunnel
body: The Lyttelton road tunnel is the quick way to the harbour and is closed to vehicles carrying certain goods, with height limits that catch some campervans. The Evans Pass road over the hill is the alternative.
From Christchurch the whole peninsula is within ninety minutes, which makes it the standard local weekend and means Friday evening arrivals compete for sites.
tips: Tunnel has height and load limits
Friday evenings are competitive

south-island-two-week-road-trip.title: South Island camping road trip: a realistic 14-day loop
south-island-two-week-road-trip.description: A two-week route that protects time for mountains, coast and Fiordland instead of collecting towns.
south-island-two-week-road-trip.imageAlt: South Island alpine road and campervan
south-island-two-week-road-trip.intro: Fourteen days is enough for a memorable Te Waipounamu loop when the itinerary accepts limits. This version chooses Mackenzie Country, Wānaka, Fiordland and the West Coast, with two flexible nights for weather.

sections.heading: Christchurch to Fiordland
body: Give Tekapo or Aoraki two nights, then travel through Wānaka to Te Anau without forcing both long walks and long drives into the same day. Queenstown can be a supply stop or a night, not an obligation.
Book the hard-to-replace nights first: Milford activities, peak DOC camps and any holiday-period stay. Leave ordinary town camps flexible around them.

sections.heading: West Coast north
body: Cross Haast Pass only after checking the road and forecast. Glacier country needs at least two nights if a flight or major walk matters, because cloud and rain frequently reorder the plan.
Hokitika or Greymouth provides the reset before Punakaiki and the alpine return. Use laundry, fuel and groceries deliberately rather than losing time to small errands every day.

sections.heading: Arthur's Pass return
body: Cross Arthur's Pass in daylight with snow chains when required and the driver's attention fresh. If the pass closes, accept the delay instead of stretching the final day into an unsafe detour.
Keep the last night near Christchurch for cleaning, refuelling and the rental handover. The spare margin also protects the trip when weather moves an earlier section.

sections.heading: A loop beats a line
body: Fourteen days is enough for a genuine South Island loop if you resist adding Stewart Island, the Catlins and Marlborough on top. A workable circuit is Christchurch, Tekapo, Aoraki, Wānaka, Queenstown, Te Anau, back up the West Coast and over Arthur's Pass.

That shape avoids backtracking, crosses the Alps twice by different passes, and leaves you finishing near where you started. Adding a second region usually means removing two nights from places you came for.
tips: Loop rather than out and back
Cross the Alps by two different passes
Adding regions costs you nights

sections.heading: Book the three things that sell out
body: Milford cruises, Aoraki accommodation and any Great Walk are the elements that will not be available late. Everything else on this loop can be arranged a few days out for most of the year.
Book those three first and build the driving around them. Trying to fit a Milford cruise into a route that was planned without it usually means an unpleasant day of driving at one end.

sections.heading: Weather will change the plan at least once
body: Over two weeks in the South Island you should expect at least one day where the pass is closed, the cruise is cancelled or the walk is unsafe. This is normal rather than bad luck, and an itinerary with no slack turns it into a crisis.
Build in two flexible days and hold a wet-weather alternative for each region. Te Papa is not an option here, but a hot pool, a museum, a brewery or simply a slower morning all are.
tips: Expect one disrupted day minimum
Keep two flexible days in the plan
Have a wet-weather option per region

sections.heading: Distances between fuel and food
body: The South Island has long stretches with no services, particularly on the West Coast, through Fiordland and over the passes. Treat Twizel, Wānaka, Te Anau, Hokitika and Greymouth as your restock points and fill up when you pass through rather than when you need to.
Reception disappears for hours at a time on several of these legs. Download the route, tell someone your plan and do not rely on being able to call ahead about a booking.

sections.heading: What to leave out
body: Two weeks does not comfortably include Stewart Island, the Catlins, Marlborough and Nelson on top of the main loop. Each of those adds two to three days properly done, and adding one usually means removing a night from Aoraki or Fiordland, which is a poor trade.

The most common regret is compressing the West Coast. It is the section with the longest distances between services, the most weather disruption and the scenery people remember, and it does not reward being rushed through in a day and a half.

If you must cut something from the standard loop, Queenstown is the easiest to shorten. It has the most expensive accommodation, the most crowding and the least that is unique to it compared with Wānaka and Te Anau nearby.

sections.heading: Where to start and finish
body: Christchurch and Queenstown are the two main entry points and both work. Starting in Christchurch and finishing in Queenstown avoids backtracking, while a Christchurch round trip avoids a one-way vehicle fee.
Queenstown flights are more weather-affected than Christchurch, so if your departure is tight, finishing in Christchurch is the lower-risk option.
tips: Queenstown flights divert more often
Weigh one-way fees against backtracking

new-zealand-three-week-campervan-route.title: 3 Week Campervan Itinerary New Zealand: Both Islands
new-zealand-three-week-campervan-route.description: A 3-week New Zealand campervan itinerary: nine days north, one Cook Strait crossing, eleven days south, with rest days and the 2026 green-warrant rule.
new-zealand-three-week-campervan-route.imageAlt: Campervan beside a New Zealand lake
new-zealand-three-week-campervan-route.intro: Three weeks can connect both main islands, but it cannot absorb every famous detour. This route keeps the north coherent, crosses Cook Strait once and concentrates the South Island on Mackenzie Country, Fiordland and the east coast.

sections.heading: Nine days in the north
body: Leave Auckland for Coromandel or the Bay of Plenty, then spend two nights around Rotorua. Continue through Taupō and Tongariro with a weather backup before reaching Wellington.

Use holiday parks for occasional laundry, power and long showers, then mix in suitable DOC or council sites. Freedom camping rules are local and vehicle-specific, not a general permission to stop anywhere.

sections.heading: Cook Strait and the south
body: Book the ferry for the correct vehicle length, arrive early and keep disruption margin. Picton deserves a recovery night after a rough crossing or late arrival.
Travel through Kaikōura and Christchurch toward Tekapo and Aoraki. Protect the alpine days from an overfilled schedule, because wind or rain may shift them by 24 hours.

sections.heading: Fiordland and finish
body: Use Wānaka or Queenstown as a transition, then base in Te Anau for Fiordland. Return to Christchurch through the southern route or central Otago only if the remaining days genuinely fit.
Plan the last 48 hours around the rental return, cleaning and fuel. A good three-week trip ends with a calm handover rather than a final overnight drive.

sections.heading: Three weeks is the first comfortable length
body: Twenty-one days is roughly the point where both islands become possible without the trip turning into a driving exercise. It allows around nine days in the North Island, one ferry day and eleven in the South, with two nights in the places that deserve them.
Resist the temptation to add Northland and Stewart Island at the ends. Either one converts a comfortable trip back into a rushed one, and both are better as their own journey.
tips: Roughly 8 north, 1 ferry, 12 south
Do not bolt on Northland or Rakiura
Two nights in the places that earn it

sections.heading: One ferry crossing, booked first
body: Cross Cook Strait once, southbound, and book it before anything else. A campervan is priced on length, summer sailings fill, and the crossing consumes most of a day once check-in and the drives at either end are counted.
Position the night before near the terminal and leave the day after soft. An evening arrival in Picton followed by a long drive is how people start their South Island leg tired.

sections.heading: Where to spend two nights
body: Rotorua, Aoraki or Tekapo, Te Anau and somewhere on the West Coast are the four places where a second night changes the trip most. Each is either weather-dependent or has more to do than a single afternoon allows.

Single nights work fine for transit stops like Taupō, Blenheim or Greymouth. The mistake is spreading single nights evenly across the whole route, which leaves you packing up every morning for three weeks.
tips: Two nights: Rotorua, Aoraki, Te Anau, West Coast
Single nights for transit towns
Packing up daily for 21 days is exhausting

sections.heading: Managing a campervan for three weeks
body: Over this length the vehicle routine matters: dump and refill on a regular schedule rather than when tanks are full, do laundry every five or six days, and plan a serviced night after each run of freedom camping. Freedom camping in a vehicle on council land needs a certified self-contained vehicle unless the council has set the site aside for vehicles that are not, many DOC notices impose the same condition, and since 7 June 2026 only vehicles with a green warrant count; blue warrants stopped counting, so check the warrant on the van at pickup. Letting these slip is what makes week three uncomfortable.
Keep the gas bottle, tyre pressures and windscreen washer topped up as you go. Small vehicle jobs are easy in a town and difficult on the Milford road.

sections.heading: Direction of travel and one-way logistics
body: Running north to south, picking up in Auckland and dropping in Christchurch or Queenstown, generally works better than the reverse because it puts the more demanding South Island driving at the end when you are used to the vehicle.

One-way rental fees between the islands vary widely and are sometimes waived in the low season when operators need vehicles repositioned. Ask directly rather than assuming the online quote is fixed, because it frequently is not.

The alternative is a round trip from Auckland, which means crossing Cook Strait twice and adds roughly two days of driving and a second ferry fare. It is only worth it if your flights are fixed to Auckland at both ends.

sections.heading: Rest days are part of the plan
body: Three weeks of moving every day is exhausting, and the trips people remember well usually include two or three days where nobody drives anywhere. Build them in deliberately rather than hoping for them.
Choose places worth staying still in: a lakeside site, a town with good food, somewhere with a walk from the door. A rest day in a transit town is not a rest day.
tips: Plan two or three no-driving days
Rest somewhere worth staying

Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Board: self-contained vehicles for private owners
DOC: freedom camping on conservation land

rakiura-stewart-island-camping-guide.title: Stewart Island Camping Guide: Rakiura Track and Oban
rakiura-stewart-island-camping-guide.description: Camping on Stewart Island: Rakiura Track campsites from $19 a night in summer and booked all year, the one-hour Bluff ferry, Ulva Island and wild kiwi.
rakiura-stewart-island-camping-guide.imageAlt: Remote beach and native forest on Rakiura
rakiura-stewart-island-camping-guide.intro: Rakiura is a trip without the campervan. Leave the vehicle on the mainland, cross with a compact pack and let walking, water taxis and island weather set the pace for three or four nights.

sections.heading: Mainland preparation
body: Buy specialist food and equipment in Invercargill, then confirm secure parking and check-in at Bluff. Ferry luggage rules and sea conditions deserve attention before the morning of departure.
Foveaux Strait can be rough and services may change. Keep essential medication, warm layers and a flexible mainland booking for any delayed crossing.

sections.heading: Oban and Ulva Island
body: Oban is the service base, not a large town. Book accommodation, camps or track huts in advance and carry what small shops may not stock.
Ulva Island is a predator-free sanctuary reached by water taxi. Clean footwear and bags, follow biosecurity instructions and keep food sealed so the visit does not introduce pests.

sections.heading: Tracks and night wildlife
body: The Rakiura Track requires the correct hut or campsite booking and gear for persistent mud and rain. Shorter Oban walks still need a torch, warm layer and realistic return time.
Kiwi viewing is quiet and patient. Use red light where guides request it, give birds space and never use food or sound to pull wildlife closer.

sections.heading: Getting there is a decision in itself
body: The ferry from Bluff takes about an hour across Foveaux Strait, which has a reputation for being rough that is entirely deserved. The alternative is a short flight from Invercargill, which costs more, carries a strict baggage limit and is weather-dependent.

You cannot take a vehicle. Leave it in secure parking at Bluff or Invercargill and plan to be on foot on the island, which has very few roads and where almost everything is within walking distance of Oban anyway.
tips: No vehicles on the ferry
Foveaux Strait is genuinely rough
Flights have strict baggage limits

sections.heading: Kiwi are actually visible here
body: Rakiura is one of the most reliable places in the country to see wild kiwi, and the Stewart Island tokoeka is active in daylight as well as at night, which is unusual. Guided evening kiwi-spotting trips run from Oban.
Use a red light rather than white, keep quiet and stay on the track. Never approach or follow a bird, and keep well back if one crosses in front of you.

sections.heading: Ulva Island is the easy highlight
body: A short water taxi from Golden Bay wharf reaches Ulva Island, a predator-free open sanctuary where saddleback, robin, kākā and weka are abundant and unafraid. It is the single best few hours available on the island and needs no tramping experience.
Check your bag for rodents and seeds before boarding, which is why the checking stations exist. A single rat reaching Ulva would undo decades of work.
tips: Check your bag before boarding
Best birdlife you will see anywhere
No tramping experience needed

sections.heading: Weather, mud and the Rakiura Track
body: The Rakiura Track is a 32 km Great Walk loop, usually walked in three days. DOC's three campsites on it cost $19 per adult a night for New Zealanders and $28 for international visitors from 1 October to 30 April, and huts $44 and $66; every hut and campsite must be booked in advance all year, with a two-night maximum at each. The North West Circuit beyond it is a serious multi-day route famous for deep mud. Neither should be underestimated because the island is small.

Expect rain on most days, whatever the season. Waterproof boots, gaiters, dry bags and a genuine change of clothes are the difference between an enjoyable walk and a miserable one, and the mud is not an exaggeration.

sections.heading: How long to stay
body: Two nights is the minimum that justifies the crossing, and three or four is better. A single night gives you an evening and a morning, which is not enough for both a kiwi trip and Ulva Island, and leaves you hostage to the ferry schedule.

Oban is the only settlement and has a hotel, a shop, a couple of places to eat and limited accommodation, all of which book out in summer. There are backpacker options, but KiwiCamping's DOC data has no campsite in Oban itself: DOC's campsites on the island are the three on the Rakiura Track. Prices reflect that everything arrives by boat.
Bring cash and anything specific you need, because the shop is small and resupply is not quick. The island runs on a slower rhythm than the mainland and that is largely the point of going.

sections.heading: Booking the crossing and the weather
body: Ferry sailings are cancelled in poor conditions and the strait is exposed. Build a spare day into the plan at each end rather than connecting the crossing tightly to a flight or another booking.
Take motion sickness medication before boarding rather than after. An hour on Foveaux Strait in a swell is a genuinely uncomfortable experience if you are prone to it.
tips: Build a spare day at each end
Take medication before boarding

sources.label: RealNZ: ferry to Stewart Island planning guide

doc-huts-new-zealand-guide.title: DOC Huts in New Zealand by Region: Types, Fees, Tickets
doc-huts-new-zealand-guide.description: Where DOC's huts are, region by region, what serviced, standard and basic huts cost in 2026/27, and how hut tickets, the Hut Pass and bookings work.
doc-huts-new-zealand-guide.imageAlt: Backcountry hut in New Zealand mountains
doc-huts-new-zealand-guide.intro: DOC looks after more than 950 huts, and KiwiCamping's DOC data lists 927 of them, from serviced huts with heating and mattresses to two-bunk bivvies. Most sit in the South Island: Canterbury alone has 180 and the West Coast 140, while the North Island's biggest clusters are in the Ruahine, Kaweka and Tararua ranges. In that data, checked on 24 August 2026, only 127 of the 927 could be booked, and although DOC has since moved every serviced hut online, most huts remain first come, first served: free if basic, paid with hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass if standard.

sections.heading: Hut categories and 2026/27 fees
body: Serviced huts have mattresses, a water supply, toilets, handwashing and heating with fuel. For 2026/27 an adult pays $25 a night from May to September, $28 on weeknights and $32 on Friday and Saturday nights from October to April, and $29 and $34 from December to February; children pay half, and camping beside one costs half the hut fee. Standard huts have mattresses, water and toilets, with wood heaters below the bush line, for $15 an adult and $7.50 a child. Basic huts and bivvies are free and offer shelter and little else. In KiwiCamping's data that splits into 96 serviced, 408 standard and 372 basic huts.

Three categories sit outside that ladder. Great Walk huts, 33 of them in KiwiCamping's data, have their own prices by track, season and residency and must be booked in the Great Walks season. Individually priced huts, including serviced alpine huts such as Mueller Hut, set their own fee, and club huts are run by clubs such as the New Zealand Alpine Club, so check the hut's DOC page. Whatever the category, the roof never replaces a sleeping bag, stove, food, head torch and warm layers.
tips: Serviced $25 to $34 by season, standard $15, basic free
Great Walk and alpine huts price individually
Carry full gear whatever the category

sections.heading: Where the huts are, region by region
body: The South Island holds most of the network. Canterbury has 180 huts, led by Lake Sumner Forest Park and Arthur's Pass National Park; the West Coast 140, many up the Whitcombe and Styx valleys; Nelson/Tasman 99, with 45 in Kahurangi National Park and 24 in Nelson Lakes; Otago 78, including 12 in Mount Aspiring National Park and 12 in Hāwea Conservation Park; Southland 70, including 30 on Rakiura; Marlborough 60; and Fiordland 55, almost all inside Fiordland National Park.

In the North Island, Hawke's Bay has 55 huts split between the Kaweka and Ruahine forest parks, Manawatū/Whanganui 43, the East Coast 38 across Te Urewera and Whirinaki, Wairarapa 36 and Wellington/Kāpiti 24, most of them in the Tararua Range. The Central North Island has 16, ten in Tongariro National Park, and Bay of Plenty, Taranaki, Northland, Waikato, Coromandel and Auckland have eight or fewer each.

sections.heading: Hut tickets, passes and bookings
body: Non-bookable huts take Backcountry Hut Tickets, bought before the trip and posted in the honesty box, or a Backcountry Hut Pass that covers most serviced and standard huts for 12 months. From 1 November 2026 hut tickets can also be bought on DOC's online booking system, and paper tickets stay valid until 1 November 2027. Bookable huts are reserved and paid on bookings.doc.govt.nz, and since 1 October 2026 that includes every serviced hut, so Serviced Hut Tickets are being retired.

The common mistake is treating a pass or a ticket as a booking. Neither reserves a bunk or gives priority in a first-come hut. The Hut Pass can pay for some bookable huts if you enter it when booking, but not Great Walk huts in their booking season or the huts on DOC's exclusion list. Read which system the specific hut uses before you leave.
tips: A pass is not a reservation
Hut tickets go online from 1 November 2026
Great Walk huts sell out months ahead

sections.heading: A full hut is still shelter in an emergency
body: At a bookable hut, DOC keeps no space for people without a booking, and you can be turned away when it is full. At non-bookable huts bunks are first come, and the convention is that a full hut means floor space rather than a closed door. Every hut stays open as emergency shelter in bad weather, so do not walk on into darkness because the bunks are taken.

Carry a mat and the means to sleep on the floor, and where the weather allows it and the site permits camping, a tent gives you a genuine alternative. On popular tracks in January, assume the hut will be full and plan accordingly.

sections.heading: Water, cooking and fire
body: Treat hut water unless current DOC information for that hut says it is safe to drink. Roof-collected supply can be contaminated, and giardia is present in New Zealand backcountry water. Boiling is the surest method, and DOC says three minutes; a filter rated for protozoa also works. Assuming is what causes problems.

Cook on your own stove, outside or in the designated area, and never inside a tent. Where a fire is provided, use it sparingly and restock the kindling for whoever arrives next in worse weather than you had.
tips: Treat the water unless told otherwise
Carry a stove regardless
Restock kindling before you leave

sections.heading: Hut etiquette
body: Boots off inside. Keep your gear consolidated on your bunk rather than spread across the table and benches. Be quiet early and move quietly in the morning, because trampers start before dawn and the whole party sleeps in one room after a hard day.
Fill in the hut book, every time, including the date and your intentions. It is a courtesy, and more importantly it can help search and rescue if someone in your party is overdue.

sections.heading: Leaving the hut
body: Sweep the floor, close the shutters and doors properly, and carry out everything you carried in, including food scraps. Rubbish left in a hut attracts rodents, and there is no collection service; whatever you leave stays until another walker removes it.

Report damage, a broken stove, a failed water supply or a hazard to DOC after your trip. Reports help DOC prioritise repairs, and a five-minute message can prevent the next party arriving to a building that does not work.
tips: Carry out all rubbish and scraps
Close shutters and doors
Report damage to DOC afterwards

faq: Do you need to book a DOC hut?

Only some. Great Walk huts, every serviced hut since 1 October 2026 and some popular huts are booked on bookings.doc.govt.nz. Most standard huts are first come, paid with hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass, and basic huts are free.
How much does a DOC hut cost per night?

For 2026/27 a standard hut is $15 for an adult and $7.50 for a child all year. A serviced hut is $25 from May to September and $28 to $34 from October to April, and a basic hut or bivvy is free. Great Walk and individually priced huts set their own fees.

sources.label: DOC accommodation prices 2026/27 by hut and campsite category
DOC media release, 1 October 2026: serviced huts bookable, hut tickets online

winter-camping-new-zealand.title: Winter camping in New Zealand: warmth, roads and realistic plans
winter-camping-new-zealand.description: Cold nights, short daylight and alpine road controls change how a campervan or tent trip works.
winter-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Campervan in a snowy New Zealand landscape
winter-camping-new-zealand.intro: Winter delivers the clearest skies, the emptiest campgrounds and the best value of the year, and it removes most of your margin for error. Cold nights, nine hours of usable daylight, chain controls and seasonal closures are not obstacles to work around afterwards; they are the things the route should be built from.

sections.heading: Rate the sleep system to the night, not the day
body: A bright Central Otago afternoon at fifteen degrees can be followed by a night below zero. Choose a sleeping bag and an insulated mat rated for the overnight minimum in the coldest place you will stop, then add a margin, because comfort ratings are optimistic and a cold night is genuinely miserable.

The mat matters as much as the bag. Most heat is lost downwards into the ground or the vehicle floor, and a summer-weight mat under a good bag will still leave you cold. In a van, insulate the floor and the windows before adding another blanket.
tips: Rate for the overnight low, not the forecast high
Insulated mat beats a warmer bag
Van floors and windows leak heat

sections.heading: Manage condensation
body: Four people breathing in a closed van produce a surprising amount of water, and it ends up in the bedding, the walls and eventually the mattress. Ventilation feels wrong when it is freezing outside, but a permanently sealed vehicle produces wet bedding by the second morning.

Crack a vent or a window on the sheltered side overnight, and air the bedding whenever the sun appears. Wipe condensation off windows in the morning rather than letting it run into the seals and soft furnishings.

sections.heading: Heat the vehicle safely
body: Use installed, manufacturer-approved heating only. Portable gas heaters, camping stoves and barbecues used indoors produce carbon monoxide, which is odourless and has killed people sleeping in vehicles in New Zealand. There is no safe way to improvise cabin heating in a closed space.

If you have a diesel or gas heater fitted, check it works before the trip and know how it vents. A carbon monoxide alarm costs very little and is worth having in any vehicle with a fuel-burning appliance.
tips: Never use a camping stove to heat a van
Carbon monoxide has no smell
Fit a CO alarm if you burn fuel

sections.heading: Chains, tyres and alpine road controls
body: The Lindis Pass, the Crown Range, Arthur's Pass, the Desert Road and the Milford Road can all require chains at short notice, and some rental agreements require you to carry them for the whole trip regardless of forecast. Fitting chains for the first time in sleet on a shoulder is genuinely difficult.

Practise fitting them in a dry driveway in daylight before you leave. Check tyre tread and pressures, confirm the battery is healthy, because cold weather finds a weak one, and read the rental company's winter restrictions before you plan a route over a pass.

sections.heading: Black ice and shaded corners
body: Black ice forms where the road merely looks wet, typically in shade, on bridges, and in the first and last hours of daylight. It gives no warning and no grip, and the standard mistake is braking or steering sharply once you feel it.

Slow down before shaded sections rather than in them, increase following distance well beyond the summer habit, and delay an alpine crossing until the sun has been on the road. Arriving two hours later is not a cost worth arguing about.
tips: Shade and bridges freeze first
Slow before the corner, not in it
Wait for sun on the road

sections.heading: Build the day around the daylight
body: Midwinter gives roughly nine hours of usable light in the south, and less in a valley. That is not much once you have packed camp, driven, stopped and found a site, so plan shorter legs than you would in February and set a firm turnaround time for any walk.

Aim to arrive with light to spare. Choosing a pitch, levelling a vehicle and checking access are all harder in the dark and colder, and a site that would be obviously wrong in daylight is easy to accept at night.

sections.heading: Expect closures and reduced facilities
body: Many DOC campsites close for winter or turn off water, some access roads shut after snow, and holiday parks in small towns can reduce hours or close entirely. A listing written for summer will not tell you this, so check the specific site and the current DOC alerts before committing to it.

Carry more water, food and charge than the plan requires, and treat a cabin or motel night as a normal weather decision rather than a failure. Winter is the season where paying for a room occasionally is what makes the rest of the trip work.
tips: Check the site is open, not just listed
Carry more water than the plan needs
A cabin night is a valid decision

faq: Can you camp in New Zealand in winter?

Yes, and it is the quietest time of year on the road. The limits are practical rather than legal: some DOC campsites and alpine roads close or become chain-only, daylight is short, and a van without insulation or a heater gets unpleasant fast.
Which parts of New Zealand are mildest in winter?

The upper North Island stays the warmest, and Northland and the Coromandel stay campable all year. Central Otago and the Mackenzie country get the hardest frosts, and the West Coast stays mild but very wet.

doc-campsite-rules.title: DOC Campsite Rules 2026: Quiet Hours, Dogs, Drones, Stays
doc-campsite-rules.description: Quiet from 10 pm to 7 am, check-out by 10 am, no pets or drones without DOC permission, and what camping unbooked costs: DOC's terms plus local rules.
doc-campsite-rules.imageAlt: Department of Conservation campsite information board
doc-campsite-rules.intro: Booking a DOC campsite means accepting DOC's booking terms and the local rules on that campsite's own page. The national ones are short: keep noise down from 10 pm to 7 am, check out by 10 am, take all rubbish away, bring no pets or drones unless DOC has authorised them, and do not smoke or vape in huts or toilet blocks. Fires, water, dogs, generators and vehicle access vary by site, so check the site's DOC page and the signs on site.

sections.heading: Use the booking honestly
body: Book the correct date, party and product, then keep confirmation available offline. Where pitches are not individually assigned, choose only from the area available on arrival.

If you miss the first night of a multi-night booking and nobody contacts the site office within 24 hours, DOC cancels the rest with no refund. Do not hold a space with an empty tent or vehicle when nobody intends to stay.

sections.heading: Respect shared hours
body: Standard DOC terms set quiet hours from 10 pm to 7 am unless local rules differ, check-out by 10 am, and check-in between 2 pm and 8.30 pm. Keep generators, music and vehicle movement within the site's limits.
A campsite booking does not guarantee use of a nearby hut's facilities, so plan around the toilets, shelters and water points that come with the campsite.

sections.heading: Leave the site ready
body: Take all rubbish, keep food secure and dispose of grey water only where the site directs. Smoking and vaping are not permitted in huts or toilet blocks.
Pets and drones require explicit permission. Check the exact campsite page rather than treating a quiet location as implied approval.

sections.heading: Booking rules and the unbooked penalty
body: Each campsite page says whether it is bookable or self-registration, and the rules follow from that. At a bookable site you need a valid booking for the night you use it, pass holders included. Without one you have no guaranteed space, and DOC charges its penalty rate: each person pays their normal fee plus a full adult fee, unless they are sheltering in adverse conditions. Campsite Pass holders who arrive without a booking pay a $10 fee instead and are turned away if the site is full.

At a self-registration site, fill in the form and pay on arrival. Either way, the booking or registration is for the people and vehicle you actually bring, and the confirmation must be available on request, so save it where you can show it without reception.
tips: A pass is not a booking
Unbooked use costs each person their fee plus an adult fee
Register and pay on arrival at first-come sites

sections.heading: Water is often untreated
body: Many DOC sites draw from streams or roof tanks and the supply is not treated. Giardia is present in New Zealand water and a clear stream tells you nothing about it. Boil for at least three minutes, filter, or use chemical treatment, and do not assume a tap is safe because it exists.
Carry enough drinking water to stay independent for a day. Tanks run dry, boil-water notices appear, and a campsite listed as having water can turn out to have a broken supply with no warning.

sections.heading: Generators, drones and dogs
body: Generator rules are set site by site, so check the campsite's DOC page before you run one. Drones require a concession on public conservation land in most circumstances, and even with a DOC permit a drone must keep away from campsites and huts.

DOC's default is no dogs on conservation land unless DOC has approved dog access, and dogs are not allowed in national parks without a permit, to protect kiwi and other ground-nesting birds. In KiwiCamping's DOC data, 207 of the 287 campsites allow no dogs and 74, about a quarter, allow them in some form, mostly on a lead or with a DOC permit. Check the specific site rather than assuming.
tips: Drones need a concession on DOC land
Dogs banned at most DOC sites
Generator rules vary by site

sections.heading: Maximum stay and site conduct
body: Some DOC campsites set a maximum stay on their DOC page to stop long-term occupation, and a Campsite Pass covers no more than 7 nights in any 30 days at one campsite, with extra nights paid at the standard rate. Moving a vehicle a few metres does not reset either limit.

Keep to the marked pitch, do not extend beyond it with awnings or gear where space is tight, and observe quiet hours. These grounds are shared, frequently full, and the enjoyment of everyone depends on people staying within their own space.

sections.heading: Arriving and settling in
body: Turn up in daylight where you can. Choosing a pitch, judging drainage, spotting overhead branches and levelling a vehicle are all considerably harder in the dark, and a site that would obviously be wrong at 4pm is easy to accept at 9pm when you are tired.

Pay on arrival where an honesty box or self-registration applies rather than intending to sort it later. Wardens do check, the fee is small, and the system only works because most people pay without being asked.

Set up within the marked pitch and leave room for whoever arrives after you. At a busy ground in summer, spreading gear across two spaces is the difference between the site holding everyone and people being turned away.

sections.heading: If the campsite is full
body: Popular DOC grounds can be full on summer evenings, so do not count on an overflow area. Creating an extra pitch on the grass, the access lane or beside the toilet block is not an option, and DOC staff can move you on.

Identify a legal fallback before you arrive rather than after. A holiday park half an hour away is a much better outcome than a late drive on an unfamiliar road looking for anywhere that will take you.
tips: Popular grounds fill in summer
Do not count on an overflow area
Know your fallback before arriving

faq: What are the rules at a DOC campsite?

Keep noise down from 10 pm to 7 am, check out by 10 am, take all rubbish away and bring no pets or drones unless DOC has authorised them. Smoking and vaping are banned in huts and toilet blocks, and each site's own page adds rules on fires, dogs, generators and vehicles.
How long can you stay at a DOC campsite?

Some campsites set a maximum stay on their DOC page, and a Campsite Pass covers no more than 7 nights in any 30 days at one campsite. Every night needs a booking or registration except at free basic campsites, and using a bookable site unbooked costs each person their normal fee plus a full adult fee, or a $10 fee for a Campsite Pass holder.

doc-hut-rules-etiquette.title: DOC hut rules and backcountry etiquette
doc-hut-rules-etiquette.description: Bookings, bunks, cooking and emergency shelter work differently from ordinary accommodation.
doc-hut-rules-etiquette.imageAlt: Interior of a shared DOC backcountry hut
doc-hut-rules-etiquette.intro: A hut booking buys access to shared shelter, not a private room or a specific bunk unless the product says otherwise. Every person still needs the equipment and judgement to cope if the hut is full, damaged or unreachable.

sections.heading: Carry the right authority
body: Book named huts and dates where reservations apply, or carry the appropriate tickets or pass for non-bookable facilities. Proof should remain available without reception.
Do not rely on unbooked space at a popular hut. Emergency use remains possible in adverse conditions, which is another reason to keep gear compact and considerate.

sections.heading: Live in one room
body: Select an available bunk, keep sleeping gear together and observe quiet hours. Cook only in the designated area, supervise flames and never leave food that attracts rodents.
Use heating fuel conservatively and follow the hut's fire instructions. Wet clothing should not block exits, bunks or the cooking space.

sections.heading: Leave safely
body: Clean benches, sweep where requested, close doors and carry every piece of rubbish out. Treat or boil water according to current advice.
Record intentions with a trusted person and carry navigation and emergency equipment. The hut does not make the track safe or guarantee rescue communication.

sections.heading: Full huts and bookings
body: Bunks in non-bookable huts are first come, and the long convention is that a full hut means floor space rather than a closed door. Bookable huts, including Great Walk huts during the Great Walks season, work differently: you need a booking, and without one you can be turned away. Do not walk on into the dark because the bunks are taken, and equally do not expect someone to give up a bunk they reached first.

Carry a mat so sleeping on the floor is genuinely viable, and where the site permits camping and the weather allows, a tent gives you a real alternative. On popular tracks in summer, plan on the assumption that the hut will be full.
tips: Full hut means floor space
Carry a mat regardless
Assume full in summer

sections.heading: Fill in the hut book, every time
body: The intentions book is one of the first places search and rescue checks when a party is overdue, and an accurate entry has shortened many searches. Record the date, your party, where you came from and where you are going next.
Sign out as well as in where the book allows it. A party recorded as arriving and never leaving generates a search that did not need to happen.

sections.heading: Fire, fuel and cooking
body: Where a hut has a stove, use the firewood sparingly and restock the kindling for whoever arrives next in worse weather than you had. Do not burn rubbish in the hut stove; it damages the flue and leaves the smell for everyone.

Cook on your own stove, in the designated area or outside, never in a tent or a confined porch. Carry enough fuel for the trip plus a margin, because there is nothing available at a hut and a borrowed stove is an imposition.
tips: Restock kindling before leaving
Never burn rubbish in the stove
Carry your own stove and fuel

sections.heading: Leaving it better than you found it
body: Sweep, close the shutters and door catches properly against wind and rodents, and carry out everything you carried in including food scraps. There is no rubbish collection at a backcountry hut, so whatever you leave stays until another walker removes it.

Report damage, a failed water supply or a hazard to DOC after the trip. Maintenance is prioritised on what gets reported, and a short message can stop the next party arriving to a building that does not work.

sections.heading: Sharing a hut with strangers
body: A backcountry hut puts a dozen people who have never met into one room after a hard day. Almost all of the etiquette follows from that: keep your gear in your own space, do not run a stove or a bright light in someone's face, and accept that somebody will snore.

Offer space on the bench and the bunks rather than waiting to be asked. Parties arriving late are usually wet and cold, and the difference between a welcoming hut and a miserable one is entirely down to whoever got there first.
Head torches on red mode after dark, and pack your bag in the porch if you are leaving before the others. Rustling a dry bag at 5am is one of the commonest complaints in New Zealand huts.

sections.heading: Booking seasons and what changes
body: Great Walk huts run a booked season with higher fees, wardens and full facilities, then revert to a lower standard and price outside it. Gas, heating and sometimes the water supply are removed in the off season.
Check what the hut actually offers for your dates rather than the summer description. An off-season Great Walk hut can be considerably colder and barer than the photographs suggest.
tips: Facilities drop outside the season
Gas and heating may be removed
Check the hut for your actual dates

faq: Can you be turned away from a full DOC hut?

On a bookable hut, yes: a bunk is only yours if you booked it. On a first-come hut nobody can be turned out, which is exactly why the etiquette matters and why you should always carry a tent or bivvy on a popular track.
What are you expected to do before leaving a hut?

Sweep the floor, replace any firewood you burned, take every piece of rubbish with you and fill in the hut book. The hut book entry matters beyond courtesy, because it is what search and rescue reads if someone is reported overdue.

sources.label: DOC: booking and paying for huts

dogs-camping-new-zealand.title: Camping With a Dog in NZ: Where Dogs Are Allowed (2026)
dogs-camping-new-zealand.description: Where you can camp with a dog in New Zealand: DOC campsites that allow dogs, national parks that do not, and how council and holiday park rules differ.
dogs-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Dog on lead beside a legal New Zealand campsite
dogs-camping-new-zealand.intro: Dog access must be checked for the exact land. Native wildlife protection means many conservation areas prohibit pets completely, including animals left inside a vehicle.

sections.heading: DOC rules are strict
body: Pets are generally not allowed at DOC camps, huts, lodges or cottages without written approval. Some campsites expressly allow dogs under listed conditions, but national parks remain no-dog environments.
A dog may travel to a hut only where dog access is allowed and must remain outside the hut. Search the exact place page before departure.

sections.heading: Councils and private parks
body: Council camping areas can combine freedom-camping bylaws with separate dog-control rules. A site may allow a vehicle overnight but prohibit dogs in the reserve.
Holiday parks set their own conditions, often by season, size or site type. Confirm in writing and disclose every animal when booking.

sections.heading: Protect wildlife and neighbours
body: Use a lead where required, prevent barking and collect all waste. Keep dogs away from nesting birds, seals, livestock and pest-control poison zones.
Carry vaccination information and a secure restraint for travel. If access is unclear, choose a dog-friendly commercial site rather than testing the rule on arrival.

sections.heading: Most conservation land is closed to dogs
body: Dogs are prohibited on the large majority of public conservation land, including most national parks, because kiwi and other ground-nesting birds have no defence against them. A single dog off a lead has killed multiple kiwi in a night, and this is why the restriction is absolute rather than discretionary.

A limited number of DOC areas permit dogs, and some require a permit obtained in advance. Check the specific place before you travel rather than assuming, because the penalties are significant and the risk to wildlife is real.
tips: Most national parks ban dogs entirely
Some areas need a permit in advance
Check the specific site, never assume

sections.heading: 1080 and pest control operations
body: Aerial 1080 is used widely for possum and rat control and is lethal to dogs, both directly and through eating poisoned carcasses, with the risk persisting for months after an operation. Warning signs are posted at access points and operations are published in advance.
