sections.heading: 1. KiwiCamping: best for DOC campsites, huts and planning the route
body: KiwiCamping is a New Zealand camping map and trip planner built on the Department of Conservation's own data. In its August 2026 data the app carried 287 DOC campsites, 927 DOC huts with 7,661 bunks and 1,453 DOC tracks, with the fees, dog rules and booking requirements DOC publishes, where it publishes them. The place details live on the phone, so a campsite's facilities and fees still open on the West Coast or in Fiordland with no reception. Map tiles, routing, weather and photos still need signal, so it does not replace a downloaded map.

Where it pulls ahead is planning. Places go into Liked, Starred, Visited, Want to Visit or your own collections, and a trip holds the ones you choose as ordered stops with dates, notes, to-dos, the total route distance and how much of the trip you have visited. Place screens add the local weather, costs converted into your own currency and Apple Look Around where Apple has it.

Price and platform: free to download, but the free version opens only BookIt stays and tours. DOC campsites, huts, tracks and dump stations, saved collections, trips and the guides all need the KiwiCamping Pass, which the New Zealand App Store lists in options from NZ$3.99 to NZ$12.99. It runs on iPhone only and needs iOS 26 or later.

The honest drawbacks: it is new, with 4 ratings on the New Zealand App Store (3.8) against Rankers' 3,322, there are no traveller reviews in the app, and there is no Android version. If you want to read what the last ten campers thought of a site, Rankers or CamperMate will tell you more.
tips: Best for: DOC-heavy trips and route planning
Pass needed for DOC places, collections and trips
iPhone only, iOS 26 or later

sections.heading: 2. Rankers Camping NZ: best for traveller reviews
body: Rankers has the most New Zealand App Store ratings of any app in this comparison: a 4.7 average from 3,322 when we checked. Its listing describes more than 1,500 campsites and 6,600 places, over 108,000 reviews, each read and checked by a person on its team, and only community-approved sites. It also lists around 500 bookable campgrounds and more than 150 activity deals.

Campsite information is built into the app from the first install, and the detailed maps download over Wi-Fi so they work beyond reception; that works in the iPhone and Android apps but not the web version. It is free to download and use, and it runs on iPhone, iPad, Android and the web.

Strengths: it publishes the largest review count of any app here, more than 108,000, and it is useful for deciding whether a free site is worth a detour. Drawbacks: the iPhone download is large at about 794 MB, its Google Play rating is lower at 3.7 from 1,771 reviews, and reviews describe someone's night rather than the current rule. Check the council bylaw or the sign on site before you settle in.
tips: Best for: reading other travellers' experience
Free to download and use
iPhone, iPad, Android and web

sections.heading: 3. CamperMate: best for booking and deals across New Zealand and Australia
body: CamperMate covers both sides of the Tasman in one free app from Outdoria. It has a filter for free and paid places, traveller reviews and photos, saved lists, campground booking with availability, local deals and links to vehicle hire partners. Version 5.8, released in mid-October 2026, added a satellite view, and its listing says maps and place information can be downloaded for use without signal.
It held a 4.4 average from 606 ratings on the New Zealand App Store and 4.0 from 12,568 on Google Play when we checked, and it is available in 27 languages. The app is free and carries ads.

Strengths: one app for a trip that crosses to Australia, and the booking and deals side earns its place on a holiday-park-heavy route. Drawbacks: commercial listings and deals share the map with free sites, so it can be busy when you only want one thing, and the app shows ads.
tips: Best for: bookings and deals, NZ and Australia
Free; contains ads
Maps and info download for use offline

sections.heading: 4. WikiCamps New Zealand: best for the largest user-built database
body: WikiCamps New Zealand is a separate app from WikiCamps Australia, and it costs NZ$7.99 once on the App Store rather than a subscription. Its developer describes more than 12,000 New Zealand sites, community reviews and photos, more than 1,000 bookable sites and a trip planner that estimates fuel spend. An Offline Mode keeps sites and trip plans available without signal.
It rated 4.5 from 137 ratings on the New Zealand App Store and 3.0 from 1,042 on Google Play. It runs on iPhone, iPad and Android.

Strengths: the largest count of New Zealand sites any developer here publishes, and no ongoing cost on iPhone. Drawbacks: almost everything is contributed and updated by its users rather than checked against an official source, and its Google Play rating is lower at 3.0. Confirm anything legally significant against the council or DOC page.
tips: Best for: maximum coverage, paid once
NZ$7.99 upfront on iPhone
Cross-check user-added sites

sections.heading: 5. Campable: best for a night on private land
body: Campable books campervans and motorhomes onto private land: vineyards, farms, orchards and sports clubs. Hosts set their own nightly price, you book and pay in the app, and you get the host's phone number once the booking is made. It rated 4.5 from 13 ratings on the New Zealand App Store and is also on Android.

Strengths: instant booking for quiet, legal nights away from busy freedom camping areas. Drawbacks: it lists hundreds of hosts rather than a full directory, and it is a booking tool rather than a way to find DOC sites or holiday parks.
tips: Best for: booked private-land stays
Hosts set the price
iPhone and Android

sections.heading: 6. NZMCA App: best for members of the motor caravan association
body: The NZMCA App is the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association's members' app, with its Travel Directory and the association's own NZMCA Parks, which charge members $5 per adult per night. The app is free, but membership costs $150 to join plus $102 a year, so $252 in the first year.

Strengths: for a long trip in a certified self-contained motorhome, the member parks change the arithmetic. Drawbacks: it requires NZMCA membership, it had no ratings yet on the New Zealand App Store, and it rated 3.2 from 156 on Google Play.
tips: Best for: NZMCA members
Membership NZ$150 plus NZ$102 a year
Member parks NZ$5 per adult a night

sections.heading: 7. AllTrails: best for the walking half of the trip
body: AllTrails is a walking and tramping app rather than a camping one, and the best rated app in this list at 4.8 from 5,198 New Zealand ratings and 4.5 from more than 388,000 on Google Play. Track maps, reviews and recordings are free, and downloaded maps for use without signal need a paid Plus or Peak subscription.

It does not cover campsites, dump stations, holiday parks or freedom camping, so it cannot be the only app on a vehicle-based trip. Pair it with a camping app and check DOC's track alerts before a remote walk.
tips: Best for: tracks and tramping
Downloaded maps need a paid tier
Check DOC track alerts too

sections.heading: Do not skip DOC's own booking system
body: DOC does not publish a national camping app, but its booking system at bookings.doc.govt.nz is the only place to book Great Walk huts and campsites and DOC's other bookable sites. Great Walks bookings for the 2026/27 season opened in May 2026, and most Great Walks charge international visitors more than New Zealanders in summer.

Whatever app you use to choose a site, make the booking with DOC and keep the confirmation on your phone. An app listing is never proof of a booking, and DOC's alerts page is the place to check closures before you drive in.

sections.heading: How we chose and checked
body: We started from the apps New Zealand travellers actually search for and download, then kept the ones that cover camping, staying or walking in New Zealand today. Roadtrippers is left out because its New Zealand listing says it is designed for the United States and Canada, and Hipcamp because we could not verify its current New Zealand listing. Gaspy belongs in a fuel-price comparison rather than this one.

For each app we read the current New Zealand App Store listing, the developer's own website and, where it exists, the Google Play listing, all on 20 October 2026. Ratings, prices and features are as listed that day. We have not counted features we could not see described by the developer, and a feature missing from this page is not a claim that the app lacks it.

sections.heading: Which combination suits your trip
body: For a self-contained van moving through remote areas, put DOC data that opens without signal first, then add a review-led app for the busier stretches where you have reception anyway. For a family trip built around powered sites and school holidays, a booking-oriented app earns its place and offline depth matters less.

For a mixed trip with serious walking, run a camping app for the vehicle nights and AllTrails or DOC's track pages for the tramping days. Carrying two apps is a reasonable outcome, not a failure to choose.

sections.heading: Check the rule, not the pin
body: Every app in this comparison, including ours, is a planning aid. The council bylaw, the DOC notice, DOC alerts and land-manager directions override anything stored on a phone, and they change more often than app data refreshes. Fire restrictions and rāhui in particular can be imposed quickly.
Before you settle in for the night, read the sign at the entrance. If it disagrees with the app, the sign wins. That habit costs nothing and is what keeps freedom camping available.
tips: Signs override app data
Recheck DOC alerts before remote legs
Fire restrictions can change overnight

faq: What is the best camping app for New Zealand in 2026?

It depends on the trip. For DOC campsites, huts and planning a route we recommend KiwiCamping, which we make; Rankers has the most New Zealand App Store ratings, CamperMate combines booking, deals and downloadable maps, and WikiCamps New Zealand publishes the biggest count of New Zealand sites. Many travellers carry two.
Is there a free camping app for New Zealand?

Rankers and CamperMate are free to download. KiwiCamping is free to download, but DOC campsites, huts, tracks and dump stations, collections and trips need its paid Pass. WikiCamps New Zealand costs NZ$7.99 once on iPhone.
Which camping apps work without reception in New Zealand?

Rankers builds its campsite information into the app and downloads detailed maps over Wi-Fi, CamperMate lets you download maps and place information, and WikiCamps has an Offline Mode. KiwiCamping keeps place details on the phone, but its map tiles, routing and weather need signal.
Which app is best for freedom camping in New Zealand?

Use an app to shortlist spots, then let the council bylaw and the sign on site decide, because no app is the authority. Rankers, CamperMate and WikiCamps all carry traveller reports on free sites, and the rules themselves are set by each council and, on conservation land, by DOC.

where-to-camp-in-new-zealand.title: Where you can camp in New Zealand: a complete location guide
where-to-camp-in-new-zealand.description: DOC campsites, conservation land, council reserves, iwi-managed places and private holiday parks each carry different rules and costs.
where-to-camp-in-new-zealand.imageAlt: Campervan parked at a coastal New Zealand campsite
where-to-camp-in-new-zealand.intro: New Zealand's camping network runs across four quite different kinds of land, and the rules, price and booking system change with each one. Knowing which type you are looking at tells you most of what you need: whether you can turn up, whether you need certification, who to ask when something is unclear, and what you should expect to pay.

sections.heading: The four land types
body: The Department of Conservation manages the largest public network, several hundred campsites and roughly 950 huts across national parks, forest parks and scenic reserves. Sites are graded from basic through standard and serviced to Great Walk, and the grade predicts both the fee and the facilities. Basic sites are free; serviced campgrounds have flush toilets, powered options and often a warden.

Council reserves are the backbone of freedom camping. They are governed by local bylaws rather than national rules, usually allow one or two nights, and are frequently restricted to certified self-contained vehicles. Because each council writes its own bylaw, a rule that applies in one district tells you nothing about the next one.

sections.heading: Holiday parks and iwi-managed places
body: Private holiday parks provide powered sites, hot showers, laundries, kitchens and cabins. They work best as reset points between remote nights, when tanks, batteries, washing and people all need attention at once. In peak season and around events they book out well ahead.

Iwi, hapū and community-managed places, marae campgrounds, showgrounds, domain reserves, offer something the commercial network does not, and they operate on their own terms. Respect tikanga, pay koha where it is requested, and confirm availability in advance rather than arriving unannounced.
tips: Match the land type to the night you need
Book holiday parks early in summer
Contact community-managed places ahead

sections.heading: North Island in outline
body: Northland pairs a long coastline of DOC and council sites with strong seasonal demand and some closures during significant cultural events. The Coromandel has beachfront DOC sites that fill immediately over summer, while Waikato, Taupō and Rotorua mix geothermal holiday parks with lakeside options.

The central plateau serves Tongariro walking from parks near Whakapapa and Tūrangi. Gisborne and Hawke's Bay blend surf-side DOC camps with council-managed areas, and Wellington's options are shaped by ferry timing more than by scenery, an early sailing is worth a duller last night.

sections.heading: South Island in outline
body: Marlborough's Queen Charlotte Drive has DOC and concession sites along the Sounds. Nelson Tasman combines Golden Bay council sites with the Abel Tasman campgrounds, most of which are booked rather than turn-up.

The West Coast rewards travellers who accept rain and sandflies for near-empty campsites. Canterbury runs from braided river country to alpine holiday parks, and Otago and Southland hold some of the best-known sites in the country. Fiordland is largely booked DOC accommodation, and freedom camping close to the fiords is not permitted.
tips: Book Abel Tasman and Great Walk sites early
Fiordland needs DOC bookings
West Coast trades weather for space

sections.heading: What each land type costs
body: DOC basic sites are free and DOC standard sites generally run $10–$20 per adult per night, charged per person rather than per site. Serviced DOC campgrounds sit around $25 per adult. Because the charge scales with people, a family is often better off at a holiday park quoting a flat site rate.

Council freedom camping areas are usually free but may require a permit, and holiday park prices vary widely with season, location and power. Iwi and community-managed places frequently operate on koha rather than a fixed rate, which is not an invitation to underpay.
tips: DOC charges per adult
Holiday parks may suit families better
Koha is not a discount

sections.heading: Booking, or turning up
body: The four land types behave differently on arrival. Great Walk and Abel Tasman campsites are booked well ahead and turning up is not an option. Most DOC sites are first-come, which works outside peak season and fails badly between Christmas and late January. Holiday parks take bookings and fill early in beach towns.

Council freedom camping areas cannot be reserved at all, which is exactly why they need a fallback. The workable pattern is to book the nights that are hard to replace, stay flexible on the rest, and always know where the nearest paid site is.

sections.heading: The legal guardrails
body: Freedom camping is allowed on council and conservation land unless a bylaw or DOC notice prohibits or restricts it, and on council land a vehicle must be certified self-contained unless a bylaw designates the site for non-self-contained vehicles. Since 7 June 2026 certification means a green warrant: blue warrants no longer count for freedom camping, whatever their printed expiry. The certification is about the vehicle's capability, not your intentions, and campgrounds, holiday parks and private land with permission do not require it.

The bylaw or DOC notice is the rule, and the sign at the site is the quickest way to read it, though not every restricted area is signposted. Where a sign and a cached listing disagree, follow the sign. DOC visitor centres and i-SITEs hold current closure and alert information that has not reached third-party data yet.

sections.heading: Season and access
body: Winter closes or restricts alpine access, Arthur's Pass, the Lindis and the Desert Road can all be affected by snow, and some DOC roads shut temporarily after heavy weather. Chains may be required, and a two-wheel-drive van is not always the right vehicle for a winter route.

Summer inverts the problem: access is easy and availability is not. Popular coastal sites fill by early afternoon between Christmas and late January. Book what you can, hold a paid alternative for what you cannot, and avoid arriving anywhere after dark with no fallback.

faq: What are the different types of camping in New Zealand?

Broadly five: DOC campsites, backcountry huts, commercial holiday parks, freedom camping areas set by local councils, and private or farm stays. They differ in price, facilities and what vehicle they will accept, and the rules attached to each are set by different bodies.
Can you just pull over and camp anywhere?

No. Not by default: freedom camping is allowed on council and conservation land unless a bylaw or DOC notice prohibits or restricts it, but popular areas usually are restricted, and breaches are enforced with infringement fees. What is allowed depends on the local council bylaw and on whether your vehicle is certified self-contained.

responsible-camping-new-zealand.title: Responsible Camping NZ: Leave No Trace Rules and Etiquette
responsible-camping-new-zealand.description: Leave No Trace in New Zealand: toilet waste, rubbish, biosecurity, rāhui and wildlife, and the habits that keep freedom camping sites open.
responsible-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Camper packing rubbish away at a New Zealand campsite
responsible-camping-new-zealand.intro: Freedom camping in New Zealand exists at the discretion of councils and land managers, and sites close when behaviour makes them expensive to maintain. Camping responsibly is not only an environmental position, it is the practical reason the next traveller will still be allowed to park there.

sections.heading: Leave No Trace, applied locally
body: The familiar principles translate directly: plan ahead, camp on durable surfaces, dispose of waste properly, leave what you find, minimise fire impact, respect wildlife and be considerate of others. What changes in New Zealand is the specifics behind each one.

Pack out everything, including food scraps. Many councils and DOC sites operate pack-in, pack-out even where there is a toilet, and organic waste left in the bush can carry seeds and pests as well as attracting animals.
tips: Pack out food scraps too
Camp on formed surfaces
Assume no bins unless you see them

sections.heading: Waste and water
body: Grey water and toilet waste belong in a dump station, not a hedge, a stormwater drain or a river. Dump stations are mapped and generally free or low cost, and using one takes minutes. Emptying a cassette anywhere else is both the single most damaging thing a camper does and the behaviour most likely to close a site.

Do not wash dishes in rivers or lakes. Carry wastewater out, or at minimum work at least 50 metres from any waterway and use biodegradable soap sparingly. Biodegradable does not mean harmless in water.

sections.heading: Biosecurity
body: Kauri dieback is spread by soil on footwear and gear. Use every cleaning station you pass, scrub soil off properly rather than rinsing, and stay on the boardwalks in kauri forest. Myrtle rust and freshwater pests such as didymo travel the same way, on gear that was not cleaned between catchments.
Check, clean and dry anything that has been in fresh water before using it in another waterway. This applies to boots, tents, fishing gear and paddleboards, not only boats.
tips: Use every cleaning station
Check, clean, dry between catchments
Stay on kauri boardwalks

sections.heading: Wildlife and rāhui
body: Do not feed kea, weka, dolphins or anything else. Human food changes behaviour, and for kea in particular it leads directly to birds being killed on roads and at car parks. Store food and rubbish where birds cannot reach it, and expect kea to open anything you thought was secure.

Dog restrictions apply widely on beaches and reserves, especially during nesting seasons for shorebirds. Rāhui and customary closures are placed for good reason, often after a death or to allow a resource to recover; treat them as absolute rather than advisory.

sections.heading: Staying on formed ground
body: Park on established pads and marked sites. Tussock, dunes and wetland margins take years to recover from a single vehicle, and the damage is what councils photograph when they propose closing an area.
The same applies on foot. Cutting corners on a track accelerates erosion badly in alpine zones, where the growing season is short and the soil is thin.

sections.heading: Being a good neighbour near towns
body: Urban and semi-urban freedom camping survives on informal agreements. Keep noise down in the evening, avoid running generators, leave reasonably early, and use the town, buy fuel, coffee and groceries locally. The economic argument is what councillors hear when a site is debated.

If you see a site being misused, report it to the council or DOC rather than leaving it. Sites are usually closed because problems went unreported until the cost of cleaning them up outweighed the benefit of keeping them open.
tips: Quiet by evening, gone early
Spend locally
Report misuse rather than ignoring it

faq: What does responsible camping mean in New Zealand?

Camping where it is permitted, carrying out every piece of rubbish, disposing of wastewater and toilet waste at a proper facility, keeping fires within the rules and leaving the site as you found it. The freedom camping restrictions that exist now are a direct response to visitors who did not.
What is the biggest mistake campers make?
Human waste. Toileting near a campsite or a waterway is the behaviour that closes free sites faster than anything else, and it is the reason the self-containment rules now require a fixed toilet.

two-week-camper-itinerary-new-zealand.title: 2 Week NZ Campervan Itinerary: North and South Island
two-week-camper-itinerary-new-zealand.description: A 14-day Auckland to Queenstown campervan itinerary: one Cook Strait crossing, the West Coast, Milford Sound and the Catlins, day by day.
two-week-camper-itinerary-new-zealand.imageAlt: Campervan on a New Zealand highway between mountains and lake
two-week-camper-itinerary-new-zealand.intro: Fourteen days is enough to see both islands properly only if you accept that it is a route, not a survey. This itinerary crosses Cook Strait once, keeps most driving legs to three or four hours, and leaves the last day soft so a delayed ferry or a closed pass does not put your flight at risk.

sections.heading: Logistics before the days
body: Book the ferry first and build the rest around it. Interislander and Bluebridge both cross Cook Strait, sailings fill in summer, and a crossing consumes most of a day once you include check-in and the drive at either end. Everything else on this route is easier to move than the ferry.

Pick up the vehicle in Auckland and drop it in Queenstown if the one-way fee is reasonable; the alternative is a long return leg that adds nothing. In winter, add time for alpine passes, carry chains where required and check road conditions each morning rather than the night before.
tips: Book the ferry before anything else
Price the one-way vehicle fee
Check passes daily in winter

sections.heading: Days 1 to 6, North Island
body: Start north of Auckland rather than in it, stock up on the way out and take the first night near Ōrewa or the Hibiscus Coast. Day two runs into the Coromandel for Cathedral Cove and Hahei, which is worth an unhurried afternoon. Day three is Rotorua and its geothermal parks, where the holiday parks are genuinely convenient.

Day four takes you to Taupō for the lake and the Huka Falls; stay at a holiday park or check Taupō District Council's freedom camping rules before parking for the night. Day five crosses to Napier for art deco and the wine trail, and day six runs down through the Wairarapa into Wellington. Position the last North Island night close to the ferry terminal.

sections.heading: Days 7 to 10, into the South
body: Day seven is the crossing and Queen Charlotte Drive, which is slower and more beautiful than the map suggests. Stop early on the Sounds rather than pushing towards Nelson in the dark.

Days eight to ten run down the West Coast to the glaciers and across to Wānaka. This is the wettest and least populated stretch of the route, the sandflies are serious, and it is also where most people's photographs come from. Fuel up more often than feels necessary.
tips: Sandfly repellent on the West Coast
Fuel early, not at the last town
Queen Charlotte Drive takes longer than it looks

sections.heading: Days 11 to 14, the south
body: Day eleven runs from Wānaka to Te Anau through Queenstown, about three hours, then Milford Sound is a long day out of Te Anau on day twelve. The Milford road is spectacular and unforgiving, leave early, expect no reception, and check for avalanche closures in winter.

Day thirteen crosses Southland to the Catlins coast at Curio Bay for penguins and sea lions, and day fourteen drives back up to Queenstown, roughly four hours, to drop the vehicle. If your flight leaves early on day fourteen, skip the Catlins and drive Te Anau to Queenstown, about two hours, on day thirteen instead.

sections.heading: Where to lose a day if you need to
body: This route has three natural compression points. The Napier leg can be cut by running Taupō to Wellington directly, the Catlins can be dropped entirely, and Milford can become a scenic flight or a shorter Te Anau day if the weather closes in.
What should not be compressed is the ferry day or the West Coast. Both punish a tight schedule, one with rebooking fees, the other with long stretches between fuel, food and reception.

sections.heading: Season changes the route more than the plan
body: Between Christmas and late January, book every night you can and treat the popular coastal sites as unavailable on arrival. In shoulder season the same route is quieter, cheaper and easier to change day to day.

In winter, the South Island half is a different trip. Alpine passes can close, some DOC sites and roads shut, daylight is short, and driving legs that work in February become uncomfortable in July. Shorten the days rather than starting earlier in the dark.

rankers-alternatives.intro: Rankers Camping NZ is the most-rated camping app on the New Zealand App Store, free, and well liked: 4.7 stars from 3,322 ratings on the New Zealand App Store when we checked on 20 October 2026. People rarely leave it because it is bad. They look elsewhere when the trip asks for something Rankers is not built around, such as planning the route day by day, DOC huts and tracks for the walking days, a night on a farm, or a crossing to Australia. Full disclosure: KiwiCamping is our own app, and that is why it heads this list; each entry below says what it does better than Rankers and when you should choose it instead.

sections.heading: Rankers alternatives at a glance
body: If you want one recommendation: keep Rankers for its reviews and add KiwiCamping when the trip becomes a plan with dates, DOC huts or tracks. Choose CamperMate instead if the trip continues to Australia, WikiCamps New Zealand if raw coverage matters more than curation, thl Roadtrip for a simple free view of what is near you, and Campable for booked stays on private land.

None of these replaces the council bylaw or the sign at the site entrance. Rankers says it only lists places the local community has approved for overnight stays, which is a real strength, and an alternative that lists more places is not automatically more useful if you then have to check each one yourself.

sections.heading: Why travellers look past Rankers
body: We read the 50 most recent Rankers reviews on the New Zealand App Store. Forty-two gave four or five stars, and the praise is for accuracy, the price and the depth of traveller comments. The complaints were few and specific: three reviewers found sites missing or out of date, three said the app failed to open or load, two wanted to combine filters rather than search one category at a time, two objected to a fee on bookings made through the app, and one could not find reviews after an update.

Rankers itself is free and earns from bookings, activity deals and campervan-hire referrals; it says the booking and activity commissions cost you nothing extra. So the honest reason to add or switch apps is usually a different job, not a fault: route planning, walking, private land or a second country.

sections.heading: 1. KiwiCamping: best for turning saved places into a dated route
body: KiwiCamping is built on the Department of Conservation's own data. In its August 2026 data the app held 287 DOC campsites, 927 DOC huts and 1,453 DOC tracks, with the fees, dog rules and booking requirements DOC lists, where it lists them. That makes it strongest exactly where a review-led app is thinnest: the hut you walk to on day four and the track that starts from tonight's campsite.

Filters combine, so a single search can ask for a type of place, a fee, facilities and access together. Saved places then become a trip with ordered stops, dates, notes, to-dos and the total distance, and place details stay readable on the phone when reception drops. Map tiles, routing, weather and photos still need signal.

What it costs and where it falls short: it is free to download, but the free version opens only BookIt stays and tours; DOC campsites, huts, tracks and dump stations, collections, trips and guides need the KiwiCamping Pass, listed from NZ$3.99 to NZ$12.99 on the New Zealand App Store. It is iPhone only and needs iOS 26 or later, it had 4 New Zealand ratings (3.8), and it has no traveller reviews. That is why we suggest it alongside Rankers rather than instead of it.

free-camping-apps-new-zealand.intro: Free camping in New Zealand comes in two forms: freedom camping, where a council or DOC allows you to stay the night somewhere that is not a campground, and campsites that charge nothing, most of them basic DOC sites. It is not first on this list, because its free DOC campsites sit behind its paid Pass. Here is where it still helps.

CamperMate adds a free or paid filter and two-country coverage, and WikiCamps New Zealand has the biggest published count of New Zealand sites, with a filter for free campgrounds, for a one-off NZ$7.99.

KiwiCamping is the one to add if you want DOC's own record of which DOC campsites charge nothing. NZMCA members get a different deal again: the association's own parks for $5 per adult a night, which is not free but is close.

sections.heading: The 2026 rule that matters most: green warrants
body: On council land, the law lets a vehicle freedom camp only if it is certified self-contained, unless a council bylaw allows other vehicles at a site, and the meaning of certified changed this year. The transition from the old blue sticker to the regulated green warrant ended on 7 June 2026, and blue stickers are no longer valid. A green warrant requires a toilet fixed in the vehicle, so a portable toilet no longer qualifies.

On conservation land DOC sets its own rules: freedom camping is not allowed in DOC scenic and recreation reserves unless DOC provides a campsite, some areas are for self-contained vehicles only or limit the number of nights, and some ban it outright. Without a green warrant, you can stay in a vehicle on council land only where a bylaw allows it, and on DOC land outside the reserves and areas DOC prohibits or restricts. Free DOC campsites are the simplest option.

body: The New Zealand Motor Caravan Association's app gives members its Travel Directory and the association's NZMCA Parks, which are for members in certified self-contained vehicles, at $5 per adult per night. Membership costs $150 to join plus $102 a year, so the parks pay off over a long trip rather than a fortnight.
It requires membership and had no ratings yet on the New Zealand App Store. For a certified self-contained motorhome on the road for months, it is often the cheapest reliable option after free sites.

sections.heading: Apps we left out
body: An App Store search for freedom camping in New Zealand turns up a free app called Freedom camping nz, last updated in 2017, with a 1.3 average from 21 ratings and reviewers saying its map shows little of New Zealand. We would not rely on it. International apps such as park4night and iOverlander list places in many countries but do not state their New Zealand coverage, so we have not ranked them.

We checked every listing, rating and price on 20 October 2026 on the New Zealand App Store and the developers' own sites. Features are described as each developer describes them, so a feature missing here is not a claim that an app lacks it.

sections.heading: Before you stay the night
body: Read the sign at the entrance, check the council's freedom camping bylaw for the district you are in, and look up DOC's list of prohibited and restricted areas for conservation land. These can change, and they outrank every app on this page, ours included.

Leave the site as you found it, use a dump station rather than a drain, and move on when the stay limit is up. Free camping in New Zealand survives on councils' goodwill, and that goodwill is easy to lose.
tips: The sign and the bylaw outrank any app
Check DOC's restricted areas list
Respect stay limits

faq: Which app shows free campsites in New Zealand?

Rankers is the best free app for it: the camping spots it shows are only ones the local community has approved for overnight stays, with traveller reviews. CamperMate filters free and paid sites, WikiCamps New Zealand has a free campgrounds filter, and KiwiCamping shows the DOC campsites DOC lists with no fee, behind its paid Pass.
Can I freedom camp in New Zealand without a self-contained vehicle?

Since 7 June 2026 only a green warrant counts as self-contained. Without one, a vehicle can stay on council land only where a bylaw allows it, and on DOC land outside scenic and recreation reserves and the areas DOC prohibits or restricts. Free DOC campsites are the simplest option.

best-travel-apps-new-zealand.intro: A New Zealand trip needs fewer apps than you might think, but the right ones save real money and trouble: the official NZeTA app costs less than the website, a fuel app pays for itself on a long drive, and a walking app can send your trip plan to someone who will raise the alarm if a tramp goes wrong. These are the ten we would install for a road trip in 2026, grouped by the job they do, with ratings and prices from the New Zealand App Store checked on 20 October 2026. We are the team behind KiwiCamping, which is why it opens the list, and we say below who will not need it at all.

sections.heading: The ten apps at a glance
body: Before you fly, the official NZeTA and New Zealand Traveller Declaration apps handle entry. On the road, KiwiCamping plans where you sleep, Google Maps drives you there, MetService warns you about the weather and Plan My Walk covers the tramping days. Gaspy and a fuel company app keep fuel costs down, AT Mobile gets you around Auckland, and Rankers adds traveller reviews of campsites.
You do not need all ten. A visitor hiring a car for a week of hotels can skip the camping apps; a campervan traveller on a month-long trip will use most of them.

Places can be saved to collections or added to a trip with ordered stops, dates, notes, to-dos and the route distance, and place details stay readable on the phone when signal drops. Map tiles, routing, weather and photos need a connection.

It is free to download, but only BookIt stays and tours are open without paying; DOC places, collections, trips and the guides need the KiwiCamping Pass, listed from NZ$3.99 to NZ$12.99. sections.heading: 2. NZeTA: the cheaper way to get your travel authority
body: Most visitors from visa-waiver countries need a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority before they travel. Immigration New Zealand charges NZ$17 when you request it in the official NZeTA app and NZ$23 on its website, and most visitors also pay the NZ$100 International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy with it.
The app scans your passport and takes the payment. Request it well before you fly, and use only the official app or immigration.govt.nz, because look-alike sites charge extra for the same thing.

sections.heading: 3. New Zealand Traveller Declaration: your arrival form
body: The New Zealand Traveller Declaration is the free digital arrival declaration everyone entering New Zealand completes; doing it before you fly saves filling in a paper one on board. The official app, from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, lets you complete it up to 24 hours before you travel, scans your passport, and has nothing to print because the declaration is linked to your passport at the border. It rated 4.7 from 3,190 New Zealand ratings.
You need a connection to start and submit it, and it must be answered in English. Do it the evening before you fly rather than at the gate.

sections.heading: 4. Google Maps: navigation, downloaded before you need it
body: Google Maps is the navigator most visitors already know, rated 4.7 from 73,470 New Zealand ratings. Download offline areas for each region before you leave a main centre: Google's help pages say offline driving directions work only when the whole route is inside a downloaded area, and offline mode has no traffic information.
Allow longer than it predicts on winding two-lane roads with a campervan, and check the NZ Transport Agency's Journeys site for closures before alpine passes.

body: MetService is New Zealand's national weather forecaster, and its app carries severe weather warnings, location forecasts and rain radar. It is free with ads, or NZ$1.99 a month without. It rates 2.4 from 1,126 New Zealand App Store ratings; its severe weather warnings are the official ones, which matters when a front closes a pass.
If you are heading onto the water, MetService's separate Marine app has coastal forecasts and tides.

body: Plan My Walk, from the New Zealand Mountain Safety Council, covers more than 3,500 tracks, huts and campsites on official topographic maps, shows official track alerts and closures, and sends your trip plan to an emergency contact. It is free and rated 4.6 from 612 New Zealand ratings.
DOC has no national visitor app of its own, so this is the easiest way to see its track alerts on your phone. Leave your intentions with someone before any walk that goes beyond reception.

Cook Strait ferries are booked on the Interislander and Bluebridge websites. Book the crossing first and build the rest of the trip around it.

The NZeTA and Traveller Declaration apps for entry, Google Maps with offline areas downloaded, MetService for warnings and Plan My Walk for walks. For a camping trip add KiwiCamping, which we make, for DOC campsites and the route plan, and Rankers for traveller reviews.

wikicamps-alternatives.title: 5 Best WikiCamps New Zealand Alternatives in 2026
wikicamps-alternatives.description: WikiCamps New Zealand costs NZ$7.99 and leans on user-added sites. KiwiCamping, Rankers, CamperMate, Campable and Overland Navigator compared on price, data and offline use. Checked October 2026.
wikicamps-alternatives.imageAlt: A house bus, cars and a small tent at Cameron Flat campsite below the forested peaks of Mount Aspiring National Park
wikicamps-alternatives.intro: WikiCamps New Zealand is a paid app with a loyal following: NZ$7.99 once on the New Zealand App Store, 4.5 stars from 137 New Zealand ratings when we checked on 20 October 2026, and more than 12,000 New Zealand sites that its own users have added. Most people who search for an alternative are not unhappy with it so much as unsure: whether to pay for an app when free ones exist, whether user-added listings are current, or whether they will need a second copy for Australia. KiwiCamping is our app, so it comes first below, but each entry says plainly what it does better than WikiCamps and when WikiCamps is still the better buy.

sections.heading: WikiCamps alternatives at a glance
body: Short answer: if most of your nights are at DOC campsites or huts, KiwiCamping gives you DOC's own details and a dated plan. If you want a free app, Rankers is the strongest New Zealand choice and CamperMate also covers Australia. Campable is for booked nights on farms and vineyards, and Overland Navigator is for gravel roads and 4WD tracks that a general camping app does not map.

WikiCamps' strength is volume. Its listings come from the people using it, which is why it has so many, and also why a fee or a closure can lag behind reality. Whichever app you choose, the sign at the site and the council or DOC page are the final word on whether you can stay.

sections.heading: What pushes people away from WikiCamps
body: WikiCamps gets few New Zealand App Store reviews, so its latest 50 there stretch back to January 2020, and only 13 of them were written in 2024 or later. Forty-one gave four or five stars; the most common praise, seven reviews each, was for the trip planner and for listing more places than free apps. The complaints: six described filters or data breaking after an update, five of them in 2023 (the current version, 6.3.0, came out on 19 October 2026), five said site details, fees or locations were out of date or wrong, and two said the app froze or would not open the trip planner.

Two practical points also come up. WikiCamps sells New Zealand and Australia as separate apps, so a trip across the Tasman means a second purchase: WikiCamps Australia costs NZ$11.99 on the New Zealand App Store. And on Android its Google Play listing rates 3.0 from 1,042 ratings and shows in-app purchase and ads labels, although its description calls it a one-time purchase.

sections.heading: 1. KiwiCamping: best for DOC campsites and huts with DOC's own details
body: In its August 2026 data, KiwiCamping's 287 DOC campsites, 927 DOC huts and 1,453 DOC tracks come from the Department of Conservation's data, with the adult fees, dog rules and booking requirements that DOC lists, and a link to DOC's own page for the place. For DOC places, KiwiCamping shows what DOC publishes.

Saved places become a trip with ordered stops, dates, notes and the route distance, and filters for cost, facilities and dogs can be combined in one search. Place details stay on the phone when you lose signal; map tiles, routing, weather and photos do not.

The limits: the free version opens only BookIt stays and tours, and DOC places, collections, trips and the guides need the KiwiCamping Pass, listed from NZ$3.99 to NZ$12.99. It runs on iPhone only (iOS 26 or later), it has 4 New Zealand ratings (3.8) and no traveller reviews, and it lists far fewer places in total than WikiCamps' 12,000-plus.

Its 108,000-plus traveller reviews are each read by a person before they appear.

That makes it narrower than WikiCamps on paper but easier to trust per listing. Campsite information is in the app from the first install, and detailed maps download over Wi-Fi. It rated 4.7 from 3,322 New Zealand ratings, the most of any camping app here.

Its makers say every route is checked and drivable rather than taken from a map.

It is free to start. Navigator All Access, NZ$7.99 a month or NZ$87.99 a year, adds full offline navigation, CarPlay and more routes. It rated 4.5 from 31 New Zealand ratings and runs on iPhone and iPad; it is a specialist tool, not a replacement for a general campsite directory.

sections.heading: When WikiCamps is still the better buy
body: If you want the largest number of New Zealand sites in one app, paid for once, WikiCamps remains hard to beat. Its trip planner estimates fuel spend, its Offline Mode keeps maps and up to three planned trips available without signal, and its filters cover free campgrounds, pet-friendly sites, water refills and dump points.

Many travellers keep it and add one of the apps above for the gap they feel most: DOC detail, curation, private land, Australia or the backcountry. Members of the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association should also install the NZMCA App, which shows the association's own parks and directory to members.

faq: Is WikiCamps New Zealand free?
No. On the New Zealand App Store it costs NZ$7.99 once, with no subscription in its listing. Its website quotes A$9.99 per platform, so check the price in your own store before you buy.
What is a free alternative to WikiCamps in New Zealand?

Rankers Camping NZ is free and lists only overnight spots the local community has approved, with traveller reviews read by its team. CamperMate is also free and covers Australia as well. KiwiCamping is free to download, but its DOC campsites, huts and trips need the paid Pass.
Do I need separate WikiCamps apps for New Zealand and Australia?

Yes. WikiCamps New Zealand and WikiCamps Australia are separate apps, each bought on its own; WikiCamps Australia costs NZ$11.99 on the New Zealand App Store. CamperMate covers both countries in one free app.

Rankers adds traveller reviews of where to park up, Camplify rents privately owned vans, Imoova lists relocation deals and the NZMCA App is for members of the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association.

sections.heading: Green warrants: the check no app makes for you
body: From 7 June 2026, blue self-containment warrants are no longer recognised for freedom camping, and the Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Board says freedom camping on public land without a green warrant can bring a $400 infringement notice. A certified vehicle needs a toilet permanently fixed and usable inside it, along with fresh water, a sink, wastewater and rubbish storage.

The rules apply to freedom camping on public land, not to campgrounds, holiday parks or private property. An app's freedom-camping pin does not tell you whether your van qualifies, so look for the green warrant card when you collect the van.

sections.heading: Other apps worth having in the van
body: Gaspy shows fuel prices reported by its users and is free, with an optional Gold subscription at NZ$1.69 a month. MetService carries the official severe weather warnings, which matter in a campervan on an exposed road, and Plan My Walk covers track alerts for the walking days.
If your van runs on diesel, ask the hire company how it charges road user charges: Spaceships, for example, bills them after the trip by the distance you drove.

body: We looked at the apps that New Zealand hire companies send their customers to, plus the apps campervan travellers use for sites, relocations and membership. It depends on the stage. For planning nights at DOC campsites we recommend KiwiCamping, which we make; thl Roadtrip suits Maui, Britz, Mighty and Apollo hirers, CamperMate is a free all-rounder, and Rankers adds traveller reviews of where to stay.
How do campervan relocations work in New Zealand?

A hire company needs a van moved, so it offers it for as little as $1 a day on fixed dates. Imoova says fuel, tolls and parking are not covered, though some suppliers add fuel or a ferry ticket, and companies such as Travellers Autobarn ask for a bond.
Do I need a green warrant to freedom camp in a campervan?

Yes, on public land where freedom camping is limited to self-contained vehicles. Since 7 June 2026 blue warrants are no longer recognised, and camping without a green warrant can bring a $400 infringement notice. Campgrounds, holiday parks and private property are not covered by the rule.

best-weather-apps-new-zealand.title: Best Weather Apps for Camping and Tramping in New Zealand 2026
best-weather-apps-new-zealand.description: MetService, Windy, Yr, Plan My Walk, Apple Weather and KiwiCamping compared for New Zealand camping and tramping, plus the mountain forecasts that live on websites. Checked October 2026.
best-weather-apps-new-zealand.imageAlt: Lenticular clouds over Lake Pukaki with Aoraki Mount Cook on the horizon
best-weather-apps-new-zealand.intro: New Zealand weather turns quickly, and the right app depends on the question: whether a severe warning covers tonight's campsite, how strong the wind will be on a ridge tomorrow, or which hut on the route will be wet. No single app answers all three. These are the weather apps we would use for camping and tramping in 2026, with ratings and prices from the New Zealand App Store checked on 20 October 2026, and the official websites that still beat every app for mountain forecasts. KiwiCamping is ours, so it is listed first; it is the right pick for one job only, and the others are better for the rest.

sections.heading: The best weather apps at a glance
body: Use MetService for the official warnings, Windy or Yr for a second forecast and for wind, and Plan My Walk on tramping days. KiwiCamping puts a forecast on each campsite and hut in your trip, which is useful for choosing between places but is not a warning service. Before going above the bushline, read MetService's mountain forecast and the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory on the web.

No independent test of weather app accuracy in New Zealand turned up in our research, so treat claims that one app is the most accurate as opinion. What can be checked is the source: MetService is the only authorised provider of severe weather warnings in New Zealand.

body: KiwiCamping shows Apple Weather on each place screen: current conditions, wind gusts, how warm it feels and seven days of highs and lows. In a trip, each stop shows the forecast for the day you plan to arrive, so you can see before you drive whether the lakeside campsite or the sheltered one in the bush suits the next two nights.

That makes it a planning tool, not a safety tool. It does not carry MetService's warnings, and it needs signal to load a forecast. Place details such as facilities and fees stay on the phone when reception drops. It is iPhone only, iOS 26 or later, with 4 New Zealand ratings (3.8).

body: MetService is New Zealand's national weather service and the only authorised provider of severe weather warnings. Its app shows warnings and watches for your location, rain radar, 48-hour forecast graphs, three-day rain maps and the UV index and fire danger, with notifications for severe weather. It is free with ads, or ad-free for NZ$1.99 a month or NZ$22.99 a year.

It is also the lowest-rated app here: 2.4 from 1,126 New Zealand ratings, with reviews on its App Store page objecting to ads and the design. Its mountain, marine and rural forecasts are on metservice.com rather than in this app, and its separate Marine and Rural Weather apps were last updated in 2023.

body: Windy offers more than 15 weather models, including the European ECMWF model, on animated maps of wind, gusts, rain and cloud. That is useful when forecasts disagree: if the models agree on a southerly change, plan around it; if they do not, keep the plan flexible. It rated 4.8 from 9,058 New Zealand ratings.

It is free, with a Premium in-app purchase that adds model comparison, forecasts at one-hour resolution, a 15-day outlook and 24-hour radar loops. It does not issue New Zealand warnings, so pair it with MetService.

body: Yr is the free app of Norway's public weather service, whose forecasts it uses worldwide, including New Zealand place forecasts. Its New Zealand listing shows no in-app purchases. It rated 3.6 from 87 New Zealand ratings.
Some trampers recommend it on forums, but we found no independent test of how it performs here. Use it as a cross-check against MetService rather than as your only source.

sections.heading: 5. Plan My Walk: best for the tramping days
body: Plan My Walk, from the New Zealand Mountain Safety Council, combines weather forecasts and warnings with official track alerts for more than 3,500 tracks, huts and campsites, and sends your trip plan to an emergency contact. The app costs nothing, and 612 New Zealand App Store ratings average 4.6.
DOC's Land Safety Code asks you to check the forecast, change your plans if needed and leave your intentions with someone, and this app covers both on one screen.

sections.heading: 6. Apple Weather: best for a quick look on an iPhone
body: Apple Weather comes with the iPhone, rated 4.7 from 18,741 New Zealand ratings. Apple lists MetService among its data sources for New Zealand severe weather, but next-hour rain forecasts are not offered here, so the minute-by-minute rain alerts some travellers expect from other countries will not appear.
It is fine for a glance at the week ahead. For a mountain day or an exposed campsite, look at MetService's own forecast as well.

sections.heading: The forecasts that are only on websites
body: MetService publishes mountain forecasts for national parks and regions such as Aoraki/Mount Cook, Arthur's Pass, Fiordland, Mount Aspiring, Nelson Lakes and Tongariro, with a New Zealand mountain forecast for areas above 800 metres that includes the freezing level. Its website also carries marine and rural forecasts.

DOC points trampers to NIWA's park forecasts on weather.niwa.co.nz, now run by Earth Sciences New Zealand, and to the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory before any trip into avalanche terrain. Save these pages before you lose signal; none of them will update once you are out of reception.

sections.heading: Warnings, watches and what they ask of you
body: MetService uses three levels. A yellow watch means severe weather is possible but not yet certain: stay alert. An orange warning means take action, and most warnings are orange. A red warning, kept for the most extreme events, means take action immediately.

For campers, an orange warning for heavy rain or wind is the moment to move away from rivers and exposed ridges and choose a sheltered site. Our guide to severe weather when camping covers what to do at each level.

sections.heading: How we chose and checked
body: We compared the weather apps most used by campers and trampers in New Zealand, favouring official sources. Ratings, prices and features come from each app's New Zealand App Store listing on 20 October 2026, and the warning definitions from MetService's own page.
We describe features as their developers do, so a feature not mentioned is not a claim that an app lacks it. Forecasts are forecasts: on the day, what you see on the hill outranks any app.

faq: What is the best weather app for New Zealand?

For official severe weather warnings use MetService, the only authorised provider of them in New Zealand. Add Windy or Yr as a second forecast, Plan My Walk on tramping days, and KiwiCamping, which we make, to compare the forecast at each campsite on your trip.
Which weather app is most accurate in New Zealand?

We found no independent test that answers this. Compare two sources, such as MetService and Windy, and treat agreement between them as more reliable than either alone. For mountains, use MetService's mountain forecasts on its website.
Where can I get a mountain weather forecast in New Zealand?

MetService publishes mountain forecasts for national parks and regions such as Aoraki/Mount Cook, Arthur's Pass, Fiordland and Tongariro on metservice.com, with the freezing level. Check the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory too before going into avalanche terrain.

fuel-price-apps-new-zealand.description: Gaspy, Z, bp, Waitomo, Gull, g.a.s., Mobil and the supermarket fuel schemes compared: what each saves per litre, what it costs and where it works. Prices and terms checked October 2026.
fuel-price-apps-new-zealand.imageAlt: State Highway 6 winding along the shore of Lake Wakatipu under grey cloud
fuel-price-apps-new-zealand.intro: Fuel has become one of the biggest costs of a New Zealand road trip in 2026. MBIE's weekly monitoring put regular 91 at 354.4 cents a litre on the price boards in the week dated 9 October 2026, against 260.4 cents a year earlier, and diesel at 323.8 cents before road user charges; the latest week's figures are provisional. At those prices it pays to know both where fuel is cheapest and which discounts you hold, so the best setup is one app that shows prices and one or two that cut them. We make KiwiCamping, a camping app that does not track fuel prices, so it is not ranked here; it appears at the end only for the planning job it can help with.

sections.heading: Fuel apps at a glance
body: Start with Gaspy to see which station near you is cheapest. Then add the app for the network you pass most: Z's app gives a daily discount and a bigger one on Wednesdays, bp's app works with Woolworths' Everyday Rewards card, and Foodstuffs' Club+ turns a supermarket shop into a discount at Z and participating Caltex sites. Waitomo and Gull reward you through in-app credit and promotion days rather than a fixed cents-per-litre discount.

Discounts are capped per fill, usually at 50 or 100 litres, and the schemes can change their amounts at short notice. Check the terms in the app before a long drive rather than relying on last month's offer.

Gaspy's help page says updates are limited to stations near you because of past misuse, which keeps prices honest but means a remote station can show an old figure.

You can tell the app which discounts you hold, and it shows your discounted price above the pump price; the free version allows one custom discount and Gaspy Gold, NZ$1.69 a month, allows as many as you like. faq: Which app shows the cheapest petrol prices in New Zealand?

Gaspy. Its users report the price on the pump and other users confirm it, so you can compare stations near you before filling up. It is free, with an optional Gold subscription at NZ$1.69 a month that lets you add more of your own discounts.
Which fuel discount is biggest in New Zealand?

It changes. On 20 October 2026 Z's app gave at least 6 cents a litre every day and 15 cents on Wednesdays, bp and g.a.s. gave 6 cents with Everyday Rewards, and Foodstuffs' Club+ gave 8 cents at Z and participating Caltex sites. Each scheme caps the litres per fill and can change its amounts.
Do diesel campervans cost more to run in New Zealand?

Diesel is cheaper at the pump, but light diesel vehicles also pay road user charges of $76 per 1,000 km, about 7.6 cents a kilometre. Add that to the fuel cost when you compare a diesel campervan with a petrol vehicle.

working-holiday-apps-new-zealand.title: Best Apps for Working Holiday Makers in New Zealand 2026
working-holiday-apps-new-zealand.description: The apps a working holiday maker in New Zealand actually uses in 2026: SEEK, Trade Me, Wise, bank and phone apps, seasonal work and farm stays, plus the official steps no app does for you. Checked October 2026.
working-holiday-apps-new-zealand.imageAlt: Autumn vineyard rows in the Awatere Valley, Marlborough, below snow-capped ranges
working-holiday-apps-new-zealand.intro: A working holiday in New Zealand runs on a handful of apps: one to find work, one to move money, a bank and a phone plan, and something to tell you where to sleep when the job is three hours from the last one. These are the apps we would install for a working holiday in 2026, with ratings from the New Zealand App Store checked on 20 October 2026, and the official steps that still happen on government websites rather than in any app. We make KiwiCamping and list it first for the travelling part of the year; for jobs, money and paperwork the other apps below do the work.

sections.heading: Working holiday apps at a glance
body: For jobs, install SEEK and Trade Me, and look at PickNZ for fruit and vegetable seasons. Wise moves money from home cheaply, a New Zealand bank app holds your wages, and a prepaid plan from Skinny, 2degrees, Spark or One NZ keeps you reachable for employers. KiwiCamping covers the nights between jobs, WWOOF and Workaway cover work in exchange for a bed, and the NZTA app helps once you own a car.

Your IRD number, tax code and visa conditions are handled on Inland Revenue and Immigration New Zealand websites. Sort those out first, because an employer needs your IRD number before your first pay.

sections.heading: 1. KiwiCamping: best for finding a bed between jobs
body: Seasonal work moves you around: kiwifruit in the Bay of Plenty, grapes in Marlborough, apples in Hawke's Bay. KiwiCamping is a map of where you can stay on the way, built on DOC's data, with 287 DOC campsites in its August 2026 data and the adult fees DOC lists, from $5 to $25 a night at the sites with a published rate. Holiday parks, stays and tours sit on the same map, and costs can be shown in your home currency alongside the New Zealand dollar figure.

We found no PickNZ app in the New Zealand App Store, so use the website. Some listings on it are for the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, which is a separate visa for workers from Pacific countries, not for working holiday makers.

body: WWOOF New Zealand connects volunteers with organic farms; online membership costs NZ$25 for one person or NZ$30 for a couple and lasts 15 months. WWOOF NZ says you need a working holiday visa to volunteer even without wages, so check the conditions on your own visa with Immigration New Zealand. The international WWOOF app had only 3 New Zealand ratings, so the website is the easier way in.

Workaway covers hosts worldwide, including New Zealand, for a yearly membership from about US$59, depending on the plan; its app rated 4.8 from 144 New Zealand ratings. Both can stretch a budget a long way, but hours and conditions vary by host, so agree them before you arrive.

sections.heading: 5. Wise and a New Zealand bank app: best for money
body: Wise moves money between currencies with a fee that starts at 0.22% of the amount, and its card gives 400 New Zealand dollars a month of free cash withdrawals, then 2.69% above that. It rated 4.8 from 23,432 New Zealand ratings and suits the first weeks before your bank account is running.

Wages go into a New Zealand account. BNZ lets you apply from overseas, ASB does too depending on your country and visa, ANZ lets you open an account before you arrive and activate it at a branch, and Westpac's migrant team can set one up up to 180 days before you move in some circumstances. Their apps rated 4.8 (BNZ, 56,574), 4.7 (Westpac, 24,380), 4.0 (ANZ, 7,946) and 3.2 (ASB, 2,106). A New Zealand bank account also helps your IRD number application.

body: Employers ring, so a New Zealand number matters. Skinny's app rated 4.4 from 18,813 New Zealand ratings and Skinny sells 52-week prepaid plans from $296; 2degrees prepay starts from $8 a month; its main 2degrees NZ app rated 1.6 from 998, and its Data Clock prepay app 4.7 from 17,570. The AA's app (4.4 from 44) holds an AA membership card and Roadservice details if you join. Before buying, check the warrant of fitness and registration dates on the vehicle; our guide to WoF and registration explains both.

sections.heading: The official steps no app does for you
body: Apply for your IRD number on Inland Revenue's website through myIR; it is free, and new arrivals can usually expect it within two days by text or email. Inland Revenue may ask for a working New Zealand bank account or a customer due diligence form (IR997). Give your employer the number and a tax code on an IR330 form, because without one you are taxed at the 45% non-declaration rate.

Know your conditions too. Since 20 April 2026 working holiday visas carry the condition that you must work for an employer, under an employment agreement or a contract for services, and you cannot employ other people. The adult minimum wage is $23.95 an hour from 1 April 2026 and applies to temporary migrants too. You cannot join KiwiSaver on a temporary or work visa, and holiday pay of 8% on each pay is only allowed for fixed-term work under 12 months or genuinely irregular work, agreed in your employment agreement.

sections.heading: How we chose and checked
body: We picked the apps that handle the jobs every working holiday maker faces, favouring the most-used option in each category. Ratings come from the New Zealand App Store on 20 October 2026, fees from each provider's own page, and every rule from Immigration New Zealand, Inland Revenue or Employment New Zealand that day.

Visa conditions, funds and lengths differ by passport, so read the page for your own country on immigration.govt.nz. We describe features as each provider does, and a feature not mentioned is not a claim that an app lacks it.

faq: What apps do I need for a working holiday in New Zealand?

SEEK and Trade Me for jobs, Wise for moving money, a New Zealand bank app and a prepaid phone plan. If you travel between seasonal jobs, KiwiCamping, which we make, shows DOC campsites and other places to stay on the way.
How do I get an IRD number on a working holiday visa?

Apply through myIR on Inland Revenue's website. It is free, and new arrivals usually receive the number by text or email within two days. Inland Revenue may ask for a New Zealand bank account or an IR997 form, so open the account early.
What is the minimum wage in New Zealand in 2026?

The adult minimum wage is $23.95 an hour from 1 April 2026, and Employment New Zealand says temporary migrants have the same minimum employment rights. Without a tax code from you, your employer must tax you at the 45% non-declaration rate.

sections.heading: 2. Gaspy: best for the fuel bill
body: With petrol above $3.50 a litre on the boards, choosing the cheaper station in each town is the simplest saving on a road trip. Gaspy shows prices that its users report from the pump and confirm, and it can show your price after a loyalty discount you hold. Its 773 New Zealand ratings average 4.0, and the optional Gold tier costs NZ$1.69 a month.
Our guide to fuel price apps compares Gaspy with the Z, bp, Waitomo and Gull apps and the supermarket fuel schemes in detail.

body: Foodstuffs' Club+ replaced the New World Clubcard in 2026. It earns Club+ Dollars, each worth $1, at 0.75% of your spend at New World and 0.38% at Four Square; PAK'nSAVE shoppers can spend them but do not earn them. Club+ also gives fuel discounts. Woolworths' Everyday Rewards works the same way with points, vouchers and bp fuel discounts. Grocer, an independent app, compares grocery prices across the major supermarkets and keeps price history and shopping lists. It rated 3.6 from 128 New Zealand ratings and was last updated in December 2025, so treat its prices as a guide and check the shelf.

sections.heading: Cheaper nights without an app
body: DOC sets the campsite fees: basic campsites are free, standard campsites cost $10 to $20 per adult a night, and serviced campsites $25 per adult unpowered. Individual campsites can differ, so check each one. Members of the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association pay $252 in the first year and can then stay at NZMCA Parks for $5 per adult a night.

For hostels, Hostelworld (4.8 from 5,114) compares beds and YHA advertises a 10% saving for its members. A campervan relocation is the cheapest vehicle of all: Imoova lists them from $1 a day, though fuel is usually extra and the dates are fixed.

body: In Auckland, AT Mobile (4.5 from 32,728) tops up an AT HOP card, and Auckland Transport caps fares at $50 over seven days with AT HOP and at $20 a day with a contactless bank card. Plan around those caps for a city stay before or after the road trip.

If you share a van, Splitwise (4.4 from 689) or Tricount (4.8 from 294) records who paid for what and settles up at the end, and TravelSpend (4.8 from 157) tracks spending against a daily budget. Wise (4.8 from 23,432) converts money from an overseas account with fees from 0.22%.

body: We ranked the apps by the size of the cost they attack, starting with accommodation and fuel. Ratings come from the New Zealand App Store on 20 October 2026; deal terms, fees and caps come from each company's own page that day, and price data from MBIE and Stats NZ.
Deals change often and some are seasonal. We describe each as the company does, and a feature not mentioned here is not a claim that an app lacks it.

faq: What is the best way to save money travelling New Zealand?

Cut the two biggest costs first: sleep at DOC campsites, where fees ran from $5 to $25 per adult a night at sites with a published rate, and use Gaspy to find cheaper fuel. KiwiCamping, which we make, shows DOC campsite fees and lets you filter by cost.
Which apps give discounts in New Zealand?

Supermarket apps such as Club+ and Everyday Rewards give points and fuel discounts, First Table gives 50% off food at early sittings, Too Good To Go sells unsold food cheaply, and Rankers offers 10% off Bluebridge ferries and 10% to 15% off some activities.

Compare Interislander and Bluebridge for your date.
