can-i-sleep-in-my-car-in-new-zealand.title: Can I Sleep in My Car in New Zealand? (2026 Rules)
can-i-sleep-in-my-car-in-new-zealand.description: Resting to beat driver fatigue is exempt, but a planned night in a car on council land is a $400 fine unless a bylaw names the spot. 2026 rules, by land type.
can-i-sleep-in-my-car-in-new-zealand.imageAlt: Lakeside rest area at Lake Taupō with a picnic table and a single car parked beneath the trees
can-i-sleep-in-my-car-in-new-zealand.intro: Sometimes: it depends on whether you are resting or camping, and on who manages the land you are parked on. The Freedom Camping Act 2011 excludes resting or sleeping at the roadside in a vehicle to avoid driver fatigue, but a planned night in a car on public land counts as freedom camping, and on council land that needs a certified self-contained vehicle unless a bylaw names a spot for other vehicles. An ordinary car lacks the fixed toilet and tanks a green warrant requires, and since 7 June 2026 an old blue warrant no longer counts either. In practice a car can sleep legally at a campground, on private land with permission, at the rare council site opened to non-certified vehicles, or on conservation land DOC has not restricted.

sections.heading: Resting to stay safe is not the same as camping
body: Section 5 of the Freedom Camping Act 2011 defines freedom camping as camping outside a camping ground, using a tent or a motor vehicle, within 200 metres of a formed road, of anywhere vehicles can reach, or of the sea or a harbour. It then carves out three things: temporary and short-term parking, day-trip excursions, and resting or sleeping at the roadside in a motor vehicle to avoid driver fatigue.

The Act gives no clock time for when a rest becomes a night, so an officer judges what they see. Pulling over because you are too tired to drive safely is the situation the exclusion protects. Picking a pretty spot at dusk and setting up to sleep until morning is the situation it does not, and stopping early rather than pushing on tired is the right call either way.
tips: Tired is a reason to stop, not a loophole
The Act sets no minimum or maximum rest time
Leave in the morning, not the next evening

sections.heading: Why a car runs into trouble on council land
body: On land a council manages, section 10 allows freedom camping in a tent or a self-contained vehicle unless a bylaw restricts or prohibits it. A vehicle that is not self-contained can camp only where a bylaw made under section 11A names the area, or under other legislation. Camping in a non-certified vehicle anywhere else is an infringement offence, and so is parking up to do it.

Self-contained now means a green warrant, which needs a toilet fixed inside the vehicle plus water, wastewater and rubbish systems. A saloon, a hatchback or a van carrying a portable toilet does not qualify. Christchurch City Council says it plainly: if you are sleeping in a vehicle without facilities, you need to stay in a camping ground that has facilities you can use.

Tents are no easier in the biggest city. Auckland Council states that freedom camping in tents in public places is not allowed in Auckland, and its roadside permission applies only to certified self-contained vehicles.
tips: No fixed toilet means no green warrant
A blue sticker has not counted since 7 June 2026
Check the council before the night, not at midnight

sections.heading: The few places that open a spot to cars
body: A council can say yes to non-certified vehicles, but it has to name the area in a bylaw, and few do. Central Hawke's Bay's 2024 bylaw lets any vehicle or tent camp at Pourerere Beach Road and at Te Paerahi Beach in Pōrangahau, and Pourerere needs a ballot permit from mid-December to the end of February. Whakatāne's 2024 bylaw permits vehicles that are not self-contained at Aniwhenua Reserve near Murupara, for a maximum of seven nights in any four-week period.

Even where a spot is open to cars, it comes with conditions a council car park would never carry. Central Hawke's Bay limits any one area to three vehicles and three tents, requires you to leave by noon and sets a one-week stand-down before you return to the same place. The council's web page can lag its bylaw, and its page still mentions blue stickers, which stopped counting on 7 June 2026, so read the schedule rather than the summary.
tips: Only the bylaw's named sites count
Expect stand-down periods and vehicle caps
Permits can be ballot-based in peak season

sections.heading: Conservation land, where cars have more room
body: On public conservation land the default runs the other way. Section 15 of the Act permits freedom camping on land DOC manages unless a notice or another law restricts it, and DOC's page says you can freedom camp on public conservation land except where it is specifically prohibited or restricted. Many of DOC's notices cover car parks beside tracks, road ends and visitor centres, so the notice list matters more than the type of vehicle.

Two limits catch people sleeping in cars. DOC-administered scenic and recreation reserves are closed to freedom camping unless DOC provides or approves a campsite, under the Reserves Act 1977, and DOC will not allow dogs to camp with you in a national park. DOC campsites are the straightforward alternative: basic ones cost nothing, and standard ones charge $10 to $20 per adult per night and list vehicle access.
tips: DOC reserves are closed unless a campsite is provided
Self-contained-only notices still apply to cars
Dogs cannot camp with you in national parks

sections.heading: What a mistake costs
body: Camping in a vehicle that is not self-contained on council land, or parking up to do it, is a $400 infringement. So is breaking a bylaw prohibition or restriction, and so is sleeping in a certified vehicle with more people than its certificate allows. Failing to display a warrant card where one is required is $200, refusing to leave when an enforcement officer tells you to is $600, and damaging the area or leaving waste outside a bin is $800. The amounts are set by the Freedom Camping (Penalties for Infringement Offences) Regulations 2023.

A notice sets a payment deadline, 28 days from delivery on the Act's default form, and explains how to challenge it. A court can fine more than the notice amount, up to $1,200 for a $400 offence. Officers can also seize and impound a vehicle where that is reasonable and necessary, for example to protect public health, wildlife or access or to stop an ongoing offence, and if you are with the vehicle they must first tell you to stop and warn you.

If the car is a rental, the notice usually goes to the company. A hire agreement can make you liable for the fee and an administration charge, and the company must send you the notice within five working days before charging the card you left at pick-up.
tips: $400 for a non-certified vehicle on council land
$600 for refusing to leave when told
Rental companies can pass the fee to your card

sections.heading: Emergencies, housing and bad weather
body: The Act includes defences where breaking the rule was necessary to save or protect life or health, prevent injury or serious damage to property, or avoid damage to the environment, and your conduct was reasonable (section 22). A medical problem or a storm that closes the road can fit. Ordinary tiredness is handled by the fatigue exclusion in section 5, not by a defence.

The Act also says a person is not freedom camping if they cannot live in appropriate residential accommodation and are living in a tent or vehicle as a result, unless they are in New Zealand on a visitor visa. Councils treat this as a welfare issue: Auckland Council points anyone worried about a person living in a vehicle to its community safety and support page.
tips: Genuine emergencies have a statutory defence
Fatigue is excluded, not defended
Welfare concerns go to the council's support page

sections.heading: Where to sleep legally instead
body: A camping ground is the simplest answer, and the Act defines it broadly: a ground registered under the Camping-Grounds Regulations 1985 or any site where a fee is payable for camping. That covers holiday parks, council-run grounds and DOC campsites that charge. Christchurch points people in cars and tents to its four council-operated camping grounds at Duvauchelle, Okains Bay, Pigeon Bay and Spencer Beach.

Private land with the owner's permission falls outside the Act, because it applies only to land managed by councils, DOC, LINZ and, by bylaw, NZTA. A friend's driveway or a farm that has said yes is lawful in a way a street never is. Agree the details first, so the arrangement is an invitation rather than an assumption.
tips: Registered grounds and paid sites count as camping grounds
Basic DOC campsites cost nothing
Written permission is the safest kind

sections.heading: Checking before you shut the door
body: Photograph the sign at the entrance, read the vehicle requirement and stay limit, and look at the council's freedom camping page or bylaw map the evening before. Auckland lists 58 prohibited areas and 20 restricted ones, so even a city that allows roadside nights can ban a particular street. If an officer asks you to leave, go: refusing is its own $600 offence.

KiwiCamping, an iPhone app, carries DOC's freedom-camping notices by district alongside its campsite and hut data, with dump stations, filters, saved places and trips. Place details, saved places and guides work without signal, while map tiles, routing, weather and photos need it, so look up a campsite before you lose reception. The notices are DOC's conservation-land ones rather than council bylaws, so the council's own page still decides a street or car park.
tips: Photograph the sign on arrival
Check the council map the evening before
Leave when an officer says so

sections.heading: The short version
body: Resting because you are too tired to drive is fine. Camping is a different act, and a car without a green warrant has no right to a council street or car park overnight, with a few named exceptions.
Use a campground or a DOC campsite, ask a landowner, or find the rare council site that welcomes ordinary vehicles. Pack a fallback so a full site never turns into a fine.

faq: Can I sleep in my caravan on the road in NZ?

Councils apply the freedom camping rules to caravans as well as vans, and Auckland's rules cover a vehicle or caravan on its land. On a council road you need a certified self-contained set-up unless the council has named the spot for others, and the street itself may be prohibited or time-limited. Auckland allows certified vehicles on most roadsides for two nights, while Christchurch bans freedom camping in its central city, so check the bylaw for the exact street.
Can you camp in NZ without a self-contained vehicle?

Yes, but not on most public land. In a council area the Act permits tents and certified self-contained vehicles, so a car or van without a green warrant needs a campground, private land with permission, a conservation area DOC has not restricted, or a site a council has named for it, such as Pourerere Beach Road in Central Hawke's Bay.
Can I sleep in my car at a rest area or lay-by?

A short rest to avoid driver fatigue is excluded from freedom camping, so pulling over to sleep because you are too tired to drive is not an offence under the Act. A planned night is different, and the owner matters: a rest area that NZTA manages is NZTA land, which falls under the Act only if a council has declared it by bylaw with NZTA's written consent. Read the sign for the owner's rules.

can-i-camp-anywhere-on-doc-land.title: Can I Camp Anywhere on DOC Land in NZ? (2026 Rules)
can-i-camp-anywhere-on-doc-land.description: No: DOC reserves ban camping outside campsites, other conservation land allows it unless a notice says no, and Great Walks need booked sites. 2026 rules.
can-i-camp-anywhere-on-doc-land.imageAlt: Open grassy DOC campsite flat with a picnic table among native trees at Siberia Flat, Kahurangi National Park
can-i-camp-anywhere-on-doc-land.intro: No. Camping on land managed by the Department of Conservation is allowed in some places and banned in others, and the rule that decides it is the kind of land you are on and whether DOC has restricted camping there. Under the Freedom Camping Act 2011, public conservation land is open to freedom camping unless DOC has prohibited or restricted it by notice, but DOC-administered scenic and recreation reserves are closed to camping outside designated campsites, and national parks and Great Walks carry their own limits. DOC publishes its banned and restricted places district by district, so the list is the thing to check.

sections.heading: Three kinds of DOC land, three different answers
body: The Act defines conservation land as land DOC controls or manages under the Conservation Act 1987, the National Parks Act 1980, the Reserves Act 1977 or the Wildlife Act 1953. On that land, section 15 says freedom camping is permitted unless a DOC notice under section 17, or another enactment, restricts or prohibits it. That makes conservation parks and ordinary conservation areas the most open category, with notices carving out the exceptions.

Reserves work the other way round. Under section 44 of the Reserves Act, nobody may use a reserve or a vehicle or tent on it for personal accommodation without the Minister's consent, except in set-apart camping grounds and a few other defined cases. DOC says freedom camping is prohibited in every DOC-administered reserve that is not listed as allowing self-contained vehicles, and national parks add their own track-by-track rules.
tips: Conservation areas: open unless a notice says no
Reserves: closed unless a campsite is provided
National parks: read the park or track page

sections.heading: DOC's notice list, district by district
body: DOC keeps a page of conservation areas where freedom camping is prohibited or restricted, grouped by district from Northland to Southland and Fiordland, with an interactive map and a PDF notice for each site. The notices are the legal instrument, so a site can be banned outright, limited to certified self-contained vehicles, capped at a number of nights in a calendar month, or restricted to certain hours or seasons. The page adds that not every restricted area has a sign.

The examples show the range. In Northland, Cape Reinga and Tapotupotu in the Te Paki reserve are prohibited, while Bland Bay is open to self-contained vehicles only. In the Central North Island, Whakapapa Village and most Tongariro National Park car parks are prohibited, but Pillars of Hercules and Umukarikari in Kaimanawa Forest Park allow certified vehicles for four nights in a calendar month. Franz Josef Glacier road car parks on the West Coast and the Kepler Track and The Divide car parks in Fiordland are prohibited.

Some entries add hours and seasons. Tukino Mountain Road in Tongariro National Park allows certified vehicles only from 5 pm to 9 am from 1 November to 30 April, and Owaka Heads in the Catlins applies a similar overnight window from 2 October to 31 March. In Canterbury, Quailburn and Round Bush are restricted to four nights a month but allow vehicles that are not self-contained, and in Otago, Rum Curries in the Gibbston Conservation Area is limited to tents for two nights a month.
tips: Look up the exact site, not the district
Four nights a month is a common cap
Some notices allow non-certified vehicles

sections.heading: Away from the road: national parks and backcountry
body: The Act's definition of freedom camping reaches only as far as 200 metres from a road, a vehicle-accessible area, a Great Walks Track or the sea. Further in, the rules come from the park or the track. They differ. On the Round the Mountain Track in Tongariro National Park, DOC says camping outside designated campsites is allowed except within 500 m of the Tongariro Northern Circuit and within 200 m of the Round the Mountain Track itself.

On the Rees and Dart tracks in Mount Aspiring National Park, DOC's brochure says camping is allowed everywhere except the fragile alpine and subalpine areas between Shelter Rock Hut and Dart Hut and on the privately owned Rees Valley Station, and that the Cascade Saddle Route is limited to the toilet area at Cascade Creek. In Abel Tasman National Park, the trip sheet says camping is permitted only in designated campsites and hammocks are not allowed.

A few rules apply nearly everywhere. DOC's freedom camping page lists the basics: obey camping restriction signs, manage your waste including human waste, light no fires, do not damage plants or animals, and be considerate. Its low-impact guide asks you to use the toilet provided, and to follow its poo-in-a-loo guidance when there is none.
tips: Beyond 200 m, the park's own rules apply
Hammocks are banned at Abel Tasman campsites
Never assume a quiet flat is allowed

sections.heading: Great Walks: the place you sleep is part of the booking
body: DOC says freedom camping is generally not permitted near Great Walks tracks, and the Great Walks themselves are built around booked huts and campsites. Camping is not permitted on the Milford Track at all. Except for Milford and Paparoa, every Great Walk offers camping near huts or in designated areas, and DOC describes nearly 60 Great Walk campsites with toilets, handwashing sinks and a water supply.

At Lake Waikaremoana the DOC page says camping on the track is permitted only at the designated campsites, and on the Abel Tasman Coast Track every hut and campsite must be booked all year, with a penalty fee or a request to leave for people without a valid booking or at the wrong site. DOC's booking terms set the penalty rate for unbooked use at the normal fee plus a full adult fee, and promise no guaranteed access without a booking except as emergency shelter in adverse conditions.
tips: Camping is not allowed on the Milford Track
Book the exact campsite named on your ticket
Unbooked use is charged at the penalty rate

sections.heading: Campsite categories and what they cost
body: DOC campsites fall into serviced, standard, basic, backcountry and Great Walk categories. Basic campsites are free and have very limited facilities, standard ones charge adults $10 to $20 a night, and serviced unpowered sites are $25. Child fees are roughly half, infants are free, and backcountry and Great Walk prices vary, so each campsite's own page is the reference.

DOC charges two adults if you book or occupy a campsite you do not intend to use, for example by leaving a vacant tent or vehicle on it. Each campsite page tells you whether the site can be booked or is first-come, and DOC's terms apply the penalty rate to unbooked use of a bookable site. Campsites are the straightforward answer where a district's notices rule out camping by the roadside.
tips: Basic campsites cost nothing
Standard campsites charge per adult
A vacant tent is charged as two adults

sections.heading: Fines, notices and the rules that bite
body: Camping where a DOC notice prohibits or restricts it is a $400 infringement, and so is making preparations to camp there by pitching a tent or parking up to do it. Failing to display a warrant card on land restricted to self-contained vehicles is $200, refusing to leave when an enforcement officer requires it is $600, and damaging land, plants or structures or leaving waste outside a bin is $800. These amounts are in the Freedom Camping (Penalties for Infringement Offences) Regulations 2023, and DOC officers can also seize and impound a vehicle in the circumstances the Act sets out.

Other DOC rules sit alongside the fines. You cannot camp or visit a hut on conservation land with a pet unless DOC has approved it in writing, even if the pet stays in your vehicle, and dogs must never camp with you in a national park. A permit from DOC is required to fly a drone on public conservation land, and fire rules at campsites are strict, so check the campfire and fire season advice before you light anything.
tips: $400 for camping against a notice
$200 for no warrant card where required
Pets need DOC's written approval

sections.heading: Cars, vans and tents on DOC land
body: The vehicle you are in matters less under DOC's freedom camping rules than on council land. Section 15 lets any freedom camper stay on open conservation land, certified self-contained or not, unless the notice says self-contained only. Where a notice does say that, a warrant card must be displayed, and since 7 June 2026 only a green warrant counts.

A tent or a car without a green warrant is therefore workable in an open conservation area, at a DOC campsite, or on the few restricted sites that allow non-certified vehicles. It is not workable in a scenic or recreation reserve, at a listed prohibited car park, or on the Great Walks. If you are unsure whether a patch of land is a reserve, a conservation area or a national park, the DOC page for the place states it.
tips: Green warrants only on self-contained-only land
Tents and cars work on open conservation land
Reserves and listed car parks do not

sections.heading: Checking on the day
body: Look for the camping restriction signs at the entrance: one means overnight camping is prohibited within 200 m, the other means only certified self-contained vehicles may camp. Then check DOC's prohibited and restricted list and the place's own page for alerts, because closures after storms change faster than printed information.

KiwiCamping is an iPhone app with DOC campsite and hut data, DOC's freedom-camping notices by district, filters, saved places and trips, so you can look up the notice for the area before you drive in. Place details, saved places and guides work without signal; map tiles, routing, weather and photos need it. DOC's page and the sign on site decide, so treat the app as a prompt to check.
tips: Check DOC's list and the place's alerts
Read the sign at the entrance
Save the notice before you lose signal

sections.heading: The short version
body: You cannot camp anywhere on DOC land. Open conservation areas allow it until a notice says otherwise, reserves allow it only at designated campsites, and Great Walks require booked huts or campsites.
Check the district notice, the park or track page and the sign at the entrance, and keep a DOC campsite in mind as the fallback if the first option turns out to be restricted.

faq: Can you freedom camp on DOC land?

Yes, on much public conservation land, unless DOC has prohibited or restricted it. DOC publishes a list of prohibited and restricted conservation areas by district, and its scenic and recreation reserves are closed to freedom camping outside campsites. Obey the signs, manage your waste, light no fires and do not damage plants or animals.
Is wild camping legal in New Zealand?

Camping away from campsites is lawful in some places and not others. Within 200 m of a road or the sea on public land it is freedom camping, governed by the Act and bylaws and notices, and on private land you need the owner's permission. Further into the backcountry the park's rules apply, such as Tongariro's 500 m buffer around the Northern Circuit or Abel Tasman's designated campsites only.
Can I camp on DOC land in a car or van that is not self-contained?

Often yes, on open conservation land, because DOC's notices restrict some sites to self-contained vehicles but the Act does not require certification everywhere on DOC land. You cannot camp in scenic or recreation reserves outside designated campsites, at listed prohibited car parks or on Great Walk tracks. Some DOC sites, such as Quailburn and Round Bush in Canterbury, specifically allow non-certified vehicles for four nights a month.

can-i-park-overnight-at-a-beach-in-new-z.title: Can I Park Overnight at a Beach in NZ? (2026 Rules)
can-i-park-overnight-at-a-beach-in-new-z.description: Usually not: most council and DOC beach car parks ban overnight stays or allow only certified self-contained vehicles for a few nights. 2026 rules.
can-i-park-overnight-at-a-beach-in-new-z.imageAlt: Orange sand and gentle surf at Langs Beach in Northland on a bright day
can-i-park-overnight-at-a-beach-in-new-z.intro: Usually not, and it depends on who manages the car park, reserve or road beside the sand. Freedom camping is lawful only where the Freedom Camping Act 2011, a council bylaw or a DOC notice allows it, so many beach car parks and reserves ban overnight stays, some allow certified self-contained vehicles for a few nights, and a few use permits or ballots. A beach is not a special category with a rule of its own, and a blue warrant has not counted since 7 June 2026.

sections.heading: A beach has no rule of its own
body: The Freedom Camping Act 2011 treats camping within 200 metres of the mean low-water springs line of the sea or a harbour as freedom camping, the same as within 200 metres of a formed road. Which rule applies then depends on who controls the land you are standing on: a council, DOC, LINZ or, if it is private, an owner whose permission you need.

That is why neighbouring beaches can have opposite answers. Council reserves are caught by section 44 of the Reserves Act, which bars personal accommodation on a reserve without the Minister's consent. DOC lists its own banned and restricted car parks, and LINZ land is closed to freedom camping unless a LINZ notice permits it. Coastal roads and car parks outside reserves are the places a council bylaw usually decides.
tips: Find the manager first, then the rule
Reserves are closed unless a campsite is provided
The sign beats any listing

sections.heading: Three councils on the coast
body: Christchurch has a City Coastal Restricted Zone running from Waimairi Beach to South New Brighton, including North Beach, North New Brighton and New Brighton. Inside it, only certified self-contained vehicles may camp, for no more than four nights in any 30 days and no more than two in one place, with the second spot at least 500 m from the first. Some coastal sites are fully prohibited: the New Brighton north and south ramp car parks, the Southshore Spit, and the North Beach car park from 7 pm Friday to 7 pm Sunday between 1 October and 1 May.

Wellington City bans camping on all land managed under the Reserves Act 1977 and the Wellington Town Belt Act 2016, which the council says includes a number of coastal car parks. Its designated sites for certified self-contained vehicles include the Evans Bay Marina car park on the harbour and the Te Kopahou Visitors Centre car park on the south coast, which is not suitable for vehicles over 7 m or caravans.

Auckland allows certified self-contained vehicles on most council roadsides and car parks but prohibits freedom camping at 58 named areas, at council reserves and in regional parks. Paid camping is available in designated areas of regional parks instead. In Ōhope, Whakatāne District Council's bylaw prohibits freedom camping at Mahy Reserve and Wharekura East Reserve, and along Muriwai Drive in Whakatāne.
tips: Christchurch coastal zone: four nights in 30 days
Reserves and many coastal car parks are banned
Check the schedule, not just the headline

sections.heading: Coastal car parks DOC has closed
body: DOC lists coastal sites where freedom camping is prohibited, and the list reads like a tour of well-known beaches. In Coromandel, the Cathedral Cove car park and the Waikawau Beach car parks are prohibited. At Cape Kidnappers in Hawke's Bay the track amenity area is closed, and in the Catlins the Papatowai picnic point is too. On the Marlborough Sounds foreshore, Broughton Bay, Anakoha Bay and Tom Canes Bay are prohibited, and so are Momorangi Bay and Ngakuta Bay on Queen Charlotte Drive.

Some sites sit in the middle. DOC allows certified self-contained vehicles at Kawatiri Beach Reserve at the Buller River mouth for four nights in a calendar month, and at Castlepoint for four nights a month between 5 pm and 9 am from 1 November to 30 April. At Owaka Heads in the Catlins a similar 5 pm to 9 am window runs from 2 October to 31 March. DOC also notes that not every restricted area has a sign.
tips: Prohibited and restricted look the same from the road
Hours and seasons can cut the allowed window
DOC's list names each car park

sections.heading: Seasons, ballots and night caps
body: A few beaches manage demand with permits. Central Hawke's Bay District Council requires a permit to camp at Pourerere Beach from mid-December to the end of February, allocated by ballot, with applications due each year by the end of October. Its bylaw allows vehicles that are not self-contained and tents at Pourerere Beach Road and Te Paerahi Beach in Pōrangahau, which makes them unusual, but they carry bylaw conditions such as a leave-by-noon rule and a one-week stand-down.

The council's web page still mentions blue stickers, which stopped counting for freedom camping on 7 June 2026, and it gives a permit year that looks out of date. Treat the bylaw and the council's current permit page as the sources, and apply early rather than turning up in January hoping for a space.
tips: Ballot permits close around the end of October
Leave by noon and respect the stand-down
Use the bylaw, not an old listing

sections.heading: Tides, tsunami and the edge of the sand
body: Check tide times before you park on or near sand, because a car left below the high-tide line can be reached by water in the night. Driving on beaches has its own rules and is not covered here. Park on firm ground above the debris line, leave room to drive out without crossing soft sand, and keep access clear for other users.

Much of the coast sits in a tsunami zone. Christchurch changed its evacuation zones in October 2026 and now has one blue zone for Christchurch and Banks Peninsula, and it tells people to leave the zone immediately if an earthquake is long or strong, if the sea level changes suddenly or unusual noises come from the sea, or if an official warning arrives. The official rule is long or strong, get gone: move to high ground or inland straight away instead of waiting for a warning.
tips: Check the tide table before parking
Know your way to high ground on arrival
Long or strong, get gone

sections.heading: Fines, tents and what an officer sees
body: On council land, camping where a bylaw prohibits or restricts it is a $400 infringement, as is camping in a vehicle that is not self-contained. Failing to display a warrant card is $200, refusing to leave when an enforcement officer tells you to is $600, and damaging the area or leaving waste outside a bin is $800. A court can fine more, and officers can impound a vehicle where the Act allows.

Waste is a common beach offence. Christchurch says it is not permitted to go to the toilet beside the road, in the bush, on the ground, on the beach or in a river, creek or lake, and the coastal zone gets regular monitoring and enforcement. Christchurch also says its parking spaces are for vehicles only, so awnings, tables, chairs and washing lines belong in a campground.

Tents are no easier at the coast. Auckland does not allow tent freedom camping in public places, and Christchurch tells tent campers and people sleeping in vehicles without facilities to use a camping ground. Fires are a risk on dry beaches, and Christchurch advises a gas cooker instead of a campfire.
tips: $400 for camping against a bylaw
$800 for waste outside a bin
Keep gear inside the parking bay

sections.heading: Where to stay instead
body: Beach camping that is allowed usually means a campground. Christchurch names Spencer Beach Top 10 Holiday Park and South Brighton Holiday Park as the closest grounds to its coastal zone, and Auckland offers paid camping in designated areas of its regional parks. In Wellington, certified self-contained vehicles can pay for overnight parking at the Barnett Street car park on the waterfront.

DOC campsites on the coast are the other reliable option. They carry categories and booking rules on each campsite page, and a booked place removes the guesswork of notices and signs. Holiday parks and council-operated grounds also take vehicles that are not certified, which is the main reason to choose one over a car park.
tips: Spencer Beach and South Brighton near Christchurch
Barnett Street in Wellington is paid and certified-only
Book DOC beach campsites ahead in summer

sections.heading: Checking on the day
body: Read the sign at the entrance, photograph it, and look at the council's bylaw map or DOC's list before you set up. If a car park is full, do not park along the access road, because overflow lines are what get beach sites closed.

Beach car parks run into DOC notices all the time, so KiwiCamping's DOC campsite and hut data, its freedom-camping notices by district, filters and saved places are the first things to open. Place details, saved places and guides work without signal, while map tiles, routing, weather and photos need it. Council bylaws are not in the app, so the council page decides when the beach is council land.
tips: Photograph the sign when you arrive
Do not create an overflow line
Council bylaws sit with the council

sections.heading: The short version
body: A beach car park is not a free campsite. It is council land, DOC land or a reserve, and each answers differently: usually no, sometimes yes for certified self-contained vehicles for a few nights, and occasionally yes by permit.
Decide before dark, keep a campground as the fallback, and treat the tide table and the route to high ground as part of the plan rather than an afterthought.

faq: Can you camp on the beach in NZ?

Not freely. Beaches are managed by councils, DOC or private owners, and freedom camping is allowed only where the Act, a bylaw or a DOC notice permits it. Many beachside reserves and car parks prohibit it, some allow certified self-contained vehicles for a few nights, and a few, like Pourerere Beach in Central Hawke's Bay, use a permit ballot over summer.
Can I park overnight at a beach without a self-contained vehicle?

Usually not on council or DOC land, because the Act allows freedom camping on council land only in tents or certified self-contained vehicles unless a bylaw names the site. The exceptions are rare and carry conditions, such as the two Central Hawke's Bay beaches. A campground or a DOC campsite is the safer option.
Is it legal to sleep on a beach in New Zealand?

Sleeping in a tent or a vehicle within 200 m of the sea on public land is freedom camping, so those rules apply. Bedding down with no tent or vehicle is outside the Act's definition, but reserves still bar personal accommodation without the Minister's consent, councils and DOC set their own limits, and Auckland allows no tent freedom camping in public places. Ask the owner if the beach is private.

can-i-camp-on-a-farm-or-private-land-in-.title: Can I Camp on a Farm or Private Land in NZ? (2026)
can-i-camp-on-a-farm-or-private-land-in-.description: Yes, with the landowner's permission. The Freedom Camping Act does not cover private land, but the Trespass Act 1980 does. 2026 guide to gates, stock and fire.
can-i-camp-on-a-farm-or-private-land-in-.imageAlt: Wooden farm gate across a grassy farm track with paddocks and fencing beyond, near Matamata in the Waikato
can-i-camp-on-a-farm-or-private-land-in-.intro: Yes, but only with the landowner's permission, and the Freedom Camping Act 2011 does not apply. That Act covers land managed by councils, DOC, LINZ and, by bylaw, NZTA, so on a farm the owner's say decides, backed by the Trespass Act 1980, which makes it an offence to stay after being warned to leave. No green warrant or council bylaw governs a paddock, but the owner can set any conditions they like.

sections.heading: Permission is the whole rule
body: Being on private land without the occupier's permission is trespass. Under the Trespass Act 1980 it becomes an offence in two ways: refusing or neglecting to leave after an occupier warns you to go, and returning within two years of a warning to stay off. The warning can be spoken or in writing, and the occupier includes anyone acting under the owner's authority, such as a farm worker or manager.

The penalty for either offence is a fine of up to $1,000 or up to three months in prison, and only the occupier or a constable can bring the charge. You must give your name and address if the occupier or a constable asks, and refusing or giving false details carries a fine of up to $500. 'Private land' in the Act includes land held under a lease or occupied by someone, so a leaseholder can say no even where the Crown owns the title.
tips: A yes from the occupier is the only permission that counts
Get it before you arrive, not at the gate
You can be warned to stay off for two years

sections.heading: Why the freedom camping rules mostly fall away
body: The Act applies to a council's own land, conservation land, LINZ land and NZTA land that a council has declared by bylaw. A farm is none of these. Southland District Council says its freedom camping bylaw applies to public places, not conservation land or private property, and that camping on private property needs the owner's consent. Christchurch says the same of its bylaw, and Auckland defines freedom camping as staying on council-controlled public land.

So the infringement fees do not apply, and the green warrant requirement does not either: nothing in the Act obliges a vehicle on a farm to be certified self-contained. An owner may still ask for it, because they may want a toilet in the vehicle. Clutha District Council notes that tent camping is allowed on private land with the landowner's permission, in contrast to its public land, where tents are limited to campgrounds and DOC campsites.
tips: No fixed toilet needed by law on private land
Owners can still require a certified vehicle
Councils' freedom camping bylaws stop at the boundary

sections.heading: Asking, and being asked to pay
body: Ask the person who occupies the land, not a neighbour or a passer-by, and say how many people, how many vehicles, how many nights and where you would park. Many farmers say yes to one or two people for a night if asked politely, and some will name a paddock or a river flat. Treat the answer as the rules for the night, and leave before you are asked.

Farm stays and online host listings turn that permission into a booking. A listing is the owner's invitation, so keep the confirmation and the directions, because gates and tracks on a farm are not signposted like a campground. If the owner charges, the arrangement is a business matter: the Camping-Grounds Regulations 1985 define a camping ground as land used, for rent or other reward, to house two or more independent parties in temporary living places, and a ground like that needs a registration from the local authority. Ask the host whether theirs is registered if you want reassurance.
tips: Say how many, how long and where
Keep the host's confirmation
Registration applies to paid grounds with two or more parties

sections.heading: Stock, gates and dogs
body: The Trespass Act treats disturbing farm animals as an offence in its own right. Disturbing horses, cattle, sheep, pigs or poultry on private land by means of a dog, a weapon or a vehicle carries a fine of up to $300 or a month in prison, and wilfully or recklessly disturbing them carries up to $500 or a month in prison. Park where the owner points, away from stock, and do not drive across paddocks with animals in them.

Leave gates as you find them. The Act separately makes it an offence for a trespasser to wilfully leave a shut gate open, or an open gate shut, on private land, with a fine of up to $200. The practical rule is the same for invited visitors: open gates stay open and shut gates stay shut unless the owner has said otherwise. Dogs belong on a lead or in the vehicle, and a farmer is entitled to refuse them.
tips: Park away from stock
Leave gates as you found them
Dogs on a lead or left at home

sections.heading: Fire, spray and poison on rural land
body: A farm is working land. WorkSafe says farmers are not responsible for the safety of people crossing non-work areas away from farm buildings, but they must manage risks from work carried out in the area, such as spraying, and visitors must take reasonable care and follow reasonable instructions. Ask about recent spraying, effluent ponds, bulls, electric fences and tracks before you set up, and accept the answer.

Fire is the owner's decision as well as the law's. Check the current fire season for the district and ask the owner before any campfire, and rely on a gas cooker when in doubt. DOC's pest control on conservation land uses 1080 with warning signs at track entrances, and DOC says dogs are highly susceptible to it, so a farm that borders conservation land is worth asking about before you bring a dog. On private land, laying poison or setting traps without the occupier's authority is an offence.
tips: Ask about spraying, ponds and electric fences
Use a gas cooker unless the owner says otherwise
Check for 1080 warnings near conservation boundaries

sections.heading: Water, waste and weeds
body: Farm water is usually untreated. DOC's own guidance for campsites says untreated water should be boiled before use, and the same sensible rule applies to a farm tank or stream. Carry your own drinking water and ask which source, if any, is meant for people.

Take rubbish with you, empty tanks at a public dump station before you arrive rather than after you leave, and use a toilet on board or ask the owner where to go. Clean gear matters on rural land: DOC asks campers to clean tents and gear between locations to stop weeds, mud and pests being carried from place to place.
tips: Boil or treat untreated water
Take every item of rubbish out
Clean tents and footwear between locations

sections.heading: Māori land, marae and land that only looks public
body: Māori freehold land is privately owned land. The Māori Land Court can hear claims for damages for trespass to it and can grant injunctions against actual or threatened trespass on Māori land or a Māori reservation, and marae and iwi campgrounds set their own terms. Ask the people who look after the place, pay any koha they request, and follow the tikanga they describe. The Freedom Camping Act also preserves rights of occupation such as nohoanga entitlements, which belong to the people who hold them.

Some land looks public but is not. LINZ land is closed to freedom camping unless a LINZ notice permits it, and a notice may not permit it on LINZ land held under a Crown lease or licence. High-country stations and similar leased land are therefore the leaseholder's to allow or refuse, with no right to camp for the public. A gate with no sign is not an invitation.
tips: Ask the marae or iwi organisation first
Koha is a gift, not a discount
Leased Crown land needs the leaseholder's yes

sections.heading: If you are told to leave, and what to do instead
body: If the owner says no, or asks you to go, leave calmly and promptly, and do not argue at the gate. Staying after a warning is an offence under section 3, and a written or spoken warning to stay off lasts two years. A trespass warning is the owner's tool and is usually avoided by a polite exit.

Have a fallback before you ask: a holiday park, a DOC campsite or a council site your vehicle qualifies for. In the KiwiCamping iPhone app, saved places can hold a host's address and gate notes beside the nearest DOC campsite or dump station, and filters help find that alternative. Saved places, place details and guides work without signal, but map tiles, routing, weather and photos need it, so write the access instructions down before the track turns to gravel.
tips: Leave when asked
Have a backup within an hour of arriving
Save the host's directions before signal drops

sections.heading: The short version
body: Private land is the one place the freedom camping rules do not reach, and the owner's permission is the rule. Ask first, follow the conditions the owner sets, look after gates and stock, and treat any refusal as final.
Treat a farm as a workplace and a favour rather than a campground, keep a backup site in mind, and the night usually goes well for everyone involved.

faq: Can I camp on private land in NZ?

Yes, if the occupier gives you permission. The Freedom Camping Act applies to public land managed by councils, DOC, LINZ and, by bylaw, NZTA, not to private farms. Without permission you can be warned to leave under the Trespass Act 1980, and refusing or returning within two years is an offence with a fine of up to $1,000 or three months in prison.
Do I need a self-contained vehicle to camp on a farm?

Not by law. The green warrant requirement belongs to the Freedom Camping Act, which does not apply to private land. The owner may still ask for a certified vehicle, a toilet or a particular spot, so ask what they require before you arrive and follow it.
Can I camp on a farm if I pay?

Yes, if the owner agrees. A farm that charges rent or other reward to two or more independent parties for camping falls within the Camping-Grounds Regulations 1985 definition of a camping ground, which usually means registering with the local council. A paid booking through a host listing is still a permission, so keep the confirmation.

can-i-park-a-campervan-on-the-street-ove.title: Can I Park a Campervan on the Street Overnight in NZ?
can-i-park-a-campervan-on-the-street-ove.description: Certified self-contained campervans may stay a few nights on some council streets, but many urban areas ban it and vans without a green warrant cannot (2026).
can-i-park-a-campervan-on-the-street-ove.imageAlt: A vintage bus converted into a turquoise and cream motorhome parked at the edge of a gravel road
can-i-park-a-campervan-on-the-street-ove.intro: It depends on the council and the street, and the answer is yes only for a certified self-contained campervan. Under the Freedom Camping Act 2011 each council decides by bylaw which of its streets allow overnight stays, which restrict them and which ban them, and a van without a green warrant cannot stay on a council street unless the bylaw names the spot. Ordinary parking rules such as time limits and clearways still apply on top, and since 7 June 2026 only a green warrant counts as self-contained.

sections.heading: A street belongs to someone, and that decides it
body: A council road counts as a local authority area under the Act, so the council's bylaw applies. Under section 10, a certified self-contained vehicle may freedom camp in a local authority area unless the bylaw restricts or prohibits it, and a vehicle that is not self-contained may only do so where a section 11A bylaw says so. That default is why some cities permit roadside nights almost everywhere while others ban them street by street.

State highways are different. NZTA land is covered by the Act only if a council has declared it a local authority area by bylaw, which needs NZTA's written consent. Elsewhere the NZTA's own powers over its land stand, so a highway shoulder or lay-by is not a safe assumption. A council can also make rules for its roads that sit outside the Act, such as time-limited parking, which is why a street can be legal for camping yet still carry a parking ticket.
tips: Council roads follow the council's bylaw
State highway land is rarely open
Parking rules sit on top of camping rules

sections.heading: Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and Queenstown
body: Auckland starts from permission. Certified self-contained vehicles can stay on most council-controlled public land, including most roadsides, for a maximum of two nights in the same road or off-road parking area, must vacate by 9 am on the day they leave, and cannot return to the same area for two weeks from 9 am on the day of departure. The bylaw prohibits freedom camping at 58 named areas, restricts 20 more with extra rules, and does not allow tents in public places. Waiheke has no public dump station, so the limit there is two nights and you must leave the island on the third day.

Wellington City allows certified self-contained vehicles but not in a single place for long: no more than four consecutive nights in a calendar month in any one area, and not within 500 m of an area where you have already stayed four nights. On-street parking is listed as a free option if you keep within any time limits, and the council's designated sites include 52 spaces at Evans Bay Marina and 16 at the Te Kopahou Visitors Centre car park. The Barnett Street car park next to Te Papa offers paid overnight parking to self-contained vehicles, except on Saturday nights.

Christchurch prohibits freedom camping on all council land in its central city, bounded by Bealey, Fitzgerald, Moorhouse, Deans and Harper avenues and Little Hagley Park, and in much of Akaroa. Elsewhere it allows certified vehicles in the areas its map marks for two nights, and within the City Coastal Restricted Zone any roadside works if you follow the limits of four nights in 30 days and no more than two in one place. Queenstown Lakes' Freedom Camping Bylaw 2025 prohibits it in urban areas, including on-road parking, and allows certified vehicles at designated car parks and on some rural roads.
tips: Auckland: two nights, out by 9 am
Wellington: four nights a month per area
Queenstown: urban streets are prohibited

sections.heading: Car parks: council, paid and supermarket
body: A council car park is council land, so the same bylaw applies, and many are excluded. Auckland says you cannot freedom camp in car parks where parking is reserved or where a fee is charged, such as council parking buildings, and Auckland Transport's car park terms state that overnight camping is prohibited. Wellington bans camping on land managed under the Reserves Act, which the council says includes a number of coastal and sports-field car parks.

A supermarket, shopping centre or pub car park is private land, so the Act does not apply and the owner's terms do. The owner or manager can ask you to leave, and under the Trespass Act 1980 a person who neglects or refuses to leave after being warned commits an offence. A sign saying no overnight parking is the owner's rule, and a manager's yes is not something to assume.
tips: Paid or reserved council car parks are usually out
Private car parks follow the owner's signs
Ask the manager, and take no for an answer

sections.heading: Time limits, clearways and the road rules underneath
body: Camping permission does not suspend the road rules. Under the Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004, a driver must not stop or park on a road without due care and reasonable consideration for other road users, or contrary to a sign or marking that prohibits, limits or restricts parking. Parking on a footpath is also prohibited, and so is obstructing a driveway, with a vehicle parked within 1 m of the prolongation of a driveway's side treated as obstructing it.

Parking within an intersection or within 6 m of one is prohibited unless signs or markings allow it, so a corner is a poor place to park a long van. Auckland points out that freedom campers must follow parking and road rules such as time limits and clearways, and the council's rules on noise, litter and fires. Park as the markings direct, keep awnings, chairs and tables inside the vehicle, and leave space for other drivers.
tips: Time limits and clearways still apply
Keep 6 m clear of intersections
Do not block a driveway

sections.heading: What it costs, and who gets the ticket
body: Camping where a bylaw prohibits or restricts it, or camping in a vehicle that is not self-contained, is a $400 infringement on council land, and so is staying with more people than the vehicle is certified for. Failing to display a warrant card is $200, refusing to leave when an officer requires it is $600, and damaging the area or leaving waste outside a bin is $800. Christchurch says it checks the warrant card in the front windscreen, the certificate or the Self-Contained Motor Vehicles Register.

A freedom camping infringement is separate from a parking ticket, and both can arrive for the same night. Wellington lets you pay or dispute a freedom camping fine through a service desk or email, and says it will only issue a waiver in special circumstances.

A rental company can pass a notice on to the hirer. A hire agreement may make you liable for the fee and an administration charge, and if it authorises a card debit the company must send you a copy of the notice within five working days of receiving it before charging the card.
tips: $400 for a non-certified van on council land
Parking tickets are separate
Rentals pass notices to the hirer

sections.heading: Dump stations, toilets and leaving a street clean
body: Councils judge a street stay by what it leaves behind. Auckland says the law requires you to dispose of human waste and grey water properly and to look for the blue dump station symbol, and Wellington lists public dump stations at Evans Bay Marina and Ngauranga Gorge. Christchurch says to empty a toilet only at a dump station and not to go to the toilet beside the road, on the ground, in the bush or on a beach.

Empty your tanks before you park rather than after, take rubbish with you or use a council bin, and do not spread out across several bays. Christchurch's bylaw prohibits taking more than one parking space with a camping vehicle, equipment or activities.
tips: Empty tanks before parking
One vehicle, one space
Use a dump station, not the roadside

sections.heading: When the street says no
body: If the street is banned, restricted or full, move on rather than squeezing in. Holiday parks and camping grounds are the usual answer for a van that is not certified, and Auckland tells people without a self-contained vehicle to use campgrounds that provide suitable facilities. DOC campsites near towns are another option, and each page states its own rules.

Paid overnight parking is an option for certified vehicles in some cities, such as Wellington's Barnett Street car park, whose price differs between two council pages at $30 and $35 per 24 hours, so check the current rate. Pick the next site before dark so a full lay-by never turns into a ticket.
tips: Holiday parks take non-certified vans
Paid city sites can be a good fallback
Choose your next stop before dark

sections.heading: Checking a street before you stay
body: Look for the signs, photograph them, and compare them with the council's page or bylaw map for that district, written the evening before. A street that was legal last year may now be in a prohibited area, and temporary restrictions can appear on the ground before any listing changes.

KiwiCamping, an iPhone app, keeps DOC campsite and hut data, dump stations, saved places, filters and trips in one place, and shows DOC's freedom-camping notices by district, which cover conservation land, not council streets. Place details, saved places and guides work without signal, but map tiles, routing, weather and photos need it, so save the alternatives you might want. The council's bylaw map is the source for a street.
tips: Photograph the sign on arrival
Council page first, then your app
Pre-select a second option

sections.heading: The short version
body: A certified self-contained campervan can stay overnight on some council streets for a night or a few, and not at all in many urban centres. A van without a green warrant needs a campground, a named non-certified site or private land with permission.
Read the sign, check the council's rules the evening before, empty your tanks, and keep the next site in mind in case the street is full.

faq: Can I park my campervan on the street in New Zealand?

Only where the council's bylaw allows it and your van is certified self-contained with a green warrant. Auckland allows it on most council roads for up to two nights, Wellington allows it with limits, and Queenstown Lakes prohibits it on urban streets. A van without a green warrant needs a campground or a site the council has named for it.
Can I park a campervan overnight in a supermarket car park in NZ?

A supermarket car park is private land, so the Freedom Camping Act does not apply and the owner sets the rules. If the signs prohibit overnight parking or a manager asks you to leave, you must go, because refusing after a warning is an offence under the Trespass Act 1980. Ask the manager first.
How long can a campervan stay in the same street in NZ?

It varies by council. Auckland allows two nights in the same road or off-road parking area and bars a return for two weeks from 9 am on departure day. Wellington allows no more than four consecutive nights a calendar month in any one area, and Christchurch's coastal zone allows four nights in 30 days with no more than two in one place.
