freedom-camping-rules-new-zealand.title: Freedom camping rules in New Zealand, region by region
freedom-camping-rules-new-zealand.description: The Freedom Camping Act, council bylaws, self-containment certification and what enforcement actually looks like on the ground.
freedom-camping-rules-new-zealand.imageAlt: Authorised freedom camping sign beside a campervan
freedom-camping-rules-new-zealand.intro: Freedom camping in New Zealand is legal where it is permitted and an infringement everywhere else, and the line between the two is drawn by whichever body manages the land under your wheels. The Freedom Camping Act 2011 sets a national frame, but councils write their own bylaws, so a rule you learned in one district tells you very little about the next one.

sections.heading: What freedom camping actually means here
body: Freedom camping is staying overnight on public land outside a formal campground, where the Freedom Camping Act 2011, a council bylaw or the landowner permits it. In practice it covers council reserves, designated car parks, lay-bys and some conservation land. It does not cover private farmland, forestry roads or national park huts, and it is a description of the location rather than a promise that the night is free.

The Act covers camping outside a camping ground within 200 metres of an area accessible by motor vehicle, within 200 metres of the sea or a harbour, or on or within 200 metres of a formed road or a Great Walks track. Beyond that you are generally in backcountry camping territory, which follows DOC's rules instead. Either way, the sign at the entrance is the final authority and overrides any app, PDF or map layer, including this page.
tips: Freedom means location, not price
Signage overrides every app
200 m of a formed road is the usual test

sections.heading: Self-containment: the transition is now complete
body: The rules changed in stages. The national green warrant system opened on 7 December 2023 and requires a toilet fixed inside the vehicle. Rental vehicles needed green warrants from 7 December 2024, and the transition for privately owned vehicles ended on 6 June 2026. Since 7 June 2026 a blue warrant no longer makes a vehicle self-contained for freedom camping, whatever expiry date it shows, so a van carrying only a blue sticker is treated as uncertified.

Certification is regulated by the Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Board, and key details of every certified vehicle go onto a national register that enforcement officers check on the spot. If you are hiring or buying, use the register's public vehicle search to confirm the certificate is current and matches the plate rather than trusting the card on the glass, and read the card for how many people it covers. On council land, camping with more people than the vehicle is certified for is a separate $400 infringement.
tips: Blue warrants stopped counting on 7 June 2026
Look the vehicle up on the national register
Certified occupancy must match your party

sections.heading: Enforcement and what it costs
body: Most freedom camping breaches carry a $400 infringement fee: camping where a bylaw or DOC notice prohibits or restricts it, using an uncertified vehicle where self-containment is required, or carrying more people than the certificate allows. Not displaying a warrant card is $200, refusing to leave when an officer tells you to is $600, and depositing waste or damaging the area is $800. On council and conservation land, officers can also seize and impound a vehicle where that is reasonable and necessary, for example to protect public health or safety, significant wildlife or access, or to stop an ongoing offence; if you are with the vehicle, they must first tell you to stop and warn you it can be taken.

Enforcement officers check the warrant card, the plate and the posted stay limit. When the vehicle is a rental, the notice usually goes to the company, and under the Freedom Camping Act a hire agreement can make you liable for the fee; if it authorises a card debit, the company must send you the notice within 5 working days before charging the card you left at pick-up, and you can still ask for a court hearing.

sections.heading: Council land versus conservation land
body: Council bylaws set stay limits, define self-contained-only zones and prohibit camping outright in many urban areas. They vary enormously: some districts publish a handful of permitted sites, others operate a general permission with named exclusions. Because each bylaw is a local instrument, the only reliable source is the council whose boundary you are inside.

On conservation land, freedom camping is generally allowed except where it is prohibited or restricted, but national parks and many reserves require you to use designated DOC campsites or recognised backcountry areas instead. DOC publishes alerts for closures, and those change faster than third-party data refreshes.

sections.heading: North Island, in outline
body: Northland councils use designated zones with short stay limits, so check the Far North, Whangārei or Kaipara bylaw for the site. Auckland allows certified self-contained vehicles on most council roadsides and car parks for up to two nights, leaving by 9am, but reserves, regional parks and 58 listed areas are prohibited and 20 more are restricted. Waikato and Bay of Plenty mix limited council reserves with a strong holiday park network, and Rotorua's lakeside sites are signed tightly.

Gisborne and Hawke's Bay permit specific beaches, sometimes with an overnight permit that has to be arranged in advance. Through Taranaki, Manawatū-Whanganui and Wellington, coastal parking is frequently restricted to certified vehicles with short stay limits, and Wellington City enforces no-camping zones around the central city, so plan for a harbour-side or Hutt Valley alternative rather than improvising near the terminal.
tips: Auckland and Wellington CBDs are largely prohibited
Some east coast sites need a permit in advance
Two nights is a common maximum

sections.heading: South Island, in outline
body: Tasman's 2025 bylaw limits freedom camping to designated sites for certified self-contained vehicles, and tent freedom camping is not allowed on council land. The Marlborough Sounds are largely served by DOC campsites, so book ahead, and Kaikōura's designated sites fill early in summer. Christchurch allows certified self-contained vehicles outside its listed prohibited and restricted areas and bans freedom camping in the central city, while the Mackenzie and Waitaki districts are more permissive but firm about certification.

Otago is strict where demand is highest: Queenstown-Lakes and Central Otago enforce defined zones, and Dunedin offers coastal reserves with two-night limits that fill before dusk. In Southland and Fiordland, freedom camping near Milford Sound is prohibited and DOC campsites are the answer; Southland District's bylaw sets out where you can stay, which is worth checking before you are tired and looking.

sections.heading: A workable routine on arrival
body: Research narrows the options, but the decision happens at the entrance. Pull in, find the freedom camping board, read the stay limit and the vehicle requirement, and photograph the sign. It takes a minute and it is the evidence that settles any later dispute. If the sign and your app disagree, the sign wins, every time.

Councils install temporary restrictions after floods, slips and events, and those appear on the ground long before they reach any dataset. If a site is full, do not create an overflow row along the access lane; move to a paid campground instead. Holding one legal paid option in reserve is what stops a tired driver making an expensive decision at 9pm.
tips: Photograph the sign
Hold a paid fallback
Never form an overflow row

faq: What are the freedom camping rules in New Zealand?

On council and conservation land, freedom camping is allowed unless a bylaw, a DOC notice or another law prohibits or restricts it, and on council land the vehicle must be certified self-contained unless a site is designated otherwise. Councils write their own bylaws, so stay limits and banned areas change between districts.
How much is the fine for illegal freedom camping?

Most breaches carry a $400 infringement fee, including camping where it is prohibited and using an uncertified vehicle where self-containment is required. Depositing waste is $800, and a rental company can pass the fee to the hirer.

freedom-camping-new-zealand-guide.title: Can you camp for free in New Zealand? Where it is legal and safe
freedom-camping-new-zealand-guide.description: Which land types allow a free night, what certification you need, and the etiquette that keeps these places open.
freedom-camping-new-zealand-guide.imageAlt: Certified campervan at an authorised freedom camping area
freedom-camping-new-zealand-guide.intro: Yes, free camping is still genuinely possible across Aotearoa, and it is also the part of a trip most likely to earn a $400 infringement. The difference comes down to understanding which kinds of land allow it, whether your vehicle meets the certification standard, and following an etiquette that most travellers never think about until a council closes a site.

sections.heading: Free and freedom are different words
body: Freedom camping describes where you are, outside a formal campground, not what you pay. Most authorised freedom camping areas cost nothing, and a few require a permit arranged in advance; a site that charges a camping fee is legally a camping ground. Conversely, some of the cheapest legal nights in the country are DOC basic campsites, which are designated DOC campsites that happen to be free.

Getting this distinction right saves money and trouble. Travellers looking only for the word 'free' miss the $0 DOC sites entirely, and travellers assuming every freedom camping area is free occasionally discover a permit requirement after they have settled in.

sections.heading: Where a free night is actually legal
body: Public reserves specifically signed for freedom camping are the most reliable option, and councils publish the lists. DOC operates a substantial number of basic campsites at no charge, typically with a long-drop toilet and an untreated water source, which are ideal if you are equipped to be self-sufficient. Some communities also provide designated car parks, gravel lay-bys or showgrounds where certified vehicles can stay a night or two.

NZTA rest areas exist for driver fatigue rather than as campgrounds; a sleep break is a different thing from setting up camp, and local restrictions may still apply. Private land, a friend's paddock, a farm, a marae, counts as free camping when you have the owner's permission, which should be explicit rather than assumed. Never treat farmland or forestry roads as open by default.
tips: DOC basic sites are often free
Rest areas are for fatigue breaks
Private permission must be explicit

sections.heading: The certification requirement
body: On most public land the default is that a vehicle used for freedom camping must be certified self-contained, unless the site is designated for vehicles that are not. Only a green warrant counts: the transition ended on 6 June 2026, and since 7 June a blue warrant has not made a vehicle self-contained for freedom camping, whatever expiry date it carries. Certification requires a toilet fixed inside the vehicle, so a car or van conversion with a portable toilet does not qualify.

Camping without certification is possible: on council land, only at sites a bylaw designates for non-self-contained vehicles; on conservation land, anywhere a DOC notice does not prohibit camping or restrict it to certified vehicles. Campgrounds, holiday parks and most DOC campsites take uncertified vans too. If you are in a car, a tent or an uncertified van, plan around sites that specifically allow your setup rather than hoping a general area will do.

sections.heading: The restrictions you should expect
body: Stay limits are short, commonly two to four nights, often with arrival and departure windows, commonly park after early evening, leave by mid-morning. Noise curfews apply at most urban sites. Councils in high-demand districts such as Queenstown-Lakes patrol freedom camping sites, and officers can check a vehicle's certification on the national register by its plate.

Read the specific bylaw wording rather than a summary. Where a listing says permit required, the permit has to be arranged before you arrive, sometimes for a fee, and turning up without it is still an offence. Where it says no overnight camping, that applies regardless of how quiet or discreet you intend to be.
tips: Expect 1–2 night limits
Permits must be pre-arranged
Patrols run at dusk and dawn

sections.heading: Etiquette is what keeps sites open
body: Free camping runs on public tolerance, and sites close when that tolerance runs out. Keep the footprint small: park within the marked bay, keep awnings and chairs in unless the signage allows otherwise, arrive without ceremony and leave early. Two vehicles is a sensible maximum at an urban freedom spot, and a convoy of six will end that site for everyone.

Empty tanks at a dump station before you arrive rather than after you leave, because grey water odour is the single most common trigger for a complaint. Rotate destinations instead of settling into one spot for a week. If residents or kaumātua ask you to move on, move on courteously, the conversation that follows a refusal ends up in a council submission.

sections.heading: Safety, not just legality
body: A legal site is not automatically a good one. Prefer places with other travellers present, avoid isolated lay-bys with a single blind entrance, and think about whether you could drive out quickly if you needed to. Park facing out where the site allows it.

Check the forecast against the ground itself. River flats flood faster than people expect, exposed coastal car parks get uncomfortable in a southerly, and a site that is pleasant in February can be genuinely unsafe in a winter storm. Keep enough fuel to leave, and do not rely on reception being available to make that decision.
tips: Prefer sites with others present
Park facing out
River flats flood quickly

sections.heading: A ninety-second check before you switch off
body: Read the sign and confirm the stay limit, the hours and whether certification is required. Confirm your warrant is current and covers the number of people staying. Check whether waste facilities exist here or whether you need to arrive already empty.

Then look at the practical questions: is the ground firm, is anything overhead, can other vehicles get past you, and where is the nearest paid alternative if this turns out to be full or wrong. If any of those answers is unclear, the campground twenty minutes away is cheap insurance.

faq: Is free camping legal in New Zealand?

In designated areas, yes. Freedom camping is legal on council and conservation land unless a bylaw or DOC notice prohibits or restricts it, and on council land a vehicle must be certified self-contained unless the site is designated otherwise, which is why the same layby can be fine in one district and a fine in the next. The site signage is the authority, not a map.
Do you need a self-contained vehicle to camp for free?

For a large share of free sites, yes. Many councils restrict free camping to certified self-contained vehicles, and since the 2023 changes that certification requires a fixed toilet. Without certification you are limited to council sites designated for non-self-contained vehicles, conservation land that no DOC notice restricts to certified vehicles, and campgrounds, holiday parks and most DOC campsites.

sources.label: DOC freedom camping on conservation land

self-contained-campervan-green-warrant.title: New Self-Containment Rules NZ 2026: Green Warrant Only
self-contained-campervan-green-warrant.description: Blue warrants stopped counting on 7 June 2026. What a green warrant needs, the $400 fine, rental vans and where uncertified vans can stay.
self-contained-campervan-green-warrant.imageAlt: Green self-contained vehicle warrant on a campervan
self-contained-campervan-green-warrant.intro: Since 7 June 2026, only a vehicle with a green warrant counts as self-contained for freedom camping in New Zealand. The blue warrant transition is over: a blue card or sticker no longer qualifies on any public land restricted to self-contained vehicles, whatever expiry date is printed on it. To earn a green warrant, a vehicle needs a toilet permanently fixed inside it, a sink and wastewater tank, fresh water, ventilation and secure rubbish storage for three days. Without one you can still stay at campgrounds, holiday parks, on private land with permission, at council sites set aside for non-self-contained vehicles, and on conservation land that no DOC notice restricts to certified vehicles.

sections.heading: Blue warrants ended on 7 June 2026
body: The Self-contained Motor Vehicles Legislation Act 2023 amended the Freedom Camping Act 2011 and moved certification to a national system run by the Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Board. The green warrant system opened on 7 December 2023, rental vehicles had to switch by 7 December 2024, and privately owned vehicles had a transition period that ran until 6 June 2026. From 7 June 2026 the Board is explicit: vehicles with the old blue warrant cannot be used for freedom camping.

That makes the expiry date on a blue card irrelevant. A blue warrant issued in 2023 with years left to run stopped counting on the same day as one that was about to lapse. Many older conversions relied on a portable toilet that could be lifted out, and those never qualified for green certification. If your vehicle still carries only a blue sticker, treat it as not self-contained until a certification authority has inspected it and issued a green card.
tips: Blue warrants stopped counting on 7 June 2026
The printed expiry on a blue card no longer matters
Rental vehicles needed green warrants from 7 December 2024

sections.heading: What a green warrant requires
body: The Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers (Self-Contained Vehicles) Regulations 2023 set eight requirements: a water supply system that keeps water from contamination, a fixed toilet, a wastewater system that holds both grey and black water, a sink that drains to the wastewater tank, a clean way to load water, a way to empty wastewater at a proper outfall, secure rubbish storage and ventilation. Each has to work for at least three days for the maximum number of people the vehicle is certified for.

The toilet is the part that ruled out most older vans. It must be permanently fixed to the vehicle and usable inside it, so a portable unit stored in a cupboard does not count. Size alone does not decide the outcome: the Board says some smaller vehicles can meet every requirement and others will not, so each vehicle is assessed on its own fittings. A certificate of self-containment lasts for up to four years and expires on the date printed on it, or sooner if the vehicle's self-containment fittings are materially changed or the certificate is revoked.
tips: Toilet must be fixed and usable inside the vehicle
Systems must last three days for the certified occupancy
Certificates run for up to four years

sections.heading: Rental campervans and the green warrant
body: Rental fleets moved first. During the final stage of the transition the law stopped recognising old-standard certification on vehicles owned by a rental company, so from 7 December 2024 any hired campervan sold as self-contained has needed a green warrant. A hired van without one is legal to drive and to sleep in at a campground, but it is not self-contained and cannot use self-contained-only freedom camping areas.

Before you drive away, find the green warrant card displayed in the vehicle, check the expiry date covers the whole hire, and confirm how many people the certificate covers. Ask whether the toilet is fixed or portable if the listing is vague. Read the infringement clause in the hire agreement too: under the Freedom Camping Act, a hirer who agrees to it can be made to pay any freedom camping infringement fee, and the company can charge the card on file if the agreement authorises it, after sending you the notice within 5 working days.
tips: Check the green card, expiry and certified occupancy
No green card means not self-contained
Fines can be charged to the hirer's card

sections.heading: Fines for camping without certification
body: Councils, the Department of Conservation and Land Information New Zealand enforce freedom camping on the land each of them manages. Under the Freedom Camping (Penalties for Infringement Offences) Regulations 2023, freedom camping in a vehicle that is not self-contained where certification is required carries a $400 infringement fee. Breaching a prohibition or restriction in a bylaw or DOC notice is also $400, and on council land so is camping with more people than the vehicle is certified for.

Failing to display a warrant card is $200. Depositing waste or damaging the area while freedom camping is $800, and refusing to leave when an enforcement officer tells you to is $600. If an offence is prosecuted in court instead, the maximum fine is three times the infringement fee. Since 7 June 2026 a blue card is no defence: it does not make the vehicle self-contained, and it does not count as the warrant card you must display.

sections.heading: Where a non-self-contained van can stay
body: The certification rule applies only to freedom camping on public land. The Board is clear that it does not apply at a campground, a holiday park or on private property where you have the owner's permission. Holiday parks are the most reliable option, with toilets and showers, and many have a dump station. Paid DOC campsites are camping grounds rather than freedom camping, and most take tents and uncertified vans, and a few DOC sites, such as the free Whakaipo campsite near Taupō, are for certified self-contained vehicles only, so check the campsite's DOC page.

Some councils also designate sites for vehicles that are not self-contained, usually with a toilet nearby, a short stay limit and sometimes a permit or fee. On conservation land, DOC notices prohibit camping at some places and restrict others to certified vehicles, and DOC-administered scenic and recreation reserves need a designated campsite. KiwiCamping shows DOC's conservation-land notices as prohibited, restricted or permitted on the map, but the council bylaw or DOC notice is what decides the night, and not every restricted area is signposted.
tips: Campgrounds and holiday parks need no certification
Most DOC campsites take uncertified vans
Some councils set aside non-self-contained sites

sections.heading: What the green warrant does not cover
body: A green warrant is not permission to camp. It does not override a bylaw that prohibits overnight stays, does not reserve a bay, and does not extend a stay limit. Where a council or DOC prohibits freedom camping, a certified vehicle is as prohibited as any other.

It also says nothing about roadworthiness. Warrant of Fitness or Certificate of Fitness, registration, gas certification and the rental company's own conditions are separate obligations. The Board notes that modifications made to fit a fixed toilet or tanks may also need low volume vehicle certification, which is a different process from self-containment.
tips: Certification is not permission
WoF, registration and gas are separate
Structural changes may need LVV certification

sections.heading: Getting a vehicle certified, and what it costs
body: Only a certification authority appointed by the Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Board can issue a green warrant. The register site at certification.nzscv.co.nz lists the authorities operating in each region, and they are the people to ask whether your layout is likely to pass and what needs changing first. The Board expects inspections to be done in person, with remote inspection only in exceptional cases such as a vehicle in a remote area with no nearby authority.

There are two charges. The certification authority sets its own inspection fee, and every certification also carries a $120 self-containment levy, including GST, which the authority passes to the Board. If you are converting a van, involve a certifier before you build: tank sizes, toilet mounting, sink drainage and ventilation are far cheaper to get right during the build than to retrofit.
tips: Use a Board-appointed certification authority
Budget the inspection fee plus the $120 levy
Talk to a certifier before converting

sections.heading: Checking a warrant before you buy, hire or camp
body: Key details from every certificate go onto the national self-contained vehicle register, which enforcement officers can check on the spot, and the register has a public vehicle search. Look the vehicle up to confirm the certificate is current and belongs to that plate rather than trusting a card in the window, then read the card or certificate for how many people it covers.

When buying a used campervan, ask for the certificate itself, check the vehicle details on it match the van in front of you, and price in recertification if the warrant expires soon. A van advertised as self-contained with only a blue sticker has not been self-contained for freedom camping since 7 June 2026, and the asking price should reflect the cost of a fixed toilet and a green inspection.

faq: Are blue self-containment warrants still valid in NZ?

Not for freedom camping. Since 7 June 2026 only a green warrant makes a vehicle self-contained on public land restricted to certified vehicles, whatever expiry date a blue card shows. Campgrounds, holiday parks and private land with permission need neither.
What is the fine for freedom camping without a green warrant?

Camping in an uncertified vehicle where self-containment is required carries a $400 infringement fee, and failing to display the warrant card is $200. With a rental, the hire agreement can make you pay and let the company charge your card.

doc-campsites-new-zealand-guide.title: DOC Hut & Campsite Bookings 2026: How to Book, Fees, Dates
doc-campsites-new-zealand-guide.description: Book DOC huts, campsites and Great Walks at bookings.doc.govt.nz. 2026/27 fees, Hut Pass vs Campsite Pass, first-come huts and what to do when full.
doc-campsites-new-zealand-guide.imageAlt: Tent at a Department of Conservation campsite
doc-campsites-new-zealand-guide.intro: DOC huts, campsites and Great Walks are booked on the Department of Conservation's own booking system at bookings.doc.govt.nz, or through a DOC visitor centre. You need a free account, you pay in full when you book, and the confirmation email is your proof on site. Bookings for the 2026/27 season, covering stays from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, opened in May 2026. Most backcountry huts and many basic campsites cannot be booked at all and run first come, first served. Below: the fees, the two passes, which places need a booking and what to do when the one you want is full.

sections.heading: Where and how to book
body: Go to bookings.doc.govt.nz, create an account and log in before you search. Find the hut, campsite or Great Walk, choose dates and party size, add the vehicle registration for a campsite, and pay by Visa or Mastercard. Full payment is taken at the time of booking and every price includes GST. DOC visitor centres can book many of the same places in person or by phone, for a $10 service fee.

The confirmation email is the booking. Download or print it before you leave reception, along with any pass, because rangers and hut wardens can ask for it and most DOC huts and many campsites have no signal. Bunks in bookable huts are not allocated, so a booking buys a bed rather than a particular one, and campsite bookings without numbered sites let you pick from whatever pitches are free when you arrive.
tips: Create and test your account before opening day
Pay in full at booking, Visa or Mastercard
Save the confirmation for use without signal

sections.heading: Great Walks 2026/27: when bookings opened and what is left
body: DOC opened 2026/27 Great Walk bookings in a staggered run: Paparoa Track on 12 May, Milford on 13 May, Abel Tasman Coast on 14 May, Routeburn on 15 May, Kepler on 19 May, Heaphy, Whanganui Journey and Lake Waikaremoana on 20 May, and Tongariro Northern Circuit and Rakiura on 21 May, each at 9:30 am. Other huts and lodges opened on 12 May, North Island campsites on 14 May, South Island campsites on 15 May and Tōtaranui on 22 May. The Hump Ridge Track is booked separately through its own trust.

DOC's figures from the 2025/26 summer suggest the Milford, Abel Tasman and Kepler peak dates are the hardest to find: huts ran at around 95 per cent occupancy on Milford and Abel Tasman and 91 per cent on the Kepler. DOC points walkers with flexible plans towards the Heaphy, Lake Waikaremoana and the Whanganui Journey, which often have space, and says many campsites still had good availability when huts were full. On opening days a virtual queue gives everyone in the lobby at 9:30 am a random place, so arriving early does not help, but anyone logging in after 9:30 joins the back.
tips: Bookings cover stays from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027
Milford, Abel Tasman and Kepler fill first
Hump Ridge is booked through its own trust

sections.heading: Fees by category, and how they are charged
body: DOC charges per person per night, not per site, so four adults at a $15 standard campsite pay $60. Basic campsites and basic huts are free. Standard campsites cost $10 to $20 an adult and serviced campsites $25 unpowered. Standard huts are $15 all year, and serviced huts $25 from May to September but $28 to $34 from October to April, highest on Friday and Saturday nights over December to February. Camping beside a serviced hut costs half the hut fee: $12.50 from May to September and $14 to $17 from October to April. Great Walk prices depend on the track, the season and whether you are a New Zealand resident: between 1 November and 30 April a night in a Milford Track hut is $106 for a resident adult and $152 for an international adult.

Residency has to be provable. The resident rate applies to New Zealand citizens and people ordinarily resident here, and DOC can ask for a passport, driver licence or similar on the track; a party that cannot show it pays the difference plus $50 a person. Turning up without a valid booking at a bookable place costs more again: DOC's penalty rate is the normal fee plus a full adult fee. Booking a campsite you do not intend to use, or holding a pitch with an empty tent, is charged at two adults.
tips: Fees are per person, not per site
Carry proof if you book the resident rate
Unbooked use attracts DOC's penalty rate

sections.heading: Hut Pass, Campsite Pass or pay per night
body: The Backcountry Hut Pass costs $160 for an adult for 12 months and covers most serviced and standard huts, plus most campsites outside serviced huts. At $15 a night in a standard hut it pays for itself after 11 nights, or after 5 to 7 serviced-hut nights depending on the season. Some bookable huts accept it, entered when you book, and in non-bookable huts you write your name and pass number in the hut book. Great Walk huts are priced separately, and DOC publishes a list of huts where the pass is not accepted.

The Campsite Pass costs $295 for an adult for one year and covers most DOC campsites, bookable and not, for up to 7 nights in any 30 days at a single campsite, plus $3 per pass holder per night at a powered site. At bookable campsites you must still book through the system before you arrive, or pay a $10 fee and risk being turned away if the ground is full. Neither pass is a reservation, and neither gives you priority at a first-come hut or campsite, so for a single short trip, paying per night is usually cheaper.
tips: Hut Pass: about 11 standard-hut nights to break even
Campsite Pass: still book bookable sites first
Neither pass holds a bed or a pitch

sections.heading: Which huts and campsites are first come, first served
body: Most of DOC's network still cannot be booked: DOC says the majority of its roughly 950 huts are non-bookable. In KiwiCamping's DOC data, checked on 24 August 2026, that included 350 basic huts and bivvies and 401 standard huts. Basic huts are free. For a non-bookable standard hut you pay with a Backcountry Hut Ticket or a Hut Pass, and paper tickets go in the honesty box at the hut. Huts stay unlocked as emergency shelter in bad weather, but shelter is not a bunk, so carrying a tent on busy tracks is sensible.

Two changes land this season. Since 1 October 2026 every DOC serviced hut is on the booking system, and Serviced Hut Tickets are being retired; tickets already bought can be applied to a booking until they expire. From 1 November 2026 Backcountry Hut Tickets for non-bookable huts can be bought on DOC's online booking system, still $15 an adult a night for a standard hut; they are payment, not a booking, and paper tickets stay valid until 1 November 2027. On the campsite side, 110 of the 287 DOC campsites in KiwiCamping are self-registration: mostly basic and backcountry sites, plus some standard ones where you fill in an envelope and pay on arrival.
tips: Basic huts are free; standard huts take tickets or the pass
Hut tickets move online from 1 November 2026
Every serviced hut is bookable since 1 October 2026

sections.heading: Changing or cancelling a booking
body: Cancel on the day you book or the following day, provided arrival is more than two days away, and DOC charges nothing. From 48 hours after booking to 15 days before arrival the fee is 10 per cent. Inside 14 days it climbs by type: huts 20 per cent, then 30 per cent from three days out; campgrounds 20 then 75 per cent; Great Walks 50 then 75 per cent; lodges, cabins and sole-occupancy huts 100 per cent. Cancelling the day before, on the day or after it forfeits the whole amount, and so does a no-show.

If you miss the first night of a multi-night booking and do not contact the site office within 24 hours, DOC cancels the rest without a refund. Weather refunds are not automatic. If DOC closes the place or cancels your stay, for example for a storm, flooding or an orange or red MetService warning for the area the day before, email DOC's booking team within 7 days, before changing the booking yourself, for a full refund of the unused nights or, if your stay has not started, a transfer to available dates in the same season. If the weather is merely bad and the place stays open, normal cancellation fees apply, which is why DOC recommends travel insurance.

sections.heading: When the hut or campsite you want is fully booked
body: Check the same place again on other dates, especially shoulder-season weeks either side of the school holidays, and look at campsites: DOC says many still had good availability when huts were full, although the Milford and Paparoa tracks have none. Swap a booked-out Great Walk for one with more room, or walk a non-bookable hut track nearby. DOC's own advice is to keep checking over the following months, because people cancel and even the Milford Track has cancellations across the year.

For a vehicle-based night, a holiday park or a self-registration DOC campsite is the realistic fallback. KiwiCamping shows every DOC hut and campsite in its data with its category, fee and whether it takes bookings, alongside holiday parks you can book through BookIt in the app, so you can find the nearest alternative without signal. DOC places in the app need the Pass; BookIt stays are free to browse and book.
tips: Try shoulder dates and nearby campsites
Heaphy, Waikaremoana and Whanganui often have space
Hold a holiday park or first-come site as plan B

sections.heading: Before you go
body: Read the place's own DOC page as well as the booking: it lists the facilities, whether water is treated, fire and dog rules, road access and current alerts. Track and road closures after storms are common, and the alert on the DOC page outranks anything you booked months ago. Check-out is 10 am, check-in runs from 2 pm to 8.30 pm, and quiet hours are 10 pm to 7 am unless the site sets different ones.

Pack for the place rather than the booking. A bed in a serviced hut still needs a sleeping bag, food, a stove for most huts and warm layers, and a booked campsite does not include the hut beside it. Take all rubbish out, fill in the hut book, and leave the bunk or pitch ready for the next party.

faq: How do you book a DOC hut or campsite?

Online at bookings.doc.govt.nz with a free DOC account, or through a DOC visitor centre. You pay in full when you book and the confirmation email is your proof. Basic huts are free, and non-bookable standard huts are paid with hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass.
When did 2026/27 Great Walk bookings open?

On seven opening days between 12 and 21 May 2026, at 9:30 am, for stays from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027. Peak Milford, Abel Tasman and Kepler dates go first, but cancellations come back on sale through the season.

holiday-parks-new-zealand-guide.title: Holiday Parks NZ 2026: Memberships, Costs and How to Book
holiday-parks-new-zealand-guide.description: TOP 10 Club costs $55 for two years and saves 10% a stay. How holiday park rates are built, when to book, late arrival, and the cost against DOC sites.
holiday-parks-new-zealand-guide.imageAlt: New Zealand holiday park beside the coast
holiday-parks-new-zealand-guide.intro: A holiday park is a commercial campground with powered and tent sites, hot showers, a shared kitchen, laundry and usually cabins, and it is the night that resets a camping trip: after a wet week, before an early ferry, or whenever power and a dependable shower matter more than solitude. Most charge per site or per person, so the price only means something for your own party. The industry association, Holiday Parks New Zealand, lists 230 member parks, and the biggest chain, TOP 10, sells a $55 two-year club card that takes 10 percent off each stay. Below: how rates work, what a membership is worth, when to book and how to arrive late without trouble.

sections.heading: Understand how the rate is built
body: Holiday parks price in three different ways and the comparison collapses if you mix them up. Some charge per person, some per site with a stated occupancy, and some quote a base rate with additional guests charged separately. As an example, a $56 site for two and a $28-per-person rate are the same price for a couple and very different for a family of five.

Then check what is bundled. Power, linen, kitchen equipment, showers, Wi-Fi and booking fees vary between parks, and a cabin quoted without linen is not comparable to one that includes it. Work out the total for your actual party and nights before deciding anything.
tips: Compare per-person against per-site
Check whether linen is included
Include booking and card fees

sections.heading: Holiday park or DOC campsite: cost it for your party
body: DOC charges per person, so the cheaper option depends on who is travelling. At a serviced DOC campsite an adult pays $25 a night unpowered and a child $12.50, so two adults and two children pay $75. At a standard DOC campsite the same family pays $30 to $60, and at a basic site nothing. Hold that against the park's quoted total for the same night, power and party, not against its headline site price.

For a couple, DOC usually wins on price and a park on facilities. For a family, a park charging per site often closes the gap or beats a serviced DOC ground, and adds laundry, a kitchen, hot showers and somewhere for children to burn off energy. Many trips work best mixing the two: DOC sites for the scenery, a holiday park every few nights for the reset.
tips: DOC charges per person, parks often per site
Two adults and two children: $75 at a serviced DOC site
Mix DOC nights with a park every few nights

sections.heading: Chains, networks and memberships
body: TOP 10 Holiday Parks is the largest chain. Its club card costs $55 for two years and takes 10 percent off accommodation at TOP 10 parks, capped at $40 a stay, plus 10 percent at more than 130 BIG4 parks across the Tasman, Interislander ferry savings and regional deals. The card pays for itself once your discounts pass $55, which at 10 percent means about $550 of TOP 10 stays over the two years: good value on a long trip, rarely on a weekend.

Holiday Parks New Zealand is the industry association rather than a chain. It lists 230 member parks, many of them independent, and arranges an Interislander discount for its member parks' guests. Motorhome owners who join the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association get its members-only parks and travel directory instead. Independent parks run their own discounts, so ask at booking rather than assuming a card applies.
tips: TOP 10 Club: $55 for two years, 10% off up to $40 a stay
It pays off after about $550 of TOP 10 nights
Independent parks set their own discounts

sections.heading: Book the vehicle you are actually bringing
body: Site dimensions matter more than travellers expect. A long motorhome, a caravan with an awning or a vehicle towing a trailer needs a site that physically fits, and parks allocate by the length you declared. Under-declaring produces an awkward conversation at check-in and sometimes no site at all.

Say whether you need drive-through access, power, and proximity to amenities if anyone in the party has mobility needs. These are easy to arrange in advance and nearly impossible to fix on a full Saturday in January.

sections.heading: Peak season changes the rules
body: Between Christmas and late January, and over Easter and school holidays, popular coastal parks can set minimum stays, higher rates and stricter cancellation terms, and the best sites go early. If your route passes through a beach town in that window, book it as early as you book the ferry.

Local events compress availability just as hard and with less warning: a regional sports tournament or a concert can fill every park in a district. Where dates are uncertain, pay for refundable terms and note the cancellation deadline against the trip stop rather than trusting memory.
tips: Book beach towns very early
Watch for local events
Note cancellation deadlines

sections.heading: Arriving after hours
body: Most parks close reception in the evening, and a long driving day frequently ends after that. Ask for the late-arrival procedure when you book: many leave an envelope with a site number and a gate code, but you need to know that before you are standing at a locked barrier at 10pm with no reception.
Confirm the gate arrangement for vehicles too. Some parks close a boom gate overnight, which matters if you have an early ferry or a dawn start planned.

sections.heading: Use the facilities deliberately
body: A holiday park night is worth most when you use what you paid for. A communal kitchen saves gas and keeps cooking smells out of a small van, the laundry resets a week of damp clothing, and the dump station and potable water taps let you leave with full tanks and empty ones in the right order.

Learn the layout before connecting anything: never fill drinking water from a tap near the dump point, and ask which taps are potable, because not all of them are. Rinse and stow hoses separately, and wash your hands after handling waste equipment.
tips: Never fill water near the dump point
Ask which taps are potable
Keep hoses separate

sections.heading: Shared space, shared rules
body: Quiet hours are enforced, and holiday parks are dense environments where sound carries between sites. Keep site boundaries, supervise children around internal roads and pools, and check the pet policy before arriving with a dog, because many parks restrict animals, especially in peak season.
Secure valuables as you would anywhere with public access. A holiday park is convenient and generally safe, but it remains a busy site with vehicles moving through it all day.

sections.heading: Finding and booking parks in KiwiCamping
body: KiwiCamping shows holiday parks and tours from BookIt on the same map as DOC campsites and dump stations. The BookIt places are free in the app: open one to see its facilities and photos, then use Book now to check live availability and price. That makes it quick to find a powered site within an hour of where you are, even when you are choosing on the road.

DOC campsites, huts, dump stations and DOC's freedom camping notices are part of the Premium pass. Place details are stored on the phone, so you can compare a park against the nearest DOC site without signal, while live availability, maps and booking pages need a connection.

faq: What is the difference between a holiday park and a campsite?

A holiday park is a commercial site with powered sites, showers, kitchens, laundry and usually cabins, priced per site or per person. A DOC campsite is public conservation land with far fewer facilities and a much lower fee.
Is a holiday park membership worth it in New Zealand?

The TOP 10 Club costs $55 for two years and takes 10 percent off each TOP 10 stay, up to $40 a stay, so it pays for itself once you spend about $550 at TOP 10 parks. That suits a long trip; for a weekend it rarely does.

sources.label: TOP 10 Holiday Parks: club membership and member benefits
Holiday Parks New Zealand: find a member park
DOC campsite categories, facilities and fees

camping-wastewater-rubbish-new-zealand.title: Dump Stations NZ: Locations by Region, Costs and Rules
camping-wastewater-rubbish-new-zealand.description: Where to empty a campervan toilet in NZ: KiwiCamping's 262 dump stations by region, most of them free, how to use one and the $800 fine for dumping waste.
camping-wastewater-rubbish-new-zealand.imageAlt: Campervan using a marked dump station
camping-wastewater-rubbish-new-zealand.intro: Waste is where responsible camping becomes concrete, and where the penalties get serious. Discharging toilet or grey water in the wrong place carries substantially higher fines than an ordinary freedom camping infringement, and it is the behaviour most likely to get a popular site closed permanently.

sections.heading: Know your three waste streams
body: Black water is toilet waste and goes only into a dump station inlet designed for it. Grey water is everything from the sink and shower, it contains food particles, soap, fats and bacteria, and despite looking harmless it is not something to tip on the ground. Solid rubbish is the third stream and generally has to leave with you.

Treat all three as containment problems rather than disposal problems. The question on the road is not where you can get rid of something, but whether you have capacity to hold it until you reach the right facility.
tips: Grey water is not clean water
Plan capacity, not disposal
Rubbish usually leaves with you

sections.heading: Finding a dump station
body: Dump stations are widely distributed across New Zealand, at holiday parks, council facilities, some service stations and town reserves, and most are free or charge a small fee. They are mapped, and the sensible habit is to identify the next one on your route before you need it rather than searching when a tank is already full.

Facilities at holiday parks are often available to non-guests for a small charge, which is worth knowing on a long remote leg. Some are locked overnight, so arriving at 11pm with a full cassette is a planning failure rather than bad luck.

sections.heading: Dump stations by region
body: KiwiCamping maps 262 public dump stations. By the DOC region of the nearest DOC campsite or hut, Canterbury has 38, Otago 28, Bay of Plenty 23, Northland 19, Auckland 17, Hawke's Bay and Wellington/Kāpiti 15 each, the Central North Island and the West Coast 14 each, Marlborough 11, Nelson/Tasman and Waikato 10 each, the Coromandel 9, Southland and Taranaki 8 each, the East Coast 7, Manawatū/Whanganui 6, and Fiordland and the Wairarapa 5 each.

Of the 262, the listings show 240 as free, 8 as asking for a donation and 6 as charging a fee, and 8 give no fee. The gaps matter more than the totals: Fiordland, the Wairarapa and the East Coast have few, so empty before you head into them rather than counting on one along the way. In the app, dump stations are part of the Premium pass, with the fee note and location stored on the phone.
tips: Canterbury and Otago have the most
Most dump stations are free
Empty before Fiordland and the East Coast

sections.heading: Using one correctly
body: Park so other vehicles can still pass, dump stations are frequently on a single access lane and a badly parked van blocks everyone. Use only the inlet marked for the waste you are emptying, empty black water first, then rinse, then grey water. Rinse without spraying the surrounding ground, and leave the area cleaner than you found it.

Keep the drinking-water hose entirely separate from anything used at the dump point, and never fill fresh water from a tap at the dump station unless it is explicitly marked potable. Wash your hands afterwards, before touching anything in the vehicle.
tips: Black water first, then rinse, then grey
Keep hoses strictly separate
Never fill drinking water at the dump point

sections.heading: What not to do, and why it costs
body: Stormwater drains discharge directly to waterways with no treatment, so emptying a tank into one is a discharge to the environment rather than to a sewer. Public toilets are not designed for cassette volumes and block. Emptying into a hedge, a bush or a stream is the offence that draws the largest penalties and the most attention: depositing waste while freedom camping is an $800 infringement fee.

Use only treatment chemicals compatible with the receiving system. Many rural dump stations feed septic tanks, and harsh formaldehyde-based products damage the biological process that makes them work. Where you are unsure, choose a product marked as septic-safe.

sections.heading: Rubbish and food waste
body: DOC accommodation terms generally require all rubbish to leave with you, and many council sites operate pack-in, pack-out even where a toilet is provided. Assume there is no bin unless you can see one, and carry a sealed container so food waste does not attract birds, rodents or possums overnight.

Food scraps are not a free pass because they are organic. Left in the bush they spread seeds, alter animal behaviour and take far longer to break down than people assume. Do not burn plastic, foil or treated timber in a campfire, it produces toxic smoke and leaves residue that the next camper inherits.
tips: Assume no bins
Seal food waste overnight
Never burn plastic or treated wood

sections.heading: Building it into the routine
body: The travellers who never have a waste problem are the ones who empty on a schedule rather than on demand, typically whenever they pass a facility with tanks more than half full, regardless of whether it feels necessary. That single habit removes almost every awkward situation.

Know your capacity in days: how long the fresh water lasts, how long before grey water needs attention, how many days the toilet supports at your party size. Those three numbers determine how far off-grid you can genuinely go, and they are more useful than any tank specification in litres.

faq: Where can you empty a campervan toilet in New Zealand?

At a public dump station, at most holiday parks, and at some council facilities. Emptying a cassette into a public toilet, a storm drain or the bush is illegal and carries one of the larger infringement fees.
Can you pour grey water on the ground?

No. Sink and shower water carries detergent and food waste and must go to a dump station or a holiday park's grey water point, which is why self-containment certification requires a waste tank rather than a bucket.

sources.label: Freedom Camping (Penalties for Infringement Offences) Regulations 2023

campfire-rules-new-zealand.title: NZ Fire Season & Campfire Rules 2026: Check Fire Bans First
campfire-rules-new-zealand.description: Open, restricted or prohibited: how NZ fire seasons work, where to check today's fire ban, when you need a permit and how to cook when fires are banned.
campfire-rules-new-zealand.imageAlt: Small controlled campfire in a legal fire site
campfire-rules-new-zealand.intro: An existing fire ring and a pile of old ash prove that someone had a fire here once, not that you may have one today. New Zealand runs a three-tier fire season system that changes with conditions, and the land manager can prohibit fires regardless of what that system says.

sections.heading: The three fire seasons
body: In an open fire season you may light a fire in the open air without a permit, subject to the land manager's own rules. In a restricted fire season you need a permit from Fire and Emergency New Zealand before lighting anything in the open. In a prohibited fire season, open-air fires are banned outright and no permit will be issued.

The season is set by district and changes with conditions, sometimes at short notice during a dry spell. Check the current status for the exact district you are in on the day, not the district you drove through this morning.
tips: Check the district on the day
Restricted means permit required
Prohibited means no fire at all

sections.heading: The land manager can be stricter
body: The fire season is a floor, not a permission. DOC campsites, regional parks, council reserves and private campgrounds all set their own rules, and many prohibit open fires permanently regardless of the season. Where two rules apply, the stricter one controls.

Read the specific campsite page and the sign at the site. Some DOC campsites permit a small fire only in a provided fireplace, some prohibit solid fuel entirely, and backcountry fires carry separate conditions about location, clearance and size.

sections.heading: If a fire is genuinely permitted
body: Use the existing authorised fireplace where one is provided rather than building a new ring. Clear combustible material well back, keep the fire small, and have water immediately to hand, not in the vehicle, but beside you. Never light beneath overhanging trees, on peat, in strong wind, or near dry grass, gorse or mānuka, all of which carry fire far faster than people expect.

Burn only fuel you are permitted to use. Collecting living vegetation is prohibited on conservation land, and many sites require you to bring your own wood. Do not burn rubbish, plastic, foil or treated timber.
tips: Water beside you, not in the van
Never light in wind or under trees
Bring fuel; do not collect living wood

sections.heading: Putting it out properly
body: A fire is out when it is cold to the touch, and getting there takes longer than most people allow. Douse it, stir the ashes, douse again, and keep going until you can put your hand in the remains. Embers survive under ash for many hours and wind can restart them long after you have gone to bed.
Never leave a fire unattended, including while it burns down. Most escaped campfires start after the people who lit them decided it was nearly out.

sections.heading: Cooking when fires are banned
body: Gas cookers are the practical answer and are generally permitted when open fires are not, but check, because a prohibited fire season can restrict some appliances too. Use them on a stable, level surface, well clear of tent fabric and vegetation.

Never cook inside a closed tent, an awning or an unventilated vehicle. The risk is carbon monoxide, which is odourless and has killed campers in New Zealand. Let a cooker cool completely before it goes back into a vehicle or tent, and store gas cylinders upright and ventilated.
tips: Never cook in a closed tent or van
Carbon monoxide has no smell
Let cookers cool before stowing

sections.heading: If it gets away from you
body: If a fire spreads beyond your control, do not try to fight it beyond the first few seconds. Move away, downhill and across the slope where safe, because fire travels fastest uphill, and call 111 immediately.

Give the clearest location you can: the road, the nearest identifiable landmark, and coordinates if you have them saved offline. Being able to state where you are, quickly, is worth more than any equipment you are carrying.

faq: Can you light a campfire in New Zealand?

Sometimes, and it depends on the fire season where you are. Fire and Emergency New Zealand sets each district to open, restricted or prohibited, and in a restricted season you need a permit before lighting anything.
How do you check the fire season before camping?

Check checkitsalright.nz for the district you are actually in, on the day, then check the campsite's own rules, because many DOC sites ban fires regardless of the district season. A gas stove is unaffected by fire seasons and is the reason most campers carry one.

sources.label: Fire and Emergency: Check It's Alright

new-zealand-camping-packing-list.title: NZ Camping Packing List: What to Pack, by Region
new-zealand-camping-packing-list.description: A New Zealand camping packing list for wind, rain, sandflies, cold nights and remote roads, then adjusted for the West Coast, Otago, the north and alpine trips.
new-zealand-camping-packing-list.imageAlt: Camping equipment packed beside a New Zealand campervan
new-zealand-camping-packing-list.intro: New Zealand punishes packing lists written for a single climate. The country delivers four seasons in a day with real conviction, and the gap between a comfortable trip and a miserable one is usually three or four specific items rather than a bigger pile of gear.

sections.heading: Sleep and shelter
body: Take a sleep system rated below the coldest night you expect, then add a margin, inland and alpine sites drop close to freezing well outside winter, even after a warm day. An insulated mat matters as much as the bag, because most heat is lost downwards into the ground.

Test the whole setup at home before you leave: pitch the tent, inflate the mat, check the pump and valves. Keep one complete dry sleep layer sealed in a waterproof bag and never wear it during the day. A wet West Coast afternoon should not be able to reach the only warm clothing you have.
tips: Rate the bag below expected lows
Insulated mat, not just a bag
Seal one dry sleep layer away

sections.heading: Wind and rain, not just cold
body: The wind is the part visitors underestimate. Bring a genuinely windproof shell rather than a light rain jacket, and carry enough strong pegs and guylines to hold a tent in an exposed coastal site, the pegs supplied with most tents are not adequate here. A groundsheet and a spare tarp earn their space repeatedly.

Pack quick-drying layers and avoid cotton for anything you rely on. Merino works well for the same reason it is everywhere in this country: it stays warm damp and does not develop a smell over a fortnight.

sections.heading: Sandflies and sun
body: Sandflies are not a minor irritation on the West Coast, in Fiordland or around the Catlins. Bring strong repellent, cover ankles and wrists at dusk, and check the tent's insect mesh for holes before you leave home. Antihistamine cream is worth carrying, because the bites keep people awake for days after the fact.

The UV here is severe, the sun burns faster than most visitors expect, including on overcast days and at altitude. High-factor sunscreen, a brimmed hat and sunglasses belong in the day bag, not the boot.
tips: Repellent for the West Coast and Fiordland
Check tent mesh before leaving
UV is stronger than it looks

sections.heading: Kitchen and water
body: Carry a stable gas cooker rated for outdoor use, a reliable lighter plus a backup, simple nesting cookware and enough food to absorb a delayed day. Cook outside or in a properly ventilated space, never inside a closed tent or van.

Use separate, clearly labelled containers for drinking water and waste, and carry a reserve of drinking water that is not touched during ordinary camp use. Water at DOC sites is frequently untreated, so bring a filter or the means to boil, and do not assume a tap is potable because it exists.

sections.heading: Vehicle and emergency kit
body: Know where the jack points are on your vehicle and confirm the spare, jack and wheel brace are actually present before you leave the depot, this is a common gap in rentals. Carry a torch or headlamp, a power bank, a basic first aid kit and a paper map, with each day's route and campsite saved before you lose reception.

Alpine routes may require chains in winter, and some rental agreements mandate carrying them regardless of conditions. For remote walks or back-country roads, a personal locator beacon is cheap to hire and is the one item that genuinely changes outcomes.
tips: Check the spare and jack at pickup
Save the route before reception drops
Hire a PLB for remote legs

sections.heading: Before you fly: clean and declare your gear
body: Used tents, hiking boots, camping gear and anything that has been in soil or fresh water must be declared when you arrive in New Zealand. Clean soil, seeds and plant material off them before you pack, and still tick yes on the arrival card when the question applies: failing to declare is what draws the fine, not the clean tent itself.

Food needs declaring too, so finish the trail mix on the plane or declare it. Pack the gear you will be asked to show near the top of the bag so the inspection takes minutes rather than a full unpack.
tips: Declare used tents and boots
Clean off soil before you fly
Declare food as well

sections.heading: Adjust for where you are going
body: For the West Coast and Fiordland, weight the packing towards rain, sandflies and drying, more repellent, more dry bags, more spare socks. For Central Otago and the Mackenzie, weight it towards cold nights and sun, with a warmer bag and better eye protection than the coast requires.

For Northland and the upper North Island, the balance shifts to heat, humidity and shade. For anything alpine, or for winter anywhere in the south, add chains, extra insulation and a genuinely shorter driving day. The list does not get longer with each region so much as it gets reweighted.

faq: What do you actually need to pack for camping in New Zealand?

Layers for four seasons in a day, proper rain gear, insect repellent, a headtorch, and more warm clothing than the average forecast suggests. Then reweight it by region: the West Coast needs rain and sandfly gear, Central Otago colder nights and stronger sun.
What do visitors most often forget?
Repellent, a warm layer for summer evenings, and a way to charge things away from power. The other is a paper map, because reception disappears exactly where the driving gets interesting.

best-time-camping-new-zealand.title: Sandfly Season NZ: When They're Worst and Best Months to Camp
best-time-camping-new-zealand.description: When and where sandflies bite in New Zealand, worst on the West Coast and in Fiordland, plus how each season suits camping, region by region.
best-time-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Four seasons across a New Zealand camping landscape
best-time-camping-new-zealand.intro: There is no single best month for the whole country, because New Zealand spans a long way north to south and most of its weather is decided by altitude and which coast you are on. Choosing when to go is mostly about deciding what you are willing to trade: warmth against crowds, quiet against daylight, or scenery against certainty.

sections.heading: Summer: daylight, and everyone else
body: December to February brings long evenings, warm coastal swimming and the broadest availability of open campgrounds and services. It is also when the country goes on holiday itself. Between Christmas and late January, popular coastal sites fill by early afternoon, ferries and rentals sell out, and prices climb sharply.

Book the nights that are genuinely hard to replace (the ferry, Great Walks, beach-town holiday parks) and leave ordinary stops flexible. Note that summer does not mean warm everywhere: alpine nights stay cold, and fire restrictions and water shortages are most likely in exactly this window.
tips: Book ferries and beach towns early
Alpine nights stay cold in summer
Fire restrictions peak in summer

sections.heading: Autumn: the quiet favourite
body: March and April are, for many people who travel here regularly, the best compromise. Settled spells are common, the light is excellent, campgrounds are open but no longer full, and prices drop once school holidays end. Central Otago in particular is at its best as the poplars turn.
The trade-off is shortening daylight and cooler nights, so driving days need to be a little shorter and the sleeping bag a little warmer. Some seasonal services begin closing from April onwards.

sections.heading: Spring and winter
body: Spring brings full waterfalls, snow still on the peaks and green everywhere, but it is the least predictable season, wind and rapidly changing alpine conditions demand more caution and more flexibility. October and November can deliver a perfect week or a genuinely difficult one.

Winter is a different trip rather than a worse one. It suits ski areas, clear southern night skies and travellers properly equipped for cold. Northern lowland camping stays mild, while Central Otago, Tongariro and the alpine passes require winter driving preparation, chains and a realistic view of daylight hours. It is a poor season to improvise.
tips: Autumn is the best all-round compromise
Spring is beautiful and unpredictable
Winter needs equipment, not optimism

sections.heading: Sandflies: where and when
body: Sandflies, namu in te reo Māori, live wherever there is flowing water and bush, and two of New Zealand's 13 species bite. The West Coast and Fiordland are infamous for them, which is why the end of the Milford Track is called Sandfly Point, and beaches, lake edges and the Catlins are reliable spots too. They breed in fast-flowing streams, bite most as the light rises in the morning and fades at dusk, rarely bite in the dark, and in dull, overcast, humid weather keep biting all day.

There is no official sandfly season: in the wettest regions they are part of camping in any month, and most visitors meet them between spring and autumn, when campsites by rivers and lakes are full. An exposed, breezy pitch away from still water is usually more comfortable than a sheltered one. Bring strong repellent, cover ankles and wrists in the evening, keep the tent or van closed at dusk, and check the insect mesh before you travel. Bites can itch for days, so antihistamine cream is worth having with you rather than hunting for in a small town.

sections.heading: Regional timing in short
body: Northland and the upper North Island are pleasant from October through April and humid at the height of summer. The central plateau and Tongariro are a summer and autumn proposition unless you are equipped for alpine winter. The East Coast is driest in summer and reliably sunny in autumn.

The West Coast is wet in every season, plan for rain rather than hoping to avoid it, but rewards it with near-empty sites. The Mackenzie and Central Otago are excellent in autumn and cold and clear in winter. Fiordland is wet year-round and best approached with flexible days and no fixed expectations about seeing Milford in sunshine.
tips: West Coast: plan for rain in any season
Autumn suits Central Otago best
Fiordland needs flexible days

sections.heading: Reading the forecast properly
body: New Zealand's weather changes faster than the length of most driving days, and a forecast for a town tells you relatively little about a pass or an exposed coast twenty minutes away. Check MetService for the specific location, and check the road conditions separately, the two answer different questions.

Build the plan so that a bad forecast changes the day rather than cancelling the trip. Holding an indoor option, a shorter alternative and a serviced campground in reserve is what turns a wet week into an ordinary one.

faq: When is the best time to camp in New Zealand?

For most trips, March and April: settled spells, campgrounds open but no longer full, and prices down once school holidays end. December and January bring the longest days but the fullest campsites and the highest prices.
What is camping like in the New Zealand shoulder season?

Quiet, cheap and unpredictable. October to November and April to May give you sites without booking and roads without queues, at the cost of shorter days, colder nights and a real chance of a washed-out week.

scenic-campsites-new-zealand.title: Best Scenic Campsites in New Zealand, Region by Region
scenic-campsites-new-zealand.description: 24 DOC campsites with standout views, from Tapotupotu to Mavora Lakes, with each one's 2026 adult fee, vehicle access and whether to book ahead.
scenic-campsites-new-zealand.imageAlt: Scenic lakeside campsite beneath New Zealand mountains
scenic-campsites-new-zealand.intro: Every campsite below is a Department of Conservation site in KiwiCamping's DOC data, picked for what you see from the tent or the van door: a beach, a lake, a river or a mountain range. Each one comes with the adult fee DOC lists for it, the vehicles that can reach it and whether it takes bookings, so you can judge it as a place to sleep and not only as a photo.

sections.heading: Northland: the far north beaches
body: Maitai Bay on the Karikari Peninsula is a sheltered bay under pōhutukawa with room for about 100 unpowered pitches, cold showers and flush toilets, at $18 per adult. It does not take bookings, so in summer the rule is to arrive early in the day rather than at dusk.

Tapotupotu and Kapowairua (Spirits Bay) are the two DOC campsites at the top of the country, each with about 45 unpowered sites at $18. Tapotupotu sits beside a lagoon you can swim in, a 5 to 10 minute gravel-road drive from Cape Reinga/Te Rerenga Wairua; Kapowairua is a long beach with bush behind it. DOC is not taking bookings for either at present, so in summer arrive early; both suit campervans and cars rather than caravans.
tips: Maitai Bay is first come
Tapotupotu is 10 minutes from the Cape
No dogs at any of the three

sections.heading: Coromandel: white sand on the northern loop
body: Waikawau Bay is the big one: about 120 unpowered and 12 powered sites behind an undeveloped white-sand beach, at $18 to $23 per adult depending on the season. Stony Bay ($18) is a 5-hectare site where the Coromandel Coastal Walkway starts for Fletcher Bay, and Port Jackson ($18 to $20) sits at the water's edge at the northern tip of the peninsula.

All three take bookings, and between Christmas and late January they fill well ahead. The northern roads are narrow and partly unsealed, so check your rental agreement allows them before you plan the loop.
tips: Book for January
Waikawau has powered sites
Northern roads are partly gravel

sections.heading: Central and lower North Island
body: Mangahuia is a quiet stream-side campsite on the edge of Tongariro National Park at $18, with about 21 unpowered sites. The plateau is high and cold at night even in summer, so the view of the volcanoes comes with a warm sleeping bag requirement.

Putangirua Pinnacles on the south Wairarapa coast costs $10, can be booked and looks across Cook Strait from beside the Putangirua Stream, with the walk to the Pinnacles from the campsite and the seal colony near Cape Palliser a short drive away. It is one of the few sites here where dogs are allowed, on a leash.
tips: Tongariro nights are cold
Putangirua is $10 a night
Dogs on a leash at Putangirua

sections.heading: Nelson, Tasman and Marlborough
body: Tōtaranui Campground at the northern end of Abel Tasman National Park is the largest site on this list, with about 269 unpowered pitches on the beach at $18 to $20, a dump station and cold showers. Kerr Bay on Lake Rotoiti in Nelson Lakes National Park costs $25 to $30 and is a serviced site with hot showers and powered sites in beech forest.

In Marlborough, French Pass ($18 to $20) is a small 18-site campsite with a jetty at the end of a long, narrow road, looking across to Rangitoto ki te Tonga/D'Urville Island. Whites Bay ($15) is the easy one: a sheltered beach about half an hour from Blenheim.
tips: Tōtaranui has a dump station
Kerr Bay has hot showers and power
The French Pass road is slow

sections.heading: West Coast
body: Lake Māhinapua ($18) is a lake-edge site in forest south of Hokitika with about 100 unpowered pitches and a jetty. Lake Paringa ($18) is a small lakeside site between Fox Glacier and Haast, and Gillespies Beach ($18 to $20) is an eight-site campsite at the end of a gravel road near Fox Glacier, by an old gold-mining settlement and a seal colony; DOC lists it for cars only.
The West Coast is wet and the sandflies are serious, which is exactly why these sites are quiet. Pitch with the door away from the wind, keep the screens closed at dusk and plan to dry gear later.
tips: Gillespies Beach is cars only
Bring repellent
Expect rain

sections.heading: Canterbury and the Mackenzie
body: Lake Pearson (Moana Rua) on the road to Arthur's Pass is a $15 lakeside site in the high-country Waimakariri Basin, with about 20 unpowered pitches and long-drop toilets only. Ahuriri Bridge near Omarama is free, takes no bookings and sits on the bank of the Ahuriri River under willows.

The turquoise lakes of the Mackenzie Basin are inside the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve, which is why the stars there are so good. KiwiCamping's DOC data has no campsite on the Tekapo or Pukaki shore itself, so a lakeside night there usually means a holiday park or a council site; check the council's rules before you park.
tips: Lake Pearson has toilets only
Ahuriri Bridge is free
Dark sky reserve around Tekapo

sections.heading: Glenorchy, Queenstown and the Catlins
body: Kinloch ($18) sits on the shore of Lake Wakatipu across from Glenorchy, with a jetty and the Greenstone and Caples tracks nearby. Sylvan ($18) is beside the Routeburn River near the start of the Routeburn Track, and Twelve Mile Delta ($15) is a 100-pitch site on a river delta on the Glenorchy road out of Queenstown that takes no bookings.

On the Catlins coast, Purakaunui Bay ($15) is a beach campsite with about 40 unpowered pitches where dogs are allowed on a leash, and the region around it has waterfalls, sea lions and very few people.
tips: Twelve Mile Delta is first come
Sylvan is by the Routeburn start
Purakaunui allows dogs on a leash

sections.heading: Fiordland and Southland
body: The Milford Road campsites are the way to sleep in Fiordland National Park with a car or campervan. Cascade Creek ($18) at the lower end of Lake Gunn has about 120 unpowered sites and suits larger vehicles; Henry Creek ($18) is a smaller site on the shore of Lake Te Anau. DOC lists 24 current notices in its Te Anau district that prohibit camping, including along the Milford Road, so plan each night at one of the campsites.

Mavora Lakes ($10) is the cheap, big-sky alternative: two camping areas between South and North Mavora Lake, reached by a long gravel road, with dogs allowed on a leash. Fiordland campsites are pack in, pack out, with no rubbish bins.
tips: Camp only at Milford Road campsites
Mavora Lakes is $10
Take your rubbish with you

sections.heading: Judging a site when you arrive
body: Read the landscape rather than the photograph. Lakeshores amplify wind and it usually rises in the evening. River flats and braided riverbeds flood far faster than they look capable of. Forest sites carry falling-branch risk in wind, particularly under older trees.

Arrive in daylight and walk the pitch before committing a large vehicle: check the slope, the firmness of the ground and the soft edges, look up for overhead branches, and confirm another vehicle can still get past you.
tips: Walk the pitch before driving onto it
Wind rises on lakeshores at evening
Look up before parking under trees

sections.heading: Booking, fees and the app
body: Most of the sites above take bookings through DOC's online booking system, and the popular ones fill for weekends and the summer holidays. The sites on the list DOC was not taking bookings for in October 2026 are Maitai Bay, Tapotupotu, Kapowairua, Ahuriri Bridge and Twelve Mile Delta, so those are first come. Fees are per adult per night; check the DOC page for child rates and any change before you go.

In KiwiCamping every DOC campsite carries its fee, facilities, vehicle access and dog rules, so you can compare them on the map and save a shortlist for the trip. DOC campsites are part of the Premium pass; only BookIt stays and tours are free in the app.
tips: Book the popular sites early
Fees are per adult per night
DOC data needs the Premium pass

sections.heading: Leaving it as you found it
body: Stay on formed surfaces, use the toilets provided, and keep every waste stream contained. Do not move rocks, cut vegetation or improve a pitch to make a better photograph; these are exactly the marks that get a site closed.

Leave early if you like, but leave clean and quietly. Dawn light is not a reason to run a generator, fly a drone where it is prohibited, or wake a campground packing up. The best scenic sites stay open because the people who use them are unremarkable neighbours.

faq: Which New Zealand campsites have the best views?

Among DOC campsites, standouts include Tapotupotu near Cape Reinga, Waikawau Bay on the Coromandel, Tōtaranui in Abel Tasman, Lake Māhinapua on the West Coast, Kinloch on Lake Wakatipu and Cascade Creek on the Milford Road. Those six charge $18 to $23 per adult per night.
Do scenic campsites need booking?

Most popular DOC sites take online bookings and fill for summer weekends and January. Maitai Bay, Tapotupotu, Kapowairua (Spirits Bay), Ahuriri Bridge and Twelve Mile Delta were not taking bookings in October 2026, so arrive early in the day.
